articles.title: Alan Peter Cayetano: Impeachment trial has no time limit
articles.summary: Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano on Tuesday raised concerns regarding timeline following the decision of the prosecution to drop three out of the four Articles of Impeachment against Vice…

blocks.text: Published October 13, 2026 3:25pm

Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano on Tuesday raised concerns regarding timeline following the decision of the prosecution to drop three out of the four Articles of Impeachment against Vice President Sara Duterte, saying that the proceedings should not be hastened for the sake of fairness.
On Day 39 of the trial, Cayetano stressed that there is no limit in the Constitution when it comes to the conduct of the impeachment trial.

“We can finish this in January, we can finish this in February. We can take a break tomorrow and focus on the budget. It is our choice. Kung ako masusunod, unahin natin ang budget--may super El Niño, hindi pa tapos ang flood control investigation,” he said.
(If it were up to me, we should prioritize the budget first—there is a super El Niño, and the flood control investigation isn't finished yet.)
“It’s in the best interest of everyone that there’s fairness and we take our time. There’s no time limit. Who is saying that we have to finish this by November?"
Cayetano said he himself wants the trial to be finished, but not at the expense of deliberating on and passing the proposed 2027 national budget.

"I want it finished. But between finishing it tapos may unfairness, and finishing it na unahin ‘to kesa sa budget---Mr. Presiding Officer, Mr. Senate President, you know I’d like to put on record, I’m very uncomfortable with that. I think it will be a disservice to the Filipino people,” he added.
The Senate impeachment court on Tuesday accepted the move by the House prosecution panel to withdraw three out of the four Articles of Impeachment leveled against Vice President Sara Duterte.
The charges dropped were Articles I, III and IV, which detail allegations of misuse of confidential funds, bribery, and grave threats, respectively.
The minority leader said that the impeachment proceedings must be finished “with the basic element of fairness [and] justice.”
“Kahit anong mangyari dito---acquit or convict---may matutuwa, may magagalit. But history will judge us whether or not ‘yung elementary fairness and due process,” Cayetano said.

(Whatever happens here---acquit or convict---some will be happy, some will be angry. But history will judge us as to whether or not we applied the elementary fairness and due process.) — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: EXPLAINER: What is a mistrial?
articles.summary: According to Black's Law Dictionary, a mistrial is defined as "an erroneous, invalid, or nugatory trial; a trial of an action which cannot stand in law because of want of jurisdiction, or a wrong…

blocks.text: Published October 13, 2026 3:24pm

The House prosecution panel on Tuesday withdrew three of the four Articles of Impeachment against Vice President Sara Duterte, a move which was accepted by the Senate impeachment court and earned a strong rebuke from the defense team.

Prosecutors dropped Article I on confidential funds, Article III on bribery, and Article IV on assassination plot, grave threats and inciting to sedition against the President. They will now only pursue Article II on Duterte's alleged failure to fully declare her assets and divest from business interests, raising questions about her unexplained wealth.

Defense lead counsel Sheila Sison said the prosecution's decision to drop three of the four Articles of Impeachment against Duterte would not affect the defense panel's presentation of its own evidence.

However, Sison said that if dropping the three articles was intended to shorten the proceedings, the resulting process would "bear unmistakable characteristics of a mistrial" as they would be unable to present their own witnesses and evidence on the corresponding allegations.
Erroneous, invalid, nugatory

According to Black's Law Dictionary, a mistrial is defined as "an erroneous, invalid, or nugatory trial; a trial of an action which cannot stand in law because of want of jurisdiction, or a wrong drawing of jurors, or disregard of some other fundamental requisite."
The American Bar Association (ABA), meanwhile, defines mistrials as "trials that are not successfully completed."
"They re terminated and declared void before the jury returns a verdict or the judge renders his or her decision in a nonjury trial," ABA said.
Right to due process
Lawyer Rico Domingo, former president of the Philippine Bar Association, explained that there is a mistrial if the court procedure was not observed correctly.
"Ibig sabihin nu'n, hindi in-observe ang tinatawag na procedures correctly, kaya mistrial. So, that would impinge on the due process right ng defendant," Domingo said in an interview with GMA News.
(It means the procedures were not observed correctly, resulting in a mistrial. So, that would infringe upon the defendant's right to due process.)
"Kaya mayroong defect sa pagkaka-hear ng, let's say, criminal case, kaya mistrial, na hindi in-observe ang mga rights ng accused, for example," he added.
(So, there is a defect in the hearing of, let's say, a criminal case, resulting in a mistrial, because the rights of the accused were not observed, for example.)
Domingo also clarified a mistrial does not mean that the case is back to zero and should be refiled.
Among the characteristics of a mistrial is when a defendant was not given a chance to present their evidence.

"Hindi binigyan, for example, ng pagkakataon ang depensa na mag-present its own evidence or, mayroong nagsasabi na defective ang ruling ng judge, for example, on certain basic things, like self-incrimination or hindi binigyan ng in-admit ng mga ebidensya na hindi dapat in-admit," Domingo said.

(For example, the defense was not given the opportunity to present its own evidence, or the judge's ruling was defective regarding certain fundamental matters, such as issues of self-incrimination or the admission of evidence that should not have been admitted.) — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: SSS chief Robert Joseph de Claro is new DICT secretary
articles.summary: De Claro, who has more than three decades of corporate experience, takes over the government's technology department following the resignation of Henry Aguda

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – Social Security System (SSS) President and Chief Executive Officer Robert Joseph de Claro has been named as the new secretary of the Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT), replacing Henry Aguda.
Malacañang announced de Claro’s appointment days after President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. confirmed that he had accepted Aguda’s resignation.

De Claro has more than 30 years of professional experience across the technology, business services, and corporate sectors, including executive positions in several technology-related companies. His professional career began in Nestlé Philippines in 1993, eventually holding posts in Australia and at the company’s headquarters in Switzerland.

Before joining the government, he served as president and CEO of People4u Incorporated, operating partner at FutureNow Business Services Incorporated, and president and general manager of JMango Philippines Incorporated. He also served as general manager for the Asia-Pacific region at GlobalOne Solutions Incorporated and Cloud Sherpas, companies involved in technology and cloud-based business solutions.
De Claro holds a computer science degree, specializing in information technology, from De La Salle University.

De Claro joined the Social Security Commission (SSC), the policymaking body of the SSS, on January 11, 2023, as a representative of the employers’ sector. He also chaired the Information Technology and Collection and Contribution Committee, and participated in committees covering audit, risk, investment, and governance.
He became SSS officer-in-charge on October 11, 2024, and was formally appointed president and CEO on December 6 of the same year.
De Claro is the third DICT secretary under the Marcos administration, after Ivan John Uy and Henry Aguda.
Aguda, who assumed office in March 2025, faced criticism over several decisions during his tenure, including the temporary blocking of online communication platform Discord.

The DICT has also faced scrutiny over its Free Wi-Fi initiative, with the Office of the Ombudsman investigating allegations of a “ghost internet” scheme involving government-funded connectivity projects that were allegedly nonfunctional or never implemented despite payments being made.

De Claro takes over a department responsible for the country’s digital transformation agenda, including the expansion of broadband connectivity, development of e-government services, and implementation of policies concerning cybersecurity and information and communications technology.
His appointment marks a return to the technology sector for an executive whose most recent government role focused on social security administration. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Second wave of early prison releases under way in England and Wales
articles.summary:
About 2,000 criminals are being freed this month to ease overcrowding, while probation union moves towards strike

The second wave of early prison releases takes place throughout Tuesday,…

blocks.text: The second wave of early prison releases takes place throughout Tuesday, with hundreds of offenders walking out across England and Wales under the government’s controversial plan to ease overcrowding.

About 2,000 criminals, including domestic abusers and violent offenders, are being freed this month, with another 3,000 to follow in stages over the next year. The total was reduced from 6,000 after an intervention by Andy Burnham.
Prisoners who were convicted of manslaughter are excluded, meaning the killers of PC Andrew Harper, who died in the line of duty in 2019, will not be eligible.
The second tranche of early releases comes as members of the probation union, Napo, hold a pre-ballot meeting on taking strike action over pay and workloads.

Pay negotiations with probation officers ended with a “best and final” conditional pay offer worth 5%, which the union’s negotiating committee rejected. Members will be asked to vote for industrial action on pay, along with a question on workloads, in a formal ballot on industrial action to launch on 19 October.
The union says probation has been asked to take on huge amounts of additional work due to tens of thousands of prisoners released early from prisons since 2022.

The number of people behind bars has jumped by more than 1,700 in the past three months. The prison population in England and Wales was at 87,499 on Monday, according to Ministry of Justice (MoJ) data, up from 85,761 on 29 June, a rise of 2%.

The MoJ said released offenders would be monitored under the “toughest supervision in British history”. New restriction zones designed to control the movements of the highest-risk sexual and violent offenders should confine released prisoners to areas a few miles wide, in an effort to reassure victims of their crimes.

The MoJ also announced an expansion of electronic monitoring, with a new presumption that offenders will be electronically tagged and monitored when they leave prison. Technology rolling out this year is said to give probation near-live access to tagging data, helping staff spot breaches when offenders step out of line.
However, this month the victims’ commissioner, Claire Waxman, said the government’s confidence in the plan “is not yet matched by the reality on the ground”.

articles.title: The return of the prodigal son? Why speculation is rising over Josh Frydenberg’s future
articles.summary:
The spectre of a leadership alternative is hardly helpful for Angus Taylor. But would Frydenberg do a better job?

  • Get our

blocks.text: A reasonable query for Liberals at this point is: if Josh Frydenberg is the answer, what is the question?

There was a whiff of weariness in some corners of parliament this week, as the former treasurer and deputy Liberal leader happily stoked another round of “Josh for Canberra” speculation. With more rumoured comebacks than Oasis, Frydenberg’s latest foray into the national political arena saw him bouncing around TV, radio and podcast interviews to promote his new book, and pointedly refuse to rule out trying to rejoin the parliament.

His book – part family history, part treatise on antisemitism and social cohesion, part political manifesto – is titled A Grateful Son. But is he instead the prodigal son? The one who set out on his own but is destined to be welcomed back to the Liberal party family with joy and celebrations?

Frydenberg is young enough, bright enough and certainly energetic enough to still make a difference in public life. His addition to what is often a tired Coalition partyroom would certainly spice things up, and give a new weapon in their arsenal. The ideas in his book – a remix of the GST to fund income tax cuts, concerns about the future of his party, changes to the system of federalism, yet more calls for civic service for school leavers – are politically inconvenient for the federal Coalition as well as the Victorian Liberals headed for an election win, but are worth considering.

The talk around parliament is that Frydenberg is privately telling people he is unlikely to seek a return. But the fact he has pointedly refused to rule it out in a conga line of media interviews, saying only that he would make his mind up later, seems opportunistic. The spectre of a potential leadership alternative is hardly a help for Angus Taylor.

Labor sources have helpfully shared key quotes from Frydenberg’s book and media tour, pointing out his calls for changes to GST, the labour market, and criticisms of the Liberal trajectory – again, none helpful to the leader.

The problems facing the modern Liberal party, under Taylor’s leadership, are myriad. Its hostile right flank is barracking for Pauline Hanson and One Nation, its centre is still eyeing the teal independents, and Taylor – now eight months into the job – has a lower primary vote than when Sussan Ley was dumped. The Guardian Essential poll found the Coalition primary at a record low 22% in September, compared to 25% in January, a fortnight before Taylor rolled Ley.

These are all reasons for alarm for the centre right. It’s just not clear if Frydenberg is the answer to any of these problems. One question echoing around parliament this week was: would he do a better job than Taylor on anything substantive? In other words, is he yesterday’s man?

A return to the partyroom would give the Coalition a well-known face and a policy brain in a team which could benefit from both. Maybe Frydenberg would be content to return as a loyal soldier under Taylor, serving in an appropriately senior cabinet role. But maybe not. Few think he’d give up a well-paid job in banking to sit on the frontbench instead of the leader’s chair.

The loudest cheer Hanson got at last weekend’s Cpac conference was when she sledged Taylor, saying Australians didn’t want a “smarmy management consultant” replacing Anthony Albanese as prime minister. Would any of those voters more prefer the chairman of investment bank Goldman Sachs, the role Frydenberg currently holds? Taylor in recent times has tried throwing a bone to that fringe of the right-wing movement, producing more off-the-cuff videos with unpolished deliveries (and swearing) a la Hanson – would Frydenberg, at home in boardrooms and business lunches, be able to win back the voters furious at “politics as usual” and career politicians?

Maybe, then, Frydenberg could chart a course back to the middle for the Coalition: not chasing its right flank further to the fringe, but setting a mainstream course back toward the centre, where elections in Australia are won.

That would be a decent idea, if you forget how Frydenberg was ejected from parliament in the first place: bundled out in 2022 by Monique Ryan in the big community independents wave which swept half a dozen moderate-ish urban Liberals from their seats.

Ryan was supported by Climate 200. That group’s origin story may be relevant here: Simon Holmes à Court, a former donor to Frydenberg’s Kooyong 200 fundraising vehicle, was reportedly ejected from a supporter event and set up his own group in response. Climate 200 would hardly respond to Frydenberg’s comeback, or potential leadership, with party poppers and a “welcome back” card.

The teal wave which swept Frydenberg and several other moderate Liberals from office in 2022 hasn’t exactly swelled into a tsunami since then, and some could argue the conditions of four years ago are not there today – just ask Tim Wilson, who lost Goldstein to teal Zoe Daniel in 2022 but wrestled it back in 2025.
after newsletter promotion
No Liberals we spoke to this week were jazzed about the prospect of Frydenberg’s return, or the distraction it provides.
But if there were any people happy about his potential return, they were on the government benches.
Albanese joked to Labor’s caucus meeting today that Frydenberg was now the “shadow opposition leader”, claiming “Josh Frydenberg’s priority has always been Josh Frydenberg”.
“I’m surprised Josh Frydenberg isn’t trying to bump me off this program,” the PM joked on the ABC on Tuesday.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers claimed his old sparring partner was “stalking” Taylor for the leadership, proclaiming. One senior Labor source cheekily joked that we should call it “the Fryre Festival”, a reference to the ill-fated and chaotic Fyre Festival in 2017, which had its own short-lived and catastrophic comeback in 2024.
Frydenberg’s media tour is likely to continue over coming days. The speculation over his potential comeback will linger even longer – Labor will make sure of it.

articles.title: SC junks contempt petition vs Tito Sotto over Sara Duterte impeach ruling
articles.summary: In a statement on Tuesday, October 13, the Supreme Court en banc ruled that Sotto’s public criticisms of the Court’s decision in Duterte v. House of Representatives et al. (G.R. Nos.…

blocks.text: October 13, 2026 | 3:05pm

MANILA, Philippines — The Supreme Court has dismissed an indirect contempt petition filed against Sen. Tito Sotto over his criticisms of a high court ruling on the impeachment proceedings of Vice President Sara Duterte.

In a statement on Tuesday, October 13, the Supreme Court en banc ruled that Sotto’s public criticisms of the court’s decision in Duterte v. House of Representatives et al. (G.R. Nos. 278353 and 278359) fall within the bounds of protected free speech and expression.

The case stemmed from media interviews and social media posts in which Sotto questioned the ruling, claiming that the ponente was unfamiliar with congressional rules and arguing that the decision effectively amended the Constitution.

Petitioner Manuelito Delos Reyes Luna and several others asked the high court to cite the lawmaker for indirect contempt under Rule 71, Section 3(d) of the Rules of Court, alleging that his remarks were highly disrespectful and threatened to erode public trust in the Judiciary.

The Supreme Court, however, stressed that the Judiciary remains subject to public scrutiny and that statements concerning public officials in the discharge of their duties are protected under the doctrine of fair comment.
“The guarantee of free speech was enacted to protect not only polite speech, but even in its most unsophisticated form,” the court’s ruling read.
The court added that “political speech is accorded the greatest degree of protection” as a direct exercise of popular sovereignty.

To determine whether the speech surpassed constitutional boundaries, the high court evaluated the totality of the circumstances, including the nature of the message, the speaker’s identity, the medium, and its actual impact.

Addressing the modern digital landscape, the court observed that social media algorithms can amplify content, take statements out of context, and spread falsehoods. In light of these realities, the Court noted that it was adopting a "more egalitarian approach" to evaluating speech restrictions, acknowledging unequal access to public platforms.

Because Sotto’s statements involved political discourse, the Supreme Court said it applied the incitement test, which it described as the strictest standard in contempt cases involving speech, to examine whether the remarks intentionally incited the public to lose faith in judicial independence or obstruct justice.
The tribunal held that Sotto’s comments presented no such danger and did not meet the threshold under the clear and present danger test.

“In contempt cases involving speech, the SC explained that the key question is whether the statements intentionally incite the public to lose trust in the independence of the Judiciary or to obstruct the administration of justice, and whether, considering the totality of circumstances, there is a likelihood and imminence that the statements will produce these effects,” the Supreme Court’s statement read.
The high court held that Sotto’s public disagreement with the impeachment decision and its ponente formed part of a legitimate public debate on an issue of national importance.
While acknowledging Sotto’s significant reach and influence as a public figure, the court pointed out that his remarks were made primarily in response to reporters’ questions.
“There is no showing he intended to incite or rally the public to lose trust in the independence of the Judiciary,” the decision said, according to the high court’s statement.
“There is no sign of bad faith or malice,” it added.

The high court cautioned that penalizing public figures for expressing disagreement with judicial rulings would unduly stifle free expression, emphasizing that discussions on impeachment proceedings must remain unrestricted by fear of subsequent punishment.

“As a matter of paramount public interest, discussions on impeachment proceedings, including opinions critical of the court’s decisions, should be free and unrestricted by fears of subsequent punishment,” the high court said.

articles.title: Stronger ASEAN cooperation sought to tackle online youth radicalization
articles.summary: A recent study highlights that exposure to violent content online increases risks of radicalization, necessitating proactive measures from parents, educators, and authorities

blocks.text: BALI, Indonesia – Experts called for regional cooperation among ASEAN countries to address online radicalization affecting young people and the multiple pathways toward violence.

“There is value, I believe, in exploring a shared regional commitment, especially the leaders’ commitment to strengthening youth resilience and preventing violence,” I Gusti Agung Wesaka Puja, ASEAN Institute for Peace and Reconciliation (ASEAN IPR) executive director, told Rappler on Monday, October 12.
According to Puja, regional cooperation would enhance exchanges of research and effective practices as countries grapple with the radicalization of young people.

“Rather than just focusing only on adoptions of agreements or producing documents, declarations of covenants, whatsoever, we should consider how such a commitment should be translated into more practical measures in which youth can benefit from,” the Indonesian diplomat added.

School shootings occurred in the parts of the Philippines between June and September 2026. Indonesia recorded two separate school bombings in 2025 and 2026. Puja mentioned preventive measures through education, digital literacy efforts, and community projects.
Regional cooperation can take different layers, according to Bora Park, research fellow at Seoul-based Institute for National Security Strategy.
“[Governments] can share the intelligence about the emerging threats or the specific dangerous people or the organizations,” Bora said in a separate interview Monday.
Other layers Bora noted are interactions between practitioners and researchers, among grassroots organizers where they can share knowledge and lessons learned.

In 2017, ASEAN adopted the Manila Declaration to Counter the Rise of Radicalisation and Violent Extremism which puts strong focus on the reintegration of individuals from extremist networks to society. This was followed by a plan of action in 2018.
A recently issued baseline study from ASEAN IPR said online spaces act as multiplier of the conditions from which young people’s personal and political grievances come from.
Networks such as True Crime Community and 764 glorify violence regardless of any formal ideological framework.
“The violence is becoming more accessible and more visible among young people nowadays,” Lee Chul, ambassador of the Republic of Korea to ASEAN, said in an interview Monday.
”It no longer comes from the organized group with a clear doctrine or ideology. Nowadays young people are exposed to radicalization risk earlier than ever.”

South Korea is supporting a training program through the ASEAN-Korea Cooperation Fund and in partnership with ASEAN IPR following the publication of the study. “This is an investment in the region’s long-term peace and security,” Lee said.
The study nuanced that exposure to violent acts does not necessarily translate to violent acts.
“Exposure alone rarely produces violence; active seeking, algorithmic reinforcement, and communities that validate hostility are what convert exposure into commitment,” the study read.
Young people’s easy access to violent ideas makes it harder for authorities to prevent the phenomenon.

In their study, ASEAN IPR recommended that authorities recognize, and address accordingly, “that hate speech, discrimination and gender-based violence normalize violence long before extremism appears.”

Parents, teachers, and health care workers should be taught to “recognize early signs of distress and of hardening attitudes.” (READ: Amid rising school violence, citizens pitch solutions to keep children safe)

Human rights education should be developed and figure prominently in this conversation, according to the think tank. Moreover, the scope of violent radicalization should be clarified, so as not to be confused with legitimate protests among the youth. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Latin American organised crime ‘may operate in 16 European countries’
articles.summary:
Cocaine seizures in Europe are up more than fivefold in 10 years as a host of cartels take root. A four-month Guardian investigation reveals the true scale of a continent-wide shift

A…

blocks.text: A four-month investigation by the Guardian has revealed that the surge in cocaine trafficking to Europe is directly linked to the expanding presence of Latin American criminal networks in Europe, where they have forged close ties with local mafia organisations.

The investigation, utilising databases, police and intelligence agencies, along with interviews with judges, prosecutors and experts from eight countries, shows that cartels and factions from Colombia, Brazil, Ecuador, Venezuela, Mexico and the US are active in at least 12 European countries. Between 2014 and 2024, there was a 471% rise in the quantity of cocaine seized and more local laboratories processing cocaine derivatives were dismantled.

The figure could be even higher, as it includes only groups officially identified in Europe through police operations, transnational investigations and ongoing court cases involving brokers, active members, cells or operational networks. It does not include gangs that lack a physical presence in Europe while working in “joint ventures” with European mafias.

The identified groups include Mexico’s Sinaloa cartel and the Jalisco New Generation cartel (CJNG); the Clan del Golfo mafia, and the guerrilla organisations ELN and dissident factions of Farc in Colombia; Brazil’s Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC, or First Capital Command) and Comando Vermelho (CV, or Red Command); Venezuela’s Tren de Aragua; and the US-originated Barrio 18 and MS-13 gangs, which are also prevalent in El Salvador, Honduras, Guatemala and, to a lesser degree, in Mexico.

blocks.caption: Spanish customs officials in Vigo, Galicia, unload bundles of cocaine from a sailing boat that was seized with more than 2,000kg of the drug last month.   Photograph: Salvador Sas/EPA

blocks.text: These organisations have built a more prominent presence in Spain, Portugal, the Netherlands, Belgium and France, while their activities have also been noted in Germany, Romania, Croatia and Slovakia. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (Gi-Toc) also includes Bulgaria.

Daniel Brombacher, a political scientist and director of the Europe Observatory at Gi-Toc, said: “There is something new happening with a presence of Latin American groups in geographies where there’s no pre-existing infrastructure.

“This phenomenon is no longer limited to the traditional gateway countries,” he says. “Recent police operations have uncovered Mexican-run methamphetamine labs in southern France, north-eastern Poland and Brandenburg, south of Berlin. Latin American groups are also appearing in Romania and Bulgaria along the Balkan route.”

Latin American national authorities and experts suggest the list may be even longer. An unpublished report by the São Paulo public prosecutor’s office, partly based on data from the Brazilian intelligence agency (Abin) – which the Guardian reviewed – shows, for example, that the PCC, now Brazil’s biggest criminal group, operates in 16 European countries, including the UK, Ireland, Iceland, Serbia, Sweden, Switzerland and Turkey.

The suspicion that Latin American cartels and factions are seeking to become established in Europe is not new. Since at least the 1980s, Colombian criminal organisations such as the Cali and Medellín cartels had footholds in regions of Spain such as Galicia. In 2013, a Europol report in 2103 warned of their rise. But what authorities are witnessing now is on an another level.

blocks.caption: Drug traffickers near Boa Vista, in Brazil’s northern state of Roraima, in 2024. The First Capital Command (PCC) is South America’s largest criminal group.  Photograph: Washington Post/Getty

blocks.text: A Europol report this year states that “Latin American MTCNs [most threatening criminal networks] have also settled in the EU, from where they direct operations that affect the EU. This is particularly the case for mobile criminal networks involved in organised property crime.”
Interpol, led by the Brazilian federal police officer Valdecy Urquiza, has been approached, but has not commented.

The problem has become more visible over the past decade. Drug production in Latin America in that time has increased roughly fourfold to reach a record of about 4,100 tonnes in 2024. This comes after growth of up to 35% at the beginning of the decade. More cocaine is now produced in Colombia than during the era of the notorious drug lord Pablo Escobar. Nearly all the world’s cocaine and many related substances originate from Latin America, particularly Colombia.

Víctor Manuel Sánchez Valdés, an academic at the Autonomous University of Coahuila in Mexico who is an expert on organised crime, says: “The main ones are the Sinaloa cartel and the Jalisco cartel [CJNG] in Mexico; the Comando Vermelho and the PCC of Brazil; the Gulf Clan and different factions of the Colombian Farc; the Lobos and the Choneros of Ecuador; and Tren de Aragua of Venezuela.”

He believes that the Latin American presence in Europe is even more widespread than is generally recognised. “Sinaloa cartel and the CJNG have a presence in more than 20 European countries. Obviously, that does not mean they dominate or have large cells,” he says. “Rather, they are business emissaries.”

blocks.caption: Soldiers and police raid a house seized by drug traffickers in Duran, Ecuador, in 2024. The country has become a key trafficking route for drugs.   Photograph: Gerardo Menoscal/AFP/Getty

blocks.text: The UN Office on Drugs and Crime’s 2026 World Drug Report on illicit crimes states that global cocaine production in 2024 was between 3,800 and 4,700 tonnes – more than four times higher than it was in 2014. South America remains the main production hub, with coca cultivation covering a record 385,000 hectares over the past decade – three times the 2014 figure.

Europe has emerged as a key market because it offers organisations higher profit margins than the US. Since the beginning of the decade, European police have confiscated more drugs than American forces, and data indicates that Europe now represents about a quarter of global consumption.

Europol recently reported that out of 731 MTCNs operating across Europe, 149 are connected to Latin American organisations. Of these, 67 have Latin American members, and 22 mainly consist of Latin Americans.

articles.title: SC junks indirect contempt petition vs Sotto
articles.summary: SC junks indirect contempt petition vs Sotto on impeachment comments

blocks.text: Published October 13, 2026 2:59pm

The Supreme Court on Tuesday dismissed the petition for indirect contempt filed against Senator Vicente “Tito” Sotto III over his criticism of the Court’s ruling on the impeachment case against Vice President Sara Duterte.

Penned by Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen, the decision reaffirmed that freedom of speech and expression enjoys the highest constitutional protection, particularly when the speech involves political matters.
“The SC found that Senator Sotto’s statements did not amount to indirect contempt,” the SC said.
The senator previously claimed that the Constitution was “amended unconstitutionally” through the SC’s alleged overreach. He said it would take decades to correct the “misinterpretation.”

This came after the SC En Banc “denied with finality” in January, the motion for reconsideration filed by the House, which sought to reverse the decision that declared the previous articles of impeachment against Duterte as unconstitutional.
The petition against Sotto was filed by Atty. Ferdinand Topacio and several other lawyers.
The SC, however, pointed out that just like other branches of the government, the Judiciary remains subject to public scrutiny and criticism.

“Under the doctrine of fair comment, statements concerning public officials in the performance of their duties are protected. Such statements do not automatically become punishable simply because they are false, harsh, or offensive,” the SC said.
“As the Court explained, ‘the guarantee of free speech was enacted to protect not only polite speech, but even in its most unsophisticated form,’” it added.
The court also clarified that it found no intention in Sotto’s statement to incite distrust of the Judiciary among the public.
“There is no showing he intended to incite or rally the public to lose trust in the independence of the Judiciary. There is no sign of bad faith or malice,” the Decision stated.
In response to the Court’s dismissal, Sotto expressed gratitude for its decision and stated that he has always respected and held the institution in high regard.

“I thank the Supreme Court for dismissing the petition for indirect contempt filed against me. I disagreed with one of its decisions. That does not mean I have lost respect for the Court. I have always held it in high regard as an institution, and I return the respect it has shown me in its decision,” the senator said in a statement.
Sotto also emphasized and reaffirmed the Court in its judgment, deeming freedom of speech as one of the strongest safeguards of the people to question those in power.

“Freedom of speech and expression is one of our strongest safeguards against tyranny. When people are free to question those in power, in any branch of government, power is kept in check. This decision protects the right of every Filipino to speak freely on issues that affect the nation,” Sotto stated.
“Again, my gratitude to the Court, and I will speak freely, always with respect for our institutions. Praise God!” he added. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: India 'cockroach' leaders detained after entering barricaded protest site
articles.summary: Protesters climbed over barricades in central Delhi to demand the election chief resign over revised voter lists.

blocks.text: Leaders of India's Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) were detained early on Tuesday after they entered a heavily-guarded protest site and chanted slogans demanding the country's election chief resign over a controversial revision of electoral rolls.
Party founder Abhijeet Dipke shared a video showing Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das being taken away from Jantar Mantar in Delhi, a historic observatory popular for protests, by police.
Footage showed the two - along with others - climbing over police barricades before chanting slogans while holding the Indian flag.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi's opponents allege the voter list revision benefits his party, a charge it and the Election Commission reject.
There have been days of protests demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation.
Police have stepped up security across Delhi as demonstrators challenge restrictions on where protests can be held.
Early on Tuesday, Dipke, Das and Ranka all shared videos showing Das and Ranka entering Jantar Mantar.
"You cannot denotify the resistance," Dipke wrote on X.
Das also posted a message declaring that the site had been "reclaimed" and that they were being detained.
It was not immediately clear where police had taken the leaders.
Ranka later appeared on an Instagram live broadcast from a police bus alongside other detainees where they appeared cheerful and said they would not back down.

The detentions came a day after the federal home ministry announced that Jantar Mantar, long associated with public protests in Delhi, would no longer be a designated protest venue. Authorities instead identified three alternative locations where demonstrations can be held with permission.

Before the decision, the CJP had met Delhi Police officials to seek permission for a peaceful protest at Jantar Mantar and had warned that it would announce further demonstrations if it received no response.
"30 mins after we went to Delhi Police asking for a date when we can go to Jantar Mantar, Jantar Mantar was de-notified as a protest site," Ranka had earlier posted on X.

Most of the party's leadership has been in Delhi in recent days. Dipke, however, had travelled to his hometown in Maharashtra after the death of his grandmother. He was among several CJP leaders detained ahead of a planned demonstration on Saturday and was released the next day.
The CJP had called for a protest at Jantar Mantar on Saturday, but authorities imposed extensive security restrictions across the capital to prevent demonstrators from reaching the site.
Several metro stations were closed, train services were disrupted and thousands of police and paramilitary personnel were deployed.

Over the weekend, the police detained and released thousands of people, including several journalists. Some videos and photos from the protest show police dragging people, including women, by force and pushing them into buses.
Separately, opposition parties held a march in Delhi on Monday from Connaught Place - a major shopping district in the heart of the capital - to the Supreme Court.

The Congress, India's main opposition party, also petitioned the Supreme Court on Monday, challenging the Election Commission's voter revision exercise, which has resulted in tens of millions of names being removed from electoral rolls.
Critics say the exercise risks excluding eligible voters and making it harder for them to prove their eligibility.

Anger over the revision exercise intensified after The Indian Express reported that Kumar had disregarded concerns raised by the two other election commissioners over changes to voter registration. The Election Commission has said its decisions were unanimous.
The current protests follow student-led demonstrations earlier this year over exam irregularities and demands for education reforms.
The CJP led weeks of action that culminated in the resignation of federal Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.

The group began as online satire after Chief Justice of India Surya Kant compared some unemployed young people to cockroaches during a court hearing. He later said his remarks had been misinterpreted, but the comments had already become a rallying cry for young people.
After the summer protests, the CJP evolved into a pressure group, tapping into wider anger over unemployment, exam irregularities and government accountability.

articles.title: FACT CHECK: Video of Claire Castro calling Marcos a ‘drug addict’ is altered
articles.summary: Castro’s statement was spliced to make it appear she was talking about Marcos, when she was actually referring to former president Rodrigo Duterte

blocks.text: Claim: Palace Press Officer Claire Castro revealed that President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has been using drugs, as shown in a press briefing aired on television.

Why we fact-checked this: Facebook user Marquin B Embalzado posted a video clip taken from GMA News showing Castro’ press briefing in India on September 11, where she supposedly called Marcos an addict.

In the video, Castro is shown saying, “Si Pangulong Marcos Jr., adik, bangag, at inamin niya rin na ang paggamit niya ng fentanyl ay inabuso niya dahil masarap daw yung pakiramdam — ‘cloud nine’ ang feeling.”
(President Marcos Jr. is an addict, a drug user; he even admitted to abusing fentanyl because of the pleasurable sensation it gave him — a feeling of being on ‘cloud nine.’)
The video also has overlaid text that reads, “Ano’ng nangyari, Ante Claire? Hala ka, siniraan mo yung amo mo? Nalilito na ata si madam; stress yarn, madam, wala na sa script?”
(What happened, Auntie Claire? Oh no, you badmouthed your boss? Madam seems confused; is she stressed? Has she gone off-script?)
As of this writing, the post has 88,000 views, 1,300 likes, 118 comments, and 486 shares. Multiple users have also reposted the video, generating high engagement.
The facts: The press briefing did take place, but Castro’s statement was spliced to make it appear she was talking about Marcos, when she was actually referring to former president Rodrigo Duterte.
When asked for a reaction to Vice President Sara Duterte calling Marcos a drug addict, Castro pointed out that it was former president Rodrigo Duterte who admitted to taking drugs.

In the press briefing, Castro said: “Inamin mismo ni dating Pangulong Duterte, pangulo na siya, na siya’y gumagamit ng marijuana. At inamin niya rin na ang paggamit niya ng fentanyl ay inabuso niya dahil masarap daw ‘yung pakiramdam, ‘cloud nine’ ang feeling.”

(Former president Duterte himself admitted — while he was already president — that he used marijuana. He also admitted to abusing fentanyl because of the pleasurable sensation it provided, describing it as feeling like being on ‘cloud nine.’)

She added, “Noong umamin ba ang kanyang ama sa paggamit ng mga bawal na gamot, tinawag niya ba ang kanyang ama na adik, bangag? So kung anong ginagawa ng inyong pamilya, huwag niyo pong ipahid kay Pangulong Marcos Jr. na siyang nagtatrabaho, umaaksyon, hindi puro pagbabakasyon ang ginagawa ng Pangulo.”

(When her father admitted to using drugs, did she call her father an addict, a fool? So, whatever your family is doing, do not project it onto President Marcos Jr.; he is working and taking action — he is not just going on vacation.)
The official GMA News report, the Presidential Communications Office’s official transcript, and other news outlets that broadcast the briefing reflected these statements.
Other fact-checkers have debunked another post containing the video as an altered version of the legitimate news report.

Drug use: Castro was referring to Duterte’s admission to using fentanyl, a highly addictive opioid, for medical purposes in 2016. He said he was told to stop using it after his doctor said he was “abusing the drug” by using multiple patches more than what was prescribed.
In December 2016, Duterte said, “I’m not an addict… Only when it is prescribed. Addiction is only with regularity, my friend.”
In 2018, he also admitted to taking marijuana to keep him awake. He later said that it was a joke.
Accusations: In 2024, Duterte accused Marcos of being a drug addict, allegedly on the list of the Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency’s (PDEA) watchlist of narcotics users. PDEA denied the claim.
Marcos clapped back, suggesting that his predecessor’s allegation might be attributed to his prolonged use of fentanyl.
Other fact-checks: Rappler has previously debunked numerous fake quotes by public officials:

items: FACT CHECK: Jonvic Remulla did not say Marcoses are ‘sure to be jailed’ after 2028
FACT CHECK: Quote card of Mark Zuckerberg threatening DICT, House with lawsuit is fake
FACT CHECK: Marcos Jr. did not say protecting VP Duterte from her case is ‘corruption’
FACT CHECK: No, Malabon congressman Oreta did not slam Sara Duterte’s travels
FACT CHECK: Jonvic Remulla did not say Marcoses are ‘sure to be jailed’ after 2028

blocks.text: – Eirene Manatlao/Rappler.com

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

articles.title: Bacon, eggs and Bowie: how year 12 English students tackled ‘human strength and vulnerability’ in HSC paper
articles.summary:
Tens of thousands of high school students across New South Wales sit the first test of their final exams

  • Get our

blocks.text: “How does the composer of your prescribed text offer you opportunities to examine assumptions about human strength and vulnerability?”
This was the bamboozling English question tens of thousands of year 12 students sat down to answer on the first day of their final school exams.

Kayden Tran, 18, had a “really great breakfast” of rice, bacon and eggs – but was it enough to get through an essay exploring tenacity and sensitivity in the writings of Tim Winton, George Orwell or Malala Yousafza?
“This morning, I felt extremely stressed and I kind of gave up hope,” the student of Canley Vale high school in Sydney’s west told the Guardian.
“But after doing the exam, I feel perfectly fine, I feel content, like I did the best I possibly could,” he said after the HSC English 1 paper on Tuesday.
Mary Alnimry listened to the song Heroes by the late David Bowie to prepare.
“I discovered that song through an assessment for year 10 and, every time, before every English exam, I listen to that song and it just reminds me of English,” she said.
The pair was among about 200 Canley Vale students to sit the test, just one cohort in the roughly 75,000 students across New South Wales working to wrap up their high school careers.

“You just have to go in and believe that you know the content,” Alnimry, 17, said. “That’s how I felt in the morning. And then after the exam, obviously it’s really rewarding. I completed everything, but there’s always that curiosity lingering.
“I think that it was pretty fair, there was nothing out of the ordinary.”

blocks.caption: Canley Vale high school students finishing their first HSC English exam of 2026. Photograph: Teagan Glenane/The Guardian

blocks.text: On Reddit, other year 12 students weren’t as confident.

“Honestly I think that’ll kick most people in the ass, the fact the question had so much to unpack I personally found it hard to address it all, I focused on vulnerability and strength and sprinkled a bit of assumptions,” one student with the handle bberson wrote on Tuesday afternoon.

Another, djungleskog41, was concerned they skipped over parts of the question: “I did Orwell too and tbh I didn’t address the question at all. I only focused on how like human vulnerability and weakness forces us to submit into the regime and rebelling is a sign of human strength blah blah blah but i barely mentioned my assumption so im rlly upset about that lol.”

Alana Miller, an English teacher at Canley Vale high school, has shepherded 17 years of year 12 students through the exams. She said the nerves don’t stop with students, and she too woke up this morning with the year 12s on her mind.
“We care so much about the students, we spend so much time,” she said. “We want them to do well, we want them to feel particularly that these exams are something they could achieve in.”

Fantasy books have been a growing hit at Canley Vale high alongside Japanese manga. Miller said she’s spent the past year trying to meet students where they are to help engage the next generation of readers.

“I think the best way is to … talk to them about books, shows, films that they might see,” Miller said. “I think choosing engaging texts in the classroom can be a huge stepping stone for resistant readers. … I just try and tell them they haven’t met the book yet that will get them to love reading.”
For Zenith Diep, self-belief was key.

“I’m feeling not too bad, because I did finish everything,” the 17-year-old said. “I don’t know if I answered the questions fully as I should’ve. You just have to trust yourself with how much work you put in and that you actually remember it. I trust in myself.”
Effie Niarchos, the principal of Canley Vale high, said the HSC represented a rite of passage for year 12s, marking the past six years of high school and the next chapter in their lives.

“All of the teaching, all the learning is building towards this moment,” she said. “We want them to be ready for the world, and we look at it as we’ve achieved something to be able to successfully prepare them for this moment”.
She said students have been experiencing a bit more anxiety in recent years, possibly from community expectations, possibly from the world shifting underneath kids’ feet.
But as she saw off the last of those who sat for the exam on Tuesday, she looked back with a smile and a sense of pride.
“They’re our future,” Niarchos said.
HSC results will be released on 16 December.

articles.title: Sara Duterte stresses plan to run for president in 2028, warns of fraud
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte on Tuesday stressed her intention to run for president in 2028, saying the impeachment trial has given her a chance to be scrutinized by the electorate.

blocks.text: Published October 13, 2026 2:55pm
Vice President Sara Duterte on Tuesday stressed her intention to run for president in 2028, saying the impeachment trial has given her a chance to be scrutinized by the electorate.
At a news briefing, Duterte thanked the public for her continued high ratings despite what she called were instances of defamation and accusations against her.
Asked if she was still decided to run in 2028, Duterte said, "Yes."
"Kaya nga, in one way, nakikita ko as a blessing 'yung impeachment trial dahil diyan ay makikilatis at mas ma-scrutinize na ng mga tao 'yung mga katanungan nila sa pagkatao ko," Duterte said.
(In a way, I see the impeachment trial as a blessing because it is a way for people to scrutinize who I am.)
"At nagpapasalamat ako sa Philippine Chamber dahil simula 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, hanggang ngayon ay iniimbitahan pa rin nila ako at nakikinig pa rin sila sa mensahe ko," she added.
(I thank the Philippine Chamber of Commerce and Industry because from 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025 until now, they continue to invite me and listen to my message.)
Duterte warned of fraud and black propaganda in the 2028 elections if it pushes through.
She has claimed that there are moves for a no-election scenario.
“Kung matutuloy man ang 2028 national elections, expect ninyo na 'yung dayaan diyan at expect ninyo na tutuloy-tuloy 'yung tinatawag nilang black propaganda,” said Duterte.
(If the 2028 national elections do push through, expect election fraud there and expect that what they call black propaganda will continue.)

articles.title: Sara Duterte on dropping of bribery charge at impeachment trial: They don't have evidence
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte said on Tuesday that the dropping of bribery charges against her only means that the prosecution does not have enough evidence as her impeachment trial continues.

blocks.text: Published October 13, 2026 2:55pm
Vice President Sara Duterte said on Tuesday that the dropping of bribery charges against her only means that the prosecution does not have enough evidence as her impeachment trial continues.

“Yung pag-drop ng bribery charge sa impeachment, ito 'yung sinasabi namin sa simula pa lang na, doon pa lang sa House of Representatives, the moment they filed, the groups filed the impeachment complaint, na walang ebidensiya lahat ng kanilang akusasyon,” she told reporters.

(The dropping of the bribery charge in the impeachment is what we have been saying from the very beginning—back when it was still in the House of Representatives, the moment they filed, the groups filed the impeachment complaint—that all their accusations have no evidence.)
The vice president said that the prosecution is only after her ouster from office.

“Dahil wala silang ebidensiya, ngayon na wala silang ebidensiya, kailangan na nila i-drop o hindi talakayin. Lumalabas na parang accountability kuno, paninira, todo-todong, araw-araw na paninira. Suwerte na kung matanggal si Sara Duterte,” she added.

(Because they have no evidence, now that they have no evidence, they need to drop it or not discuss it anymore. It appears like so-called accountability, but it's just smear tactics, full-on, daily character assassination. If Sara Duterte gets removed, then lucky for them.)

The House prosecution panel in Duterte’s impeachment trial dropped the bribery charge against her on Friday. This was done to meet its timetable for presenting evidence, panel member and Bukidnon Representative Jonathan Keith Flores said Sunday.
Article III accuses the vice president of bribing officials of the Department of Education during her tenure as its secretary from 2022 to 2024.
The prosecution on Saturday raised the possibility of referring the bribery allegations to the Department of Justice (DOJ) and the Office of the Ombudsman for possible criminal proceedings.

Hours after Duterte made the statement, the House prosecution panel dropped three out of the four Articles of Impeachment leveled against her, saying its case will stand on Article II alone on alleged unexplained wealth due to non-full declaration of assets and non-divestment of business. —KG, GMA News

articles.title: Healey should ‘stay the course’ and repair UK finances, says top IMF economist
articles.summary: Fund upgrades UK’s GDP growth forecast for 2026 to 1.3%, but says it is likely to ‘edge down’ next year

blocks.text: John Healey should “stay the course” and continue repairing the UK’s public finances, the International Monetary Fund’s top economist has said, after the fund lifted its growth forecast for Britain.
Little more than a fortnight before Healey’s first budget, Silvana Tenreyro, the IMF’s economic counsellor, said the UK “stands out” among G7 countries in having a plan to narrow its deficit.
“The UK has already started a consolidation process,” she said. “The message for the UK is simply, stay the course.”

Tenreyro, a former member of the Bank of England’s monetary policy committee, was speaking at the launch of the IMF’s twice-yearly World Economic Outlook (WEO) at the Fund’s annual meetings in Bangkok.
Healey is under pressure to announce a generous energy support package in the budget, before the sharp rise in energy bills expected in January.
But in its WEO, the IMF advises member governments against across-the-board subsidies, saying any support should be “temporary, targeted and non-distortionary”.

In a fillip for the chancellor, who is poised to arrive in Bangkok later this week, the IMF has upgraded its growth forecast for the UK this year, but expects a modest slowdown in 2027 as higher energy prices take their toll.

Responding, Healey said: “conflict in the Middle East and Europe is hitting people in the UK and around the world. But Britain’s economy is showing strong international resilience in the face of these challenges.”
The IMF predicted GDP growth of 1.3% for the UK this year – up 0.3 percentage points from its most recent update in July.

UK GDP growth has been stronger than expected in early 2026, at 0.6% in the first quarter and 0.5% in the second quarter. The Office for National Statistics has pointed to the strong expansion of AI-related businesses as one factor behind the upside surprise.

However, the IMF warned that prolonged high oil prices and rising interest rates meant growth was likely to “edge down” in 2027, “as higher energy prices and long-term interest rates weigh on consumption and investment”.
It cut its UK growth forecast for next year modestly to 1.2%, from 1.3%.
Markets have been revising up their expectations of future inflation and interest rates across big economies, since the Middle East conflict re-escalated in the summer.

The Bank of England’s nine-member monetary policy committee is now widely expected to raise the policy rate at its November meeting – echoing similar moves by the Federal Reserve, European Central Bank and Bank of Japan.
Mortgage rates in the UK have already been rising in response to higher funding costs for banks in financial markets.
after newsletter promotion
BoE policymaker Megan Greene argued on Tuesday morning that the IMF’s growth upgrade was proof that UK interest rates should be higher.
Speaking to the Atlantic Council at the International Monetary Fund meetings in Bangkok, Greene argued that interest rates were currently not very restrictive.
“There’s more recently been some labour market data that has also suggested that maybe slack in the labour market has peaked, so the labour market is loose,” Greene said.

The IMF singled out the UK as among the countries – also including Japan – where core inflation, which excludes volatile commodities such as energy, is not expected to return to the 2% target until late next year.

It expects average inflation in the UK to be 3.3% this year, and to remain at 2.8% in 2027 – a challenge for Healey and the prime minister, Andy Burnham, who are promising to offer voters a “breathing space” from rising costs.
Healey will spend little more than 24 hours in the Thai capital before flying home to put the finishing touches to his 28 October budget.
He is expected to focus on plans to devolve more tax revenues to mayoralties, alongside measures to help households cope with higher energy bills before the winter.
A string of other challenging decisions, including when the UK should be aiming to spend 3% of GDP on defence, is expected to be delayed until a big spending review at some point next year.

The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) warned this week that the budget would be a “work of fiction” unless Healey explained how he would deal with what it said were £35bn of future spending pressures.

articles.title: Jinggoy Estrada faces fresh 90-day suspension
articles.summary: The Sandiganbayan Fifth Division has implemented a preventive suspension of Sen. Jinggoy Estrada amid his pending cases before the anti-graft court.

blocks.text: October 13, 2026 | 2:47pm

Sen. Jinggoy Estrada, along with three of his co-accused, arrived at the Sandiganbayan in Quezon City on June 4, 2026 for the arraignment of their plunder case in connection with the alleged P573 million in illicit payouts from flood control projects.
The Philippine STAR / Miguel De Guzman
MANILA, Philippines — The Sandiganbayan Fifth Division has implemented a preventive suspension of Sen. Jinggoy Estrada amid his pending cases before the anti-graft court.

In a resolution dated October 12, the anti-graft court’s Fifth Division imposed a 90-day suspension pending trial, following the automatic lifting of the first 90-day suspension, which was imposed in June.

“Accordingly, accused Senator Jose "Jinggoy" P. Ejercito Estrada is suspended from his position as Senator of the Republic of the Philippines and from any other public office which he may now or hereafter be holding for a period of ninety (90) days from receipt of this Resolution,” the anti-graft court’s ruling read.
The cases were originally filed by the Office of the Ombudsman on May 28.
The charges also named Manuel Bonoan, Denryl Caesar Cortuna, Manny Bulusan and Arturo Gonzales Jr. as co-accused.

While the court suspended Cortuna, Bulusan and Gonzales pendente lite in June 2026, it deferred Estrada’s suspension due to pending motions to quash and subsequent moves to amend the charges to exclude Bonoan.
Following the court’s denial of the motions for reconsideration regarding the amended charges on October 9, the anti-graft court proceeded with Estrada’s suspension.
In his comment, Estrada opposed the move, arguing that placing him under another 90-day suspension would be overly punitive.
He pointed out that he had already been serving a separate 90-day suspension issued by the Sandiganbayan’s Second Division since June 22, 2026.

Estrada also argued that the rationale for a preventive suspension no longer existed because he was detained at the New Quezon City Jail, where he had been held since June 1, and therefore could not frustrate or hamper his prosecution.
However, the Sandiganbayan Fifth Division brushed aside these arguments, reiterating established jurisprudence that preventive suspension is mandatory under the law.

It explained that under Section 13 of Republic Act No. 3019, or the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act, and Section 5 of Republic Act No. 7080, or the Plunder Law, any public officer facing pending criminal prosecution under a valid information in court must be preventively suspended from office.

“Jurisprudence is clear on the mandatory nature of preventive suspension when a public officer is charged with a valid information involving violation of R.A. No. 3019, there are no ifs and buts about it,” the Sandiganbayan said.
“The imposition of suspension, however, is not automatic or self-operative as a pre-condition thereof is the existence of a valid information, determined at a pre-suspension hearing,” it added.
Estrada is currently detained at the New Quezon City Jail in Payatas over graft and plunder charges.
These stem from allegations that Estrada received kickbacks amounting to P573 million from flood control projects.

articles.summary: The Senate impeachment court on Tuesday accepted the move by the House prosecution panel to withdraw three out of the four Articles of Impeachment leveled against Vice President Sara Duterte.

blocks.text: Published October 13, 2026 2:45pm
The Senate impeachment court on Tuesday accepted the move by the House prosecution panel to withdraw three out of the four Articles of Impeachment leveled against Vice President Sara Duterte.

Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero made the ruling after the prosecution told the Senate court that it will no longer pursue the three Articles of Impeachment and will only retain one: Article 2 on amassing of unexplained wealth due to failure to disclose assets in the Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN) and non-divestment of business interest despite Constitutional prohibition.
“The court accepts and confirm the prosecution’s manifestation,” Escudero said.

The prosecution decided to drop Article I on confidential funds, Article III on bribery, and Article IV on assassination plot, grave threats and inciting to sedition against the President after a week of testimonies from the Anti-Money Laundering Council, bank and insurance firm officials, as well as lawyer and accountant Alexander Cabrera ultimately concluding that the Vice President and her husband accumulated unexplained wealth worth P817 million at the least and P1.5 billion at the most.

Going forward, Escudero said that the impeachment court should allow the alternate presentation of evidence between the prosecution and the defense to avoid a situation wherein the defense won’t be able to rebut the allegations which evidence were presented but are suddenly withdrawn. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Shock, anger and a crackdown: why a contentious electoral revision has sparked outrage
articles.summary: Marches in Delhi against changes to voting registration led to dragnets, internet blackouts – and questions about India’s electoral independence. Plus, the cinematographer capturing the beauty of…

blocks.text: Months of simmering public anger have given rise to a season of discontent in India. In its latest iteration, the demand is for the removal of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and the scrapping of a controversial electoral rolls revision that has struck 130 million people off the register. Protests have erupted every day over the past week, prompting a violent crackdown on dissenters in the capital.

Over the weekend, Delhi was effectively under lockdown, transformed into a militarised landscape of barricades, road closures and paramilitary forces marching through the streets. Ahead of a protest led by the Cockroach Janta party on Saturday, authorities deployed a massive dragnet: 245 trains to Delhi were cancelled, 45 metro stations were shut, liquor shops were closed, internet services were cut off in the heart of the city and activists were put under house arrest.

The founders of the Cockroach party were removed from an Air India flight shortly after it landed at Delhi airport on Saturday. Opposition leaders were held for more than eight hours in various police stations. Video footage showed students and activists being manhandled, beaten and dragged off the streets while some journalists were also swept up in the detentions. A supreme court lawyer assisting those detained was carried away by police, his shirt torn in the process. The crackdown extended to Mumbai, where Tushar Gandhi, the great-grandson of Mahatma Gandhi, was whisked away by the police to prevent him from participating in a local demonstration. On Monday, the Delhi police denotified Jantar Mantar as a designated protest site, instead recommending three alternative locations.

“I have been in public life and have watched politics for four decades now, and I have never witnessed this kind of preparation for a demonstration. It was extraordinary by any stretch of the imagination,” political activist Yogendra Yadav, who was also detained, said of Saturday’s crackdown. Despite what he described as “terror unleashed by the state”, he said, small groups staged flash protests in several areas of Delhi defying the heavy security presence.

The crackdown was preceded by similarly aggressive police action against Congress party’s protests, led by Rahul Gandhi. Dramatic images of police personnel detaining Gandhi and his sister, Priyanka, amid scenes of chaos flashed across screens nationwide.

The ruling Bharatiya Janata party has defended its position, with spokesperson Ravi Shankar Prasad accusing the opposition of weaponising protests after electoral defeats. “One, Indian democracy has thwarted attempts to incite anarchy. Two, the country will be governed by parliament, not by the streets,” he said at a news briefing.

While suppression of protests is not new, what stands out this time is the scale of the crackdown in the capital. Government clampdowns in Indian-administered Kashmir have been far more severe, particularly in 2019, when sweeping restrictions were imposed after the revocation of Article 370.

blocks.caption: An activist tries to stop a police bus carrying detained protesters during a demo seeking the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner. Photograph: Priyanshu Singh/Reuters

blocks.text: The ferocity of the state response reflects the high political stakes for Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government, which faces mounting resistance over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) and questions about the credibility of the electoral process.

The latest protests began with a demand for Kumar’s resignation after an Indian Express investigation reported that the ECI’s two other commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, had raised concerns about changes to electoral rolls, registration procedures, and digital systems. While Kumar has not responded to the investigation, the ECI said in a statement that “differing views” were part of the “decision-making process”. But the anger runs deeper. The SIR exercise has faced criticism for putting citizens through a trial by fire and leaving the most marginalised in a Kafkaesque limbo. Critics and opposition leaders have gone further, charging that the exercise was designed to benefit the ruling regime.

Former election commissioner Ashok Lavasa told me that the SIR process is unprecedented and unfair, marking a departure from the Commission’s traditional emphasis on inclusion. “For more than seven decades the ECI took it upon itself, as a duty, to enrol everyone who was eligible to vote. And that was one of the basic differences between how Indian democracy works and how other democracies function, where you need to apply to get enrolled,” he said. Voters accustomed to a “friendly procedure” now face a hostile system, which he said “is not good for democracy” in the long run.

Yadav argued that the SIR controversy has exposed what he describes as a deeper process of democratic capture by the ruling party. “Elections are the only mechanism now left for the regime to stamp its legitimacy and election capture is critical to their survival. And therefore, Gyanesh Kumar is critical,” he said. He pointed to a 2023 law giving election commissioners legal immunity for actions performed in their official capacity, which he said is broader than even the protection afforded to judges.

As to what comes next, he envisions potential for three strands to find common ground: the opposition parties, organised civil society groups, and ordinary citizens. For a government that has shown no sign of budging yet, he said, the calculus will get harder. “The longer they delay, the higher the stakes.”

On Monday, the Kerelam assembly passed a resolution seeking Kumar’s removal, as opposition parties marched toward the supreme court demanding action against him. And the Cockroach movement and leftist student groups have vowed to continue protesting. “People have refused to be fearful any longer. They will come again and again,” said left-wing student leader, Danish Ali. “We are living in a democratic country, and protest is a fundamental right that no one can snatch away from us.”
What else we’re reading about

blocks.caption: South African jurist and former UN human rights chief Navanethem ‘Navi’ Pillay has won the 2026 Nobel peace prize. Photograph: Daniel Karmann/DPA/AP

blocks.text: Human rights | South African jurist and former international criminal court judge, Navi Pillay, who is of Indian Tamil heritage, has won the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize. In a first-person account published in 2023, she wrote about her grandparents, who came from India and worked on a sugarcane farm in South Africa for five years before being allowed to buy land.

Technology | The United States has suspended labour-certification processing for several major technology companies, including top Indian IT firms, as part of a crackdown on what it alleges is a misuse of its flagship green card program, fraud and the displacement of American workers. The impacted companies include Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, Capgemini, Microsoft and Adobe. “We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labour certification applications involving these companies,” the US labour secretary Keith Sonderling announced last week.

Climate| Citing a significant rainfall deficit linked to the El Niño weather phenomenon, the Maharashtra government last week announced water cuts of at least 10% across urban areas starting 16 October. The state government had previously declared drought conditions in 74% of the sub-districts.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: The Sufi shrine of Hazrat Sarmad Shaheed, beside the Jama Masjid mosque. Photograph: Mayank Austen Soofi

blocks.text: With Delhi in the news for all the wrong reasons, I turned to Mayank Austen Soofi, who writes a daily Delhi column for Hindustan Times, to share a spot he returns to for a moment of reprieve. “Whenever I can, I spend a solitary afternoon at the tiny Sufi shrine of Hazrat Sarmad Shaheed, beside the Jama Masjid mosque. The bazaar outside the shrine is the Walled City’s noisiest quarter, yet inside one can sit in silence beneath the neem tree growing beside Sarmad’s grave. An Armenian Jew from Iran, Sarmad fell in love with a Hindu boy in Sindh, eventually became a naked fakir and settled in Mughal Delhi. Executed by Emperor Aurangzeb, his grave lies beneath a red cloth that recalls his blood-soaked beheading. These days, I linger a little longer at the resting place of a man who would just not submit to power.”
Count it
A number worth knowing

blocks.caption: Koushila Markam holds a photo of her daughter, Bamita Markam, who died from measles during an outbreak in Balaghat. Photograph: BBC News

blocks.text: At least 32 children from the Indigenous community in Balaghat, Madhya Pradesh, have died since June, the Indian Express reported. An inquiry found evidence of measles and malaria. The children, aged between one and 13, experienced symptoms including high fever, skin rashes and abdominal pain.
Vibe check

blocks.caption: A quiet moment between Arbab Kamal Khan’s parents, whose everyday intimacy features in his photographs.

blocks.text: For Mumbai-based cinematographer, Arbab Kamal Khan, the fleeting, unguarded moments of everyday life offer the most honest form of documentation. His Instagram account is an extension of this cinematic vision, capturing the languor of slow days, the beauty of the mundane and the quiet air of romance.
“When someone passes away, we don’t remember the curated moments,” he told me. “We always go back to the little things, the moments that are small or intricate.”

For me, the images and videos featuring his parents – their feet across each other besides teacups resting atop an Urdu newspaper, or his dad resting under his wife’s dupatta as she brushes her hair – are particularly striking because older people are rarely afforded such tenderness in visual culture. In his frames, his parents are not only elderly figures but also lovers who continue to find intimacy in each other’s presence.
