articles.title: DPWH project relocates Pampanga community to more flood-prone site – HRW
articles.summary: DPWH spends P150 million dredging an island in Macabebe, and permanently relocating its residents to a former fishpond that chronically floods

blocks.text: DPWH spends P150 million dredging an island in Macabebe, and permanently relocating its residents to a former fishpond that chronically floods

items: Residents of Pulo Island in Pampanga were relocated for a flood control project but ended up in a more flood-prone area, facing significant hardships.
Human Rights Watch criticized the authorities for not following proper standards in the relocation process, leading to intimidation and inadequate compensation for the displaced residents.

The report highlights failures in the planned relocation process, including lack of meaningful consultation and oversight, amidst ongoing concerns about corruption in flood control projects in the Philippines.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Residents of an island in Macabebe, Pampanga, were relocated to make way to a P150-million flood control work, only to end up in a site that chronically floods, international rights group Human Rights Watch (HRW) said in a new report about the Philippines.

“The authorities responsible for moving the Pulo Island community did not follow national or international standards to protect affected people’s rights,” said HRW’s report published on Tuesday, October 13.

The island of Pulo is located in the middle of the Pampanga river in Macabebe, Pampanga, which was home to 90 families before they were removed from there in 2022. That was when the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) dredged the island as a flood mitigation program.

According to HRW, the DPWH said it heeded the request of the former mayor of Macabebe to dredge the island, which had become a “danger area.” DPWH awarded the contracts to two separate private companies worth a combined P150 million.

Most of the residents were not land owners on the island. The report found that the residents felt “intimidated” and “harassed” into demolishing their own homes, and into agreeing to move to a new site that eventually turned out to be a more flood-prone area.
All photos are courtesy of Human Rights Watch
The site, a former fishpond, is still right by the Pampanga river, located six feet below the road dike, and submerged in water coming from the river all year long.
“They removed us [from Pulo Island], and they put us in a place where we feel we were thrown here like trash,” one of the residents said, as quoted by HRW.

The residents could no longer plant crops, like they did on the island, and it has affected their everyday life from daily mobility to the unsanitary condition of wading through water everyday. Residents whose new houses were built without elevation are flooded from the inside frequently. One resident said, “I’m sick of it, so sick of it.”

HRW’s newest report on planned relocations comes amid the Philippines’ so-called “trillion-peso” flood control corruption scandal that centers around the DPWH and local politicians. “The [DPWH] officials interviewed have not been implicated, nor did Human Rights Watch investigate corruption in the Pulo Island project,” the report said.

“Communities in the Philippines living in flood-prone areas are already facing the consequences of climate change and shouldn’t have to suffer further from botched government relocations,” said Lian Buan, HRW’s Southeast Asia researcher.

Planned relocation, according to the United Nations (UN), is a government-led program to move a group of people “to protect people from risks and impacts related to disasters and environmental change, including the effects of climate change.”

items: Marcos promised a crackdown on flood control corruption. What happened a year later?
Flood control corruption: How much money has been recovered so far?
Flood control corruption: Senate blue ribbon panel’s partial findings, recommendations
Flood control corruption cleanup spooks investors, drags PH growth – World Bank

blocks.text: The UN has guidelines on how to implement a planned relocation, and the Philippines has adopted those largely in its own national resettlement policy framework. The guidelines, both of the UN and the Philippines, state that there should be meaningful consultation with the affected community, and that adequate information are given to them so they can consider their options carefully, and be involved in the process.

The report found that while there were meetings with residents, their “concerns and questions about relocation were not given due consideration.” “We had no choice. People just arrived measuring our houses, our lands. We had no choice but to agree, because you can’t be left there,” the report quotes said Mary Grace Liguid, a resident.

The residents were compensated for their houses, but the payment arrangement – 70% at first instance, and then the remaining 30% after submitting proof that the houses had been totally demolished – left the residents spending significant amounts of money on rent during transition. They were not compensated for their crops, even as HRW notes the UN guidelines state that relocated people have the right to be compensated for “other relinquished assets related to that land.”

In the report, the projects’ engineers from the DPWH said the relocation site was selected by the local government unit, and that it was “an isolated case.” The report also quotes the Department of Human Settlements and Urban Development as saying that they were not tapped for the project, even though they are the lead agency to oversee relocations, resulting in a project “with no check and balance.”
The Commission on Human Rights will conduct a fact-finding investigation, the report said. – Rappler.com

items: Meralco customers will see a 32-centavo increase per kilowatt-hour in electricity bills this October, raising the overall residential rate to P15.0615.

The increase is primarily due to higher generation costs linked to elevated fuel prices and tighter electricity supply, although some costs were offset by cheaper electricity from other suppliers and reduced taxes.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – Meralco customers will face higher electricity bills this October, as the energy giant announced a 32-centavo hike per kilowatt-hour (kWh).
The Manila Electric Company (Meralco) said on Tuesday, October 13, that its overall residential electricity rate will rise by P0.3191 per kWh, bringing it to P15.0615 from P14.7424 in September.
For a household consuming 200 kWh monthly, this translates to an additional P64 on the electricity bill, bringing the total to around P3,012.

blocks.caption: Meralco electricity rates rise in October 2026 as generation costs rise

blocks.text: Most of the increase was because of higher generation costs, which rose by P0.4973 per kWh amid elevated fuel prices, a weaker peso, and tighter electricity supply.

Meralco said electricity purchased from First Gas and Prime CoreGen became more expensive as the plants used liquefied natural gas (LNG), whose price remains elevated due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East.

blocks.caption: DRIVERS. Screenshot showing the drivers of electricity rates, taken from Meralco’s press conference on Tuesday.

blocks.text: Meanwhile, electricity purchased from the Wholesale Electricity Spot Market (WESM) also became more expensive due to tighter supply conditions in Luzon.
These increases were only partly offset by cheaper electricity from other contracted suppliers, lower transmission charges, and reduced taxes.
The removal of the 12% value-added tax on allowable system loss charges also helped reduce the overall increase.

blocks.caption: With power bills already high, Meralco wins approval to raise own fees after 15 years

blocks.text: The October rate does not yet include the newly approved increase in Meralco’s own distribution charges, which the Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC) approved following the distribution utility’s first rate review in 15 years.
Unlike generation and transmission charges, which are pass-through fees, distribution charges pay for Meralco’s own operations and allow it to earn a regulated profit.
The ERC approved an average distribution rate of P1.48 per kWh, up from the existing P1.35, although Meralco has yet to determine the exact impact on residential customers.

Meralco spokesperson Joe Zaldarriaga said the company expects to implement the higher distribution rate beginning November billing, which will be slightly offset by a newly approved P2.64-billion refund to customers.

The refund, equivalent to P0.1733 per kWh for residential customers, will run for six months or until the full amount is returned. It could offset much of the impact of the distribution rate increase, with Zaldarriaga saying the two adjustments could result in a slight net reduction in charges.
Meralco is also continuing two previously approved refunds totaling P1.0139 per kWh for residential customers.

Asked by Rappler whether Meralco’s planned investments to reduce system losses were considered in the rate reset, Meralco head of utility economics Larry Fernandez confirmed that the company had included spending proposals to bring down these losses. (READ: MAP: Where have system losses been highest from 2021 to 2025?)

However, Fernandez said Meralco could not yet identify which projects regulators had approved, reduced, or rejected. As such, the company also did not provide specific targets or timelines for reducing technical and non-technical system losses. – Rappler.com

articles.title: What is holding back Cyprus's Schengen ambitions?
articles.summary: The European Commission says Cyprus is ready to join the Schengen Area. Yet questions relating to the island's division and British military bases could still complicate its path to Europe's…

image.caption: There are nine designated crossing points between the internationally recognized Republic of Cyprus and the Turkish-controlled northern part of the island. Pictured here: the Leda Street crossing point in NicosiaImage: Mpalis/Depositphotos/IMAGO

blocks.text: Cyprus is closer than ever to joining the Schengen Area.
Together with Ireland, Cyprus is currently the only member of the European Union not to be part of Europe's border-free travel zone.
After years of preparations and the implementation of 120 technical recommendations, Nicosia received a positive assessment from the European Commission in July, confirming its technical readiness.

The recommendations, issued as part of EU evaluations dating back to 2021, covered areas including border controls, visa policy, access to European security databases and police cooperation. Their implementation required technological upgrades as well as legislative and administrative reforms.

On October 1, Cyprus's Deputy Minister for Migration and International Protection, Nicholas Ioannides, confirmed that "all recommendations made by the European Commission are now considered to have been implemented."

blocks.caption: Cyprus's Deputy Minister for Migration, Nicholas Ioannides, says Cyprus is technically ready to join Schengen, Europe's border-free travel zone, which covers 29 EU and non-EU countriesImage: Markus Lenhardt/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: According to Ioannides, Cyprus is technically ready to join Schengen, with the next step being to secure the necessary political agreement.
Austria, the Netherlands express reservations
However, a positive technical assessment alone is not enough for Cyprus to join the Schengen Area.
Accession requires a unanimous decision by the EU Council following consultation with the European Parliament.

According to information obtained by DW, Austria and the Netherlands have already informally expressed reservations over security concerns linked to the Green Line, which divides the island of Cyprus, and the special status of the British Sovereign Base Areas.
Although neither country has officially threatened to veto Cyprus's accession, their reservations carry particular weight.
Both Austria and the Netherlands have previously raised objections to the expansion of the Schengen Area to Bulgaria and Romania.
What is the Green Line?
Perhaps the most significant obstacle is the Green Line, the approximately 180-kilometer-long (112 miles) ceasefire line that has divided Cyprus since Turkey's military intervention in 1974.

blocks.caption: The buffer zone between the two parts of the island is monitored by the United Nations Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus (UNFICYP)Image: STR/NurPhoto/IMAGO

blocks.text: It separates the areas controlled by the internationally recognized Republic of Cyprus from the Turkish-controlled northern part of the island.
The buffer zone is monitored by the United Nations Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus (UNFICYP), while the Green Line itself is not an internationally recognized state border.
Crossings between the two sides take place at nine designated crossing points and are governed by a special EU regulation.

This unique arrangement poses a challenge to Schengen membership, as the Republic of Cyprus does not exercise effective control along the entire length of the line. At the same time, Nicosia rejects any arrangement that could turn the Green Line into an external border, either legally or even symbolically.

"The issue raised by some Schengen countries is that the Republic of Cyprus does not control the entire Green Line. It may control the crossing points, but there are also open stretches of land," Dr. Nasia Hadjigeorgiou, associate professor of Transitional Justice and Human Rights at the School of Law of UCLan Cyprus, told DW.

"For it to be considered to have full control, something would have to change. Either the Cyprus problem would have to be resolved, or a strictly controlled physical border would have to be established. There is no other way," said Hadjigeorgiou.
Why are the British Sovereign Base Areas an issue?

Another obstacle to Cyprus's Schengen ambitions is the presence of the British Sovereign Base Areas of Akrotiri and Dhekelia, which remained under UK sovereignty when Cyprus gained independence in 1960.
Together, the two areas cover 254 square kilometers (98 square miles), almost 3% of the island, and remain British sovereign territory.

The main complication concerns the Dhekelia base area, which borders both the territory controlled by the Republic of Cyprus and the self-declared Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, which is not internationally recognized.
Two crossing points, at Pergamos and Strovilia, are located in this area, where checks are carried out by British authorities. The UK is no longer a member of the European Union.

Dr. Nasia Hadjigeorgiou explains the difficulties arising from this unusual arrangement: "This is problematic because the area in question is controlled on one side by the authorities in the occupied north and on the other by the British Sovereign Base Areas."

"As a result, the United Kingdom would be controlling who enters and leaves the Schengen Area. This is an unusual situation, since it is normally the Schengen member states themselves that decide who can enter and leave the area," she said.

According to information obtained by DW, Nicosia and the British Sovereign Base Areas have already begun discussions on upgrading border control procedures at Pergamos and Strovilia to bring them into line with EU requirements.
Political negotiations with EU countries
In the meantime, Nicosia has stepped up its diplomatic efforts to secure the necessary consensus.

Deputy Minister for Migration Nicholas Ioannides held bilateral meetings with his counterparts from Austria, the Netherlands and Finland on October 1 on the sidelines of the EU Justice and Home Affairs Council meeting in Luxembourg. Cyprus's accession to Schengen was among the issues discussed.

blocks.caption: UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres was in Cyprus this summer in what was seen as an effort to kickstart the stalled peace process on the islandImage: Ali Ruhluel/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: Cyprus also secured significant political backing on October 7 during the summit of the nine Mediterranean EU member states (MED9) in Croatia.
In their joint declaration, the leaders welcomed the European Commission's positive assessment and called for the timely completion of Cyprus's accession process.
Nevertheless, diplomatic sources speaking to DW on condition of anonymity cautioned that despite the positive signals, Cyprus's entry into the Schengen Area should by no means be taken for granted.

The same sources consider it highly likely that the EU may choose to wait for the outcome of the ongoing efforts to resolve the Cyprus problem before making a decision that could create additional political and practical complications.

articles.title: AI models may soon self-replicate without access to data centers, Anthropic warns
articles.summary: In its experiments, Anthropic looks at whether AI models could find vulnerable devices, copy themselves into those devices, and continue spreading without human help

blocks.text: AI. 'AI Artificial Intelligence' words, a keyboard and a robotics hand in this illustration taken, September 23, 2026
Dado Ruvic/Reuters
In its experiments, Anthropic looks at whether AI models could find vulnerable devices, copy themselves into those devices, and continue spreading without human help

Anthropic said on Monday, October 12, its experiments suggested small AI models may be months away from being capable enough to self-replicate on commercial internet-of-things (IoT) devices, such as smart ovens and off-brand Android TV boxes.
In its experiments, Anthropic looked at whether AI models could find vulnerable devices, copy themselves into those devices, and continue spreading without human help.
It found that small models under 30 billion parameters could complete the many steps needed for replication.
However, the firm found that such AI models also struggled to complete the entire sequence from start to finish.
In its simplified tests, where some security steps were removed, Anthropic found that GLM-5.2 and stronger models were capable of end-to-end replication.

Replicating models would be hard to shut down as there is no central switch-off point and, unlike non-AI malware, they could also figure out unfamiliar devices on their own, targeting data center processors, Anthropic warned.
The firm focused on IoT devices like Android TVs, smart appliances, and other internet-connected gadgets in its research as these are typically poorly secured.

The AI major also warned that if small models improved at their historical rate, they would be able to autonomously replicate by the end of this year, with small weight-based replicators following suit soon after.

Anthropic also said such autonomous AI systems were likely to replicate slowly and rely on widely available, relatively insecure computing resources. It added that systems should be strengthened to make it harder for such AI agents to spread. – Rappler.com

articles.title: NFA says rice imports could prevent food insecurity amid US import plans
articles.summary: The NFA said rice imports are still needed in the country to fill supply gaps and prevent food insecurity as local production only covers about 70% to 78% of the country’s rice needs.

blocks.text: October 13, 2026 | 2:20pm
Workers load sacks of National Food Authority (NFA) rice on a truck inside a warehouse at the NFA compound in Balagtas, Bulacan on August 13, 2025.
STAR / Miguel De Guzman

MANILA, Philippines — The National Food Authority (NFA) said rice imports could help maintain supplies and prevent food insecurity in the country following reports of plans to import large volumes of rice from the United States.

NFA Administrator Larry Lacson clarified on Tuesday, October 13, that the rice importation plans were initiated by a private rice industry stakeholder group and the government has no involvement in the matter.

“Hindi po sa atin dumadaan ang mga permit or whatever niyan. Hindi rin po tayo nag-i-import. So it’s a pure private sector initiative na I don’t know kung magkakatotoo, tingnan natin,” Lacson said in an interview with Super Radyo dzBB.
(We don’t handle the permits or whatever for that. We also don’t import. So it’s a pure private sector initiative, which I don’t know if it comes true.)

Last week, it was reported that the Philippine Rice Industry Stakeholders Movement (PRISM) and the USA Rice have signed a memorandum of understanding which could reportedly allow rice imports from the US starting 2027.
The signed MOU indicated that PRISM could import 100,000 metric tonnes of bagged and bulk US rice by next year, and could increase to 200,000 metric tonnes yearly starting 2028.
Lacson said they don’t have regulatory powers over such imports.
Filling supply gaps
The NFA said rice imports are still needed in the country to fill supply gaps and prevent food insecurity as local production only covers about 70% to 78% of the country’s rice needs.
“Eh saan po natin kukunin yung ah 30%, ‘ika nga no? Eh saan po natin kukuhanin ‘yon kundi sa pag-aangkat din po. Hindi naman po natin gustong magkaroon ng food insecurity,” Lacson said.
(So where will we get the other 30%? Where else will we get that aside from imports? We also don’t want to have food insecurity.)

The administrator added that the Department of Agriculture (DA) has openly said that the target volume of local production for 2026 is five million metric tonnes, which without importation is not enough for the national buffer stock.
“Pero dahil may importation ang national buffer stock po natin ay nasa 75 days to last,” Lacos said.
(But because there are imports, our national buffer stock could last 75 days.)

October 13, 2026
Tea and game plan: Rahul Gandhi expected to host INDIA bloc MPs after Supreme Court rally

blocks.caption: Monday's opposition protest snaked through a heavily barricaded part of central DelhiImage: Priyanshu Singh/REUTERS

blocks.text: India's main opposition leader Rahul Gandhi has invited fellow lawmakers of the INDIA bloc of opposition parties over high tea on Tuesday, news agencies ANI and PTI reported.

The meeting comes after thousands of opposition demonstrators, including activists and civil society members, marched to the Supreme Court on Monday evening in a protest heralded by Gandhi and the INDIA bloc.
Monday's large demonstration was the latest in a series of protests the world's largest democracy has been witnessing over an alleged manipulation of voter rolls.

India's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar has come under public and opposition ire, with calls for him to resign amplifying, after a report last month found that Kumar took alleged unilateral decisions that resulted in a mass deletion of voters, allegedly violating the law.
Around 130 million names have been struck off so far from electoral rolls under the process called Special Intensive Revision (SIR), which began last year.
Critics say the exercise favors Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata (BJP).
The Election Commission of India and the BJP deny the allegations.
Kumar and Modi have not yet given a statement on the issue.
On Saturday, another protest called by the youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) movement was thwarted by a mammoth deployment of police and paramilitary, leading to mass detentions,
BJP has slammed the CJP and INDIA bloc as 'anarchists'.

"There are no parallel protests. It's one protest, and it's a protest where everybody is standing together. Every single person is going to stand against these killers of our Constitution, these killers of our democracy. And we're not going to back down," Gandhi wrote on X after the rally.

Monday's opposition protest, that snaked through a heavily barricaded part of central Delhi, culminated with the opposition filing a joint petition in the Supreme Court against the SIR and the alleged irregularities.
On Tuesday, the opposition MPs are expected to discuss further plans in their joint protest, PTI reported.

articles.title: Palace defends Marcos' rainwater buckets remarks: 'Sit down and listen'
articles.summary: Malacañang on Tuesday defended President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr.'s remarks about using buckets to collect rainwater, saying people need to listen to what he had to say.

blocks.text: Published October 13, 2026 2:15pm
Malacañang on Tuesday defended President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr.'s remarks about using buckets to collect rainwater, saying people need to listen to what he had to say.

Interviewed by the media in Singapore, Marcos urged the Filipino public to collect rainwater amid the ongoing El Niño phenomenon, which is expected to intensify in the coming months. To collect rainwater, Marcos said people need to buy buckets.

"Hindi po ito pakanya-kanya. Kung ito lang po ang nadinig na tungkol sa balde, ang mas maganda po, umupo sila at makinig. Sit down and listen kung ano ang sinasabi ng Pangulo. Bakit 'yung balde lang ang kanilang nakita at narinig?" Castro said in a press briefing.

(This is not about every man for himself. If the bucket is the only thing they heard about, it is better for them to sit and listen. Sit down and listen to what the President said. Why did they just hear and see about the bucket?)
People should avoid just seeing negative things about the government, particularly obstructionists, Castro said.
"Sa mga obstructionists po itong sasabihin ko. Kailangan po talaga natin ng balde, baldeng utak. Para po maintindihan niyo po kung ano ang plano ng Pangulo," she added.
(To the obstructionists, this is what I have to say. We need a bucket. A bucket of brains. So you can understand the plans of the President.)

Castro urged the public not to make a laughing matter out of Marcos' statement, saying that it was important to collect rainwater, saying that other high-ranking officials have already laughed at it while forgetting that it has been practiced for a long time.

The Palace executive stressed that collecting rainwater was important, adding that Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) Secretary Rex Gatchalian is set to release a video tutoring people how to filter the water.

"Mayroon akong kilala, isang mataas na opisyal, tinawanan ang pag-iipon ng tubig baha. Kilala niyo ba? Tinanong sa kanya, tinawanan niya, mataas na opisyal. Hindi niya batid ang pag-iipon ng tubig-ulan ay matagal ng ginagawa. At iyan ay ang Bise Presidente," Castro said.

(I know someone, a high-ranking official who laughed at collecting floodwater. Do you know her? It was asked to her, she laughed at it, a high-ranking official. She did not know that the collection of rainwater had long been done for a long time. And that is the vice president.)
GMA News Online has reached out to Vice President Sara Duterte's office for a statement, but it has yet to respond as of posting time. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Defense seeks to present evidence despite 3 dropped articles
articles.summary: Defense lead counsel Sheila Sison on Tuesday said the prosecution"s decision to drop three of the four Articles of Impeachment against Vice President Sara Duterte would not affect the defense panel"s…

blocks.text: SARA DUTERTE IMPEACHMENT TRIAL
Published October 13, 2026 2:02pm Updated October 13, 2026 2:19pm

Defense lead counsel Sheila Sison on Tuesday said the prosecution’s decision to drop three of the four Articles of Impeachment against Vice President Sara Duterte would not affect the defense panel’s presentation of its own evidence.

Sison made the statement on Day 39 of the impeachment trial after House lead prosecutor and Batangas Rep. Gerville Luistro manifested that the prosecution would no longer pursue Articles I, III and IV, which detail allegations of grave threats, misuse of confidential funds and bribery.

With the decision, the prosecution will pursue only Article II, which concerns allegations that Duterte failed to fully declare her assets and divest from business interests, raising questions about her unexplained wealth.

“We respect the decision of the prosecution. However, whether this will affect how the defense plans to proceed with its presentation of evidence is something that we must make clear: It will not,” Sison said.

“Because the prosecution cannot make decisions for the respondent and the defense. In other words, the prosecution cannot be allowed to have the benefit of its accusations without bearing the burden of having those accusations tested,” she added.
Sison argued that after 38 days of trial, the prosecution had already spent considerable time and government resources presenting its witnesses and evidence.

She said the public had also been exposed to the allegations through the direct examinations of prosecution witnesses, interjections, and the conclusions and opinions some witnesses expressed before the impeachment court.
“And therefore, the accusations have already entered the consciousness of those who must ultimately render judgment," the defense lawyer said.

"In other words, the prosecution would thus retain the benefit of having its evidence heard, while the respondent would be at risk of being denied the benefit of having that evidence contradicted,” she added.

According to Sison, allowing the prosecution to withdraw three impeachment articles after presenting its evidence could undermine Duterte’s right to due process and a meaningful opportunity to rebut the allegations against her.

“And we feel and we believe that this is not fairness, and it is not in keeping with the guarantees of due process, because the right to be heard is not merely satisfied by allowing the respondent some room to present evidence on her behalf," she said.
"It necessarily includes a meaningful opportunity to answer material accusations already publicly advanced against her,” the defense counsel added.
Sison stressed that the prosecution’s decision to drop three impeachment articles “cannot unilaterally determine” how the defense would proceed with its presentation of evidence.

“It cannot make decisions for us and for the respondent because to allow this would be to confer upon the prosecution the extraordinary and impermissible power to control not only the presentation of its own case, but also the scope and substance of the defense case,” she said.

Sison maintained that the prosecution’s decision to drop three impeachment articles should not deprive Duterte of the opportunity to rebut the allegations already presented before the impeachment court.

“That prerogative to withdraw an accusation is not the power to suppress its rebuttal on the part of the respondent. The authority to streamline, or to achieve speed in a trial, is not the authority to diminish due process, or to altogether disregard fundamental rules of fairness," she said.
"And the desire to reach a verdict expeditiously can never justify reaching it unfairly,” Sison added.
Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero then asked whether the defense was objecting to the prosecution’s manifestation.
Sison clarified that she was merely making a manifestation on behalf of the defense and Duterte, saying they “will proceed as we deem fit.”
“Even if it's not an objection, it's still subject to the court's decision and discretion as to how to act on the motion of the prosecution,” Escudero said.—MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Coastal erosion in England has claimed at least 183 homes in past 16 years
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Homes demolished along east coast after being deemed too vulnerable to live in, figures reveal

Seaside communities along the east coast of England have lost at least…

blocks.text: Seaside communities along the east coast of England have lost at least 183 homes to coastal erosion and landslides over the past 16 years, figures obtained by the Guardian reveal.
After councils judged properties across the Yorkshire and East Anglian coasts too vulnerable to remain safely occupied, the homes were proactively demolished.

The demolitions cost £1.1m, with the Environment Agency contributing about £482,000 towards clearing 61 homes at risk of collapsing and the rest paid for by councils and at times by homeowners themselves.

Coastal erosion is the gradual wearing away and retreat of the sea shoreline, which can destabilise cliffs and eventually force homes and infrastructure to be demolished before they collapse. While it is a natural process, scientists said the climate crisis was accelerating the retreat of the UK’s shores.
The Guardian requested data from nine councils noted in a House of Commons environment, food and rural affairs committee (EFRA) report as being some of the most vulnerable to coastal erosion.
East Riding of Yorkshire council, which includes vulnerable communities in Skipsea, Aldbrough and Mappleton, has demolished 66 homes since 2010 – the most of these nine local authorities.

Great Yarmouth borough council (GYBC) has demolished 64 homes since 2010, with all the houses located in the village of Hemsby. Since December 2025, the council has removed 41 properties in the seaside resort.
A GYBC spokesperson said: “Last winter, the dunes in Hemsby saw about 50% of the erosion predicted for the entirety of the next 30 years. More than 10 metres of land was lost in just over 12 months.
“Council staff continue to liaise with people to make sure residents and the public are safe and work closely with people to offer support and advice and explain the options available.”
North Norfolk council has proactively demolished 21 homes over the same period.

East Suffolk council, which only held data for the past six years, recorded a sharp rise in demolitions last year. Eight homes were demolished between 2020 and 2024, and 16 between May last year and April this year.

Most of East Suffolk’s homes demolished this year are understood to be in Thorpeness. Hilary Lightfoot’s home, in which she lived and raised a family for 20 years, was demolished this year. “I’ve lost £650,000 – that was what my flat was worth,” she said. “I’ve had to dig into my pension savings to buy a house, of which I still owe money on. I’ve borrowed money. It’s just disastrous.”
The Environment Agency estimates that 3,500 properties in England are at risk from coastal erosion by 2055, increasing to more than 10,000 properties by 2105.

More than 6 miles (10km) of major roads, 107 miles of minor roads and 3.5 miles of railway – many serving small, coastal communities – are also at risk from erosion over the next 80 years, according to the EA.

Unlike flood damage, which can be covered by the Flood Re scheme, there is no UK insurance product for coastal erosion because insurers treat coastal retreat as a “virtual certainty” for some seaside homes rather than an accidental risk, according to the EFRA committee’s report.

East Suffolk council said that although some government funding was available towards demolition, “there are currently limited mechanisms to support the wider costs of adaptation and relocation” for residents.

The authority said it had invested about £1.5m in short-term measures designed to slow erosion and give residents more time to prepare, while also testing new approaches through the government’s flood and coastal innovation programme.
after newsletter promotion
Sophie Day, senior research associate at the University of East Anglia, said because the east coast was made up of “very sandy, gravelly, silty material”, it was more vulnerable to erosion.

She said wetter winters, made more likely by the climate crisis, would saturate and destabilise soft cliffs such as those on the east coast, while increased storminess and rising sea levels would worsen the impact of high tides and leave beaches with less time to recover between storms.

While councils have increased spending on sea defences over the decades, Day said these protections have created an “illusion of permanence” for what is an accelerating issue. The scale of the threat from coastal erosion meant “we are going to have to shift to more of an acceptance of not intervening any more and enabling retreat”, she added.
Day said adapting to a retreating coastline meant planning for the loss of homes and infrastructure before the next emergency, while working more closely with communities.

“Having skilled people who are able to engage, who have the time, the training, the skills, to go and sit at somebody’s kitchen table and talk to them about the fact that, in a year, even five months’ time, their home may not be livable. What are the options? How can we find ways of giving people choices and support?”

North Norfolk district council (NNDC) said: “Households in all 21 homes were supported by NNDC. Nineteen of these properties were proactively demolished before they reached the cliff edge and became an emergency.

“NNDC continues to work with the Environment Agency and Defra … to better prepare communities. A number of pilot opportunities are under development. It is hoped that through this work, more targeted support for those impacted can become part of the business as usual and supported by government for the whole coast into the future.”

A spokesperson for East Riding council said: “East Riding of Yorkshire has some of the fastest eroding coastlines in Europe, resulting in the loss of homes, businesses and roads. Through the Changing Coasts East Riding project, the council is working directly with residents, businesses and communities to find out the full economic, environmental and social impacts of these losses.”
An Environment Agency spokesperson said it was “very aware” of how erosion was affecting coastal homeowners and communities.

They said: “While local authorities are best placed to support affected residents, we’re backing them with £36m for coastal erosion adaptation pilots, slashing planning regulation red tape in vulnerable areas and offering £10,000 grants to fund the safe demolition of affected properties – with scope to go further for more complex jobs.”

articles.title: Same-sex couple sue over Slovakia’s refusal to register marriage
articles.summary:
Case of couple who wed legally in Austria exposes clash between EU court ruling and national restrictions

A same-sex couple are suing authorities in Slovakia for refusing to register their…

blocks.text: A same-sex couple are suing authorities in Slovakia for refusing to register their Austrian marriage, testing whether a landmark EU court ruling can turn recognition abroad into legal security at home.
Their fight exposes a clash between European obligations and national restrictions – and what that means for LGBTQ+ people living under Robert Fico’s populist-nationalist government.
Ivan Novotný, 31, and Metod Špaček, 51, married in Austria in 2020, but six years on, their marital status at home remains unrecognised.
There is no same-sex marriage in Slovakia, a socially conservative, predominantly Catholic country; neither is there any form of civil partnership.

But Novotný and Špaček, who are both lawyers and former diplomats, are not asking for that. They want the Slovakian authorities to recognise a marriage that was concluded legally in another EU country – something the bloc’s top court has said is mandatory for all EU members.

“I’ve said this publicly several times, and [LGBTQ+] activists in Slovakia have criticised me for it: Metod and I are not discriminated against here. We have a lovely life here in Bratislava, in Slovakia,” Novotný said. “So, we don’t actually need [recognition of marriage] for our day-to-day lives.”
For example, said Novotný, when Špaček was hospitalised during the Covid pandemic he was treated by a “lovely” doctor who recognised Novotný’s official relationship to her patient.

He added: “She put me down on the report as ‘husband’ and gave me all your [Špaček] medical information. The problem is: that was because she was nice, not because she had to do it. If someone wanted to make trouble for us, they could do it.
“That’s not how the rule of law should work.”
The couple argue they are on solid legal ground after a ruling by the EU’s highest court in November 2025 in response to a case brought by a Polish same-sex couple who had married in Berlin.

Jakub Cupriak-Trojan and Mateusz Trojan had challenged the Mazovia provincial governor’s refusal to recognise their German marriage. The court ruled that member states must recognise such marriages where couples had exercised their right to move and reside in another EU country, and created or strengthened family life there.
The European court of justice ruling does not require member states to allow same-sex weddings at home.

blocks.caption: Marián Žáry Kukelka, who is also suing Slovakian authorities, holds his Austrian marriage certificate.  Photograph: Rob Cameron

blocks.text: The Slovakian authorities explained why Novotný and Špaček’s request to register their Austrian marriage had been turned down in a letter signed by the interior minister, Matúš Šutaj Eštok.

“[The letter] says that since the constitutional definition of marriage [in Slovakia] is a bond between a man and a woman, they lack the legal basis for formally recognising the marriage certificate. That’s essentially it,” said Špaček, who served as chief of staff to the country’s liberal former president Zuzana Čaputová.

Across town, in the house his grandparents built on a hill overlooking the Danube, Marián Žáry Kukelka, 44, recalled his wedding to his partner, Ondrej, in 2023. The couple married in Hainburg an der Donau, an Austrian town visible from their terrace.
after newsletter promotion

Žáry Kukelka, a radio presenter for the public broadcaster STVR, is also suing Slovakian authorities. He uses his full married name on air (Žáry is Ondrej’s surname) and is supported by his colleagues. But his official documents refer to him as Marián Kukelka. He said: “It’s a court case for love. I don’t need that surname to live my life, but for me it’s a kind of tribute to my partner, that I can carry his surname too.”.
Žáry Kukelka lives behind Bratislava Castle, not far from Zámocká street – the scene of the homophobic attack in 2022 where two people were shot dead outside the LGBTQ+ bar Tepláreň.
The anti-LGBTQ+ rhetoric of many Slovakian politicians, especially in the government, was contributing to an atmosphere of increasing hostility, he said.

Last year, Fico’s government backed constitutional changes recognising only two sexes and tightening adoption restrictions. Žáry Kukelka told the Guardian that Hainburg an der Donau had been “overwhelmed” with LGBTQ+ couples from Slovakia wanting to get married since a change to Austrian legislation made it possible.
He himself had experienced little in the way of abuse as a gay man, he said, although he admitted he thought carefully before using the words “my husband”, depending on whom he was talking to.
“Two weeks ago, we were in Switzerland, and there we held hands in public for the first time in a long time,” he said. “We felt it was different there.”
Slovakia’s interior ministry said it was bound by the country’s existing constitutional and legal framework, regardless of whether a marriage was valid abroad.

It acknowledged the primacy of EU law but argued that recognition for freedom of movement purposes did not require registration as a marriage. Its administrative work “cannot replace decisions by the legislature or the constitutional legislature,” the ministry told the Guardian.

articles.title: Palace: Marcos never said Philippines can't do business with China
articles.summary: The Palace on Tuesday said President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. never said that the country could not do business with China, adding that the issue was whether the money was used to meddle with…

blocks.text: Published October 13, 2026 1:59pm

The Palace on Tuesday said President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. never said that the country could not do business with China, adding that the issue was whether the money was used to meddle with politics.

Amid accusations of receiving money from China through various organizations, Vice President Sara Duterte said that there was nothing wrong with doing business with Beijing. She raised the issue after Marcos called the transactions a national threat if proven true.

“Kung national threat ang pag-uusapan natin, sinabi niya ay delikado na makipagnegosyo sa China — mayroon bang sinabi ang Pangulo na hindi puwedeng makipagnegosyo ang Pilipinas sa China? Parang wala, so, fake news,” Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said.

(If we are talking about a national threat, and she is talking about doing business with China — did the President say something about the Philippines being prohibited from doing business with China? There is none, so it is fake news.)

“Ang pinag-uusapan dito ay ang pakikipag-negotiate sa ibang bansa na ang pondo kung mapapatunayan ay para pondohan ang pamumulitika nila,” Castro added. (What we are talking about here is the negotiation with other countries for funds that, if proven, is being used for their politicking.)
Castro also pointed out that Duterte allegedly received P150 million from China through her Tapat and Malasakit Foundation, which is not a business in the first place.
“And one more thing, with that statement of the Vice President it means she is really into business with China,” she added.
Military-to-military communications with China

During the same press briefing, Castro was also asked about the Chinese Embassy in the Philippines’ claim that Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro had shut down military-to-military communications with Beijing.
While Castro deferred the matter to Teodoro himself, she said that China and the Philippines still needed each other in terms of trade.

“Definitely hindi naman natin sinasara ang ating relasyon sa China. Hindi naman po gugustuhin iyan ng Pangulo. Kasi tuluy-tuloy pa rin ang pakikipag-ugnayan natin sa China dahil nais din po natin magpatuloy din iyong trade and investment natin sa bansang China,” Castro said.

(Definitely, we will not close off relations with China. The President does not want that. Our talks with China continue because we want our trade and investment with China to continue.) — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: SC junks 2025 impeachment-related contempt case vs Tito Sotto
articles.summary: 'Democracy is founded on respect. With this decision, we double down not only on freedom of expression but on full respect for the respondent,' the High Court says

blocks.text: SOTTO. Senator Tito Sotto speaks during the plenary session on May 12, 2026.
Senate Social Media Unit
'Democracy is founded on respect. With this decision, we double down not only on freedom of expression but on full respect for the respondent,' the High Court says

items: The Supreme Court dismissed the indirect contempt case against Senator Tito Sotto III, stating his remarks about Vice President Sara Duterte's impeachment were protected by freedom of speech.
The Court emphasized that public criticism of its decisions, especially regarding political matters, is constitutionally protected and does not constitute indirect contempt.

This ruling aligns with previous cases where the Court upheld the right to free speech, reinforcing that statements about public officials in their official capacity are safeguarded, regardless of their nature.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The Supreme Court (SC) dismissed the indirect contempt case filed against Senator Vicente “Tito” Sotto III over the latter’s statement related to Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment in 2025.

“The Supreme Court has dismissed the petition for indirect contempt against Senator Vicente ‘Tito’ Sotto III over his public criticism of the Court’s ruling on the impeachment case against Vice President Sara Duterte (G.R. Nos. 278353 and 278359, Duterte v. House of Representatives et al.), holding that his statements are protected by the constitutional freedoms of speech and expression,” said the SC, based on the ruling penned by Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen.

Under Philippine laws, indirect contempt is a type of contempt or violation against a tribunal committed out of the court’s presence. The punishment varies, but penalties may include a fine. Rule 71, Section 3(D) of Rules of Court states that conduct that impedes or obstructs the administration of justice may be punished with indirect contempt.

Duterte v. House of Representatives was the High Court’s 2025 ruling that dismissed the first impeachment complaint against the Vice President. There, the High Court, through Leonen, ruled that the articles of impeachment or the allegations from the House of Representatives were unconstitutional.

After this ruling, Sotto aired several remarks where he questioned the SC decision and even said that the ponente or Leonen “was unfamiliar with congressional rules and that the decision effectively amended the Constitution.”
Lawyer Manuelito Luna and others then went to the High Court and asked the SC to cite the senator for indirect contempt, claiming that the lawmaker’s remarks were disrespectful to the Court.

But in the current ruling, the SC said Sotto’s statements did not violate the indirect contempt rule. The Leonen ruling said that “freedom of speech and expression enjoys the highest constitutional protection, particularly when the speech involves political matters.”

The Court explained that when the alleged contemptuous speech involves speech, the tribunal must also consider the constitutional protections of free speech and expression in its ruling. In assessing situations like this, the SC said courts must also consider not only what was said, but also “how, when, where it was expressed, and who spoke it.”

“Citing Tolentino v. Heydarian (G.R. Nos. E-01742 and E-01747), also penned by Senior Associate Justice Leonen, the SC reiterated that the Judiciary, like the other branches of government, remains subject to public scrutiny and criticism,” said the High Court.

“Under the doctrine of fair comment, statements concerning public officials in the performance of their duties are protected. Such statements do not automatically become punishable simply because they are false, harsh, or offensive. As the Court explained, ‘the guarantee of free speech was enacted to protect not only polite speech, but even in its most unsophisticated form’,” it added.

As said by the SC, this is the latest impeachment-related contempt case that was dismissed by the High Court. In July, the SC en banc unanimously dismissed the petition for indirect contempt filed by lawyers Mark Tolentino and Rolex Suplico against Akbayan Representative Perci Cendaña and political analyst Richard Heydarian.

blocks.caption: SC declines to punish personalities who criticized ruling on Sara impeachment

blocks.text: Duterte is currently in the middle of her impeachment trial after the failed proceedings in 2025. The House prosecution team had finished presenting its evidence against Duterte over alleged grave threats, misuse confidential funds, and unexplained wealth.

“The Court regards Senator Tito Sotto with the greatest respect and understands his frustration with some of our Decisions, or even with one member of the Court. Courts must be receptive to all forms ofcriticisms,” said the SC. “Democracy is founded on respect. With this decision, we double down not only on freedom of expression but on full respect for the respondent.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: Tuesday briefing: Could Burnham take Britain back towards the EU?
articles.summary:
In today’s newsletter: The prime minister is calling for closer ties with the EU, but what could this actually amount to?

Good morning. After a holiday spent contracting nursery bugs from an…

blocks.text: Good morning. After a holiday spent contracting nursery bugs from an 11-month-old, it’s good to return. Yesterday, Andy Burnham marked his first day back after party conference by calling for a closer relationship with the EU and drawing a line under a decade of “drift and division”. On Sunday, he said it was “clear” the Kremlin had been involved with the 2016 Brexit referendum vote.

Both statements mark a break, rhetorically at least, from his predecessors. Conservative governments long insisted there was no evidence of Russian interference in the Brexit vote. Keir Starmer attempted to put the entire issue of Brexit behind him, treating it as a historic event rather than a cause of economic pain.

But for all his words about a closer relationship with the EU, Burnham has kept the details pretty vague. Today’s newsletter, with the help of the Guardian’s Brussels correspondent Jennifer Rankin and our senior political correspondent Peter Walker, asks what his stance might actually amount to. That’s after the headlines.
Five big stories

items: UK | Andy Burnham said Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps were “almost certainly” behind threats to RAF Fairford, the firmest attribution of responsibility made so far by the UK after an incident late last month.
UK politics | A close adviser to Nigel Farage had an influential role at a national polling company despite not being publicly associated with the firm, the Guardian revealed.

Ukraine | Volodymyr Zelenskyy has vowed to respond to Russia’s continuing attacks on the Ukrainian power grid as European leaders rally around Kyiv amid a feud with Donald Trump over Ukraine’s strikes on oil refineries.

Israel | Benjamin Netanyahu has ordered the country’s attorney general and the head of the Shin Bet security service to reveal the identities of soldiers and officers interviewed in the documentary NAZA and prosecute them for causing “harm to Israel’s diplomatic and security interests”.
US news | RJ Mitte, the young actor best known for playing Walter White Jr in the award-winning TV series Breaking Bad, died on Monday. He was 34.

blocks.text: In depth: What does Burnham want from Europe?

blocks.caption: The UK’s relationship with the EU has remained a source of political debate a decade after the Brexit referendum. Photograph: Susannah Ireland/Reuters

blocks.text: In the years after it voted to leave the European Union, Britain became something of a laughing stock among EU member states. “It was like a box set TV drama. People in Brussels would be staying up to watch votes in the House of Commons,” Jennifer Rankin, who moved to Brussels to cover the EU for the Guardian in January 2016, tells me. Civil servants in Brussels grew to regard the UK as one might regard a belligerent and ungrateful elderly relative, an impression that reached its apotheosis when the former Northern Ireland secretary Brandon Lewis admitted that the UK’s Brexit arrangements for Northern Ireland would break international law (albeit in a “very specific and limited way”.)

“From 2016 to 2020, the UK was seen as a model of how not to run your country,” Jennifer says. This impression softened after the passing of the Withdrawal Agreement Act in early 2020, and the Windsor framework deal, which amended the arrangements under the Northern Ireland protocol in 2023. “That was a turning point in drawing a line under the bad blood of the Brexit years,” Jennifer says. Keir Starmer’s government then sought to cooperate with the EU on various issues such as security, food and fishing, but the “reset” he pledged to deliver was tightly circumscribed by his red lines: no rejoining the single market, no customs union, no freedom of movement.

After his conference speech, Burnham suggested he might be open to reconsidering this when he suggested, somewhat cryptically, that the UK could go “all the way” (presumably towards full EU membership), and yesterday he called for a “longer-term discussion” about Britain’s relationship with the EU. But what might that actually mean?
Could the UK rejoin the EU?

Burnham has been “showing a lot of ankle” to remainers over the last few weeks, Peter Walker tells me. During his Labour conference speech, he promised to lay out “different options” for Britain’s long-term relationship with Europe, and acknowledged that Brexit had caused “more harm than good”.

“It’s pretty clear that a decent majority of people would like to push a switch that meant Brexit had never happened,” Peter says. Indeed, a YouGov poll in January 2025 found that just 11% of people thought Brexit had been more of a success than a failure. And as recently as last week, the Messina Group, a polling company, reported that half of voters say they would like to rejoin the EU. The economic consequences of Brexit are now well known, and research has estimated that, a decade after the referendum, UK GDP per head is between 6% and 8% lower than it would have been without Brexit. Yet reversing this decision would require another referendum, which would be politically fraught, reigniting a debate that splintered the country a decade ago, and reducing a highly complex and technical issue to a binary decision.

It’s hard to imagine Burnham – or any politician, for that matter – wanting to fight the next election while pledging something so divisive. Notably, even the Liberal Democrats, the most pro-EU of the major parties, favour rejoining the single market and customs union but describe UK membership of the EU as a “long-term goal” rather than an immediate priority.
What other options are on the table?

If a second referendum seems like a vanishingly distant prospect, other changes could take place without one. In the combustive years after Brexit, there was a short-lived hope that the UK might pursue its own version of the Norway model, allowing it to become a member of the European Economic Area. “It was the Conservatives who decided to pursue the hardest Brexit possible,” Peter reminds me.

In theory, a softer deal could mean rejoining the single market and customs union. But this would mean breaking Labour’s red lines, which Burnham has said he will stick to. And if the UK was to rejoin the single market but remain outside the EU, it would be forced to accept rules that it had no power to shape. “As soon as you look at the democratic deficit that comes with single market membership, the case for rejoining the EU becomes stronger,” Jennifer tells me.

The debate over rejoining the EU is often conducted in relatively parochial terms, as if it only concerns Britain. But the UK’s future relationship with the EU will be largely shaped by the member states of a union that has changed significantly since the referendum. Far-right parties are gaining power in France and Germany, while the mercantilist politics of China and the US have inspired the EU’s Made in Europe agenda, a series of protectionist laws designed to bolster European industry and reduce reliance on Chinese imports.

In this context, Burnham may decide it’s better to be inside the tent than outside it. The Made in Europe agenda is particularly concerning for the government, since UK industry could suffer if exports were legally classified as “non-European” goods under these new laws. But as Mujtaba Rahman wrote in an interesting opinion piece for the Guardian in July, “any serious rejoin debate must start from an honest assessment of what the EU has become”.
What happens next?

Right now, the longer term outcome is anyone’s guess. In his statement to the Commons, Burnham confirmed that the planned UK-EU summit will go ahead in November. Negotiators are expected to discuss a trade deal on food and drink, a deal on emissions trading, a plan to link the energy systems of the EU and UK and the new youth mobility scheme. These areas were all discussed at last years’ UK-EU talks, so Burnham wasn’t announcing anything we didn’t already know.

“There’s a lot of frustration in Brussels that the UK has been talking a big game on a reset with the EU, without actually changing very much,” Jennifer says. “The theme over the last ten years is that the EU has always been waiting for the UK to define what it wants. The rhetoric may be warmer, but the substance has stayed the same.”
What else we’ve been enjoying

blocks.caption: ‘I was reminded of the world beyond my bubble’ … Georgina Elliott at Genesis cinema, London. Photograph: Ethan Parker/The Guardian

items: I have always found that TV – with its twisting plotlines, and lack of demands – is a good cure for grief. Today’s one change that worked, by writer Georgina Elliott, on how the cinema gave her some focus after the death of her brother, poignantly depicted what it’s like to muddle through such times. Poppy Noor, newsletters team

Chloe Kerleroux’s photo essay about Atlanta’s Bill Pickett rodeo is a beautiful window into a competition which encompasses athleticism, hip-hop, fashion and the celebration of contemporary Black cowboy and cowgirl culture. Lucinda Everett, newsletters team

Here’s a line I didn’t expect to read today: professor Devi Sridhar, chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh, is worried about the pneumonic plague (although it might not be for the reasons you suspect). Poppy
Kiran Sidhu was touching, on considering who to pass her most prized possessions down to in her will since she doesn’t have children. Poppy

I, too, have been had by the myth that my (small amount of) muscle will turn into fat if I don’t force myself into a few push-ups every week. Not so, according to this week’s Is it true that … column – although what does happen when you stop exercising isn’t that much more reassuring. Poppy

A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

blocks.caption: Naffah Naffah checks the finish on the outer mould, ready for casting a new bell.  Photograph: Gabriel Ferneini/The Guardian

blocks.text: The Naffah family has been making church bells in the Lebanese town of Beit Chabab for three centuries. Led by master bell-maker Naffah Naffah and his two sons, their workshop is the last remaining production centre for church bells in Lebanon and the only source of church bells for much of the Middle East.

Crafted using a mix of modern and ancient tools, each bell takes about two months to make and bears the names of those who worked on it. Naffah and his sons Charbel and Youssef are determined to preserve the tradition. Charbel will succeed his father as master of the workshop and Youssef helps alongside studying medicine, but says he would take Charbel’s place if needed.
“Traditions are important to us,” he says. “We are living and breathing tradition here in this workshop.”

articles.title: Cale88, banana chips firm, has no inventory despite 100M+ cash flows — analyst
articles.summary: A banana chip exporter linked to Vice President Sara Duterte's husband reported that it had no raw materials in stock and owed no money to buyers, even as large sums moved in and out of its accounts,…

blocks.text: October 13, 2026 | 1:41pm

Lawyer and financial analyst Alexander Cabrera was cross examined by the Defense regarding his report and testimony on the financial, property and corporate records relating to Vice President Sara Duterte and her husband, Manases Carpio on Oct. 12, 2026.
Senate of the Philippines / Wendell Alinea

MANILA, Philippines — A banana chip exporter linked to Vice President Sara Duterte's husband reported that it had no raw materials in stock and owed no money to buyers, even as large sums moved in and out of its accounts, the prosecution's financial expert witness told the Senate impeachment court on Monday.

Lawyer Alexander Cabrera, the forensic financial analyst presented as the House prosecution's last witness for its evidence-in-chief, flagged Cale88 Foods Corp. for being a "revolving door," when Sen. Raffy Tulfo asked whether he had examined the company's payables and receivables.
"Pagpasok po ng pera, lumalabas po," Cabrera said on Day 38 of Duterte's trial. (When the money comes in, it goes out.)
Manases Carpio held a 47.5% stake in Cale88 from 2021 to 2024, according to the company's general information sheet.
Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) records presented at the trial also show Cale88 received P319.33 million in remittances from mainland China and Hong Kong.

This is a finding that has since drawn a reaction from President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., who said that if Duterte was proven to have received funds from China, it "now rises to a national security issue."
Much of Cale88's financial statements appear out of place, Cabrera said.
The company listed no payables and no receivables, odd for a supposed manufacturer or exporter of manufactured goods, Cabrera said.
"Manufacturer siya o exporter siya ng manufactured goods [pero] wala siyang inventory ng raw materials or work in process," Cabrera said.
Its property, plant and equipment were also small, Cabrera said. If Cale88 had other firms make its products, its notes did not say so given they disclosed no toll manufacturing arrangement.
"Kahit po gaano kalaki 'yung perang pumapasok at lumalabas, nananatili po siyang lugi," Cabrera said. (No matter how much money comes in and goes out, it remains at a loss.)

Why is this a red flag? Cabrera explained that an exporter with no receivables would have to be paid in cash each time its goods were delivered abroad. A company with no payables would have to pay suppliers in cash on delivery of every large order.
Tulfo also pressed on whether Cale88 actually shipped any goods or products.
He said he had checked with the Bureau of Customs whether the company had documents covering shipments to the countries he had cited.
Cabrera said he had put the same question to the prosecution but did not follow up on the answer. He, too, wanted to know whether real inventory was going out, he said.
Bureau of Customs export records show that Cale88 shipped banana chips to 13 Chinese companies from 2023 to 2026, totaling approximately P217.3 million in customs value.
AMLC Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura testified that the company was the subject of three suspicious transaction reports on remittances that had no apparent legal, trade or economic basis.
Carpio's name was dropped off Cale88's general information sheet in 2025, replaced by Pikimong Pikimong Philippines Corp. But the BIR told the court it had no record of any transfer of Cale88 shares.

articles.title: Sara Duterte: I will never resign
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte on Tuesday said that she has no plan to step down from her post amid the ongoing impeachment trial and allegations against her.

blocks.text: Published October 13, 2026 1:32pm
Vice President Sara Duterte on Tuesday said that she has no plan to step down from her post amid the ongoing impeachment trial and allegations against her.
“I will not resign, will never resign from the Office of the Vice President,” she told reporters.
The impeachment trial is already on its 39th day with the prosecution presenting its case. The defense panel will start presenting its evidence and witnesses starting November 9.
The Senate, acting as the impeachment court, is currently discussing the alleged unexplained wealth of Duterte as well as of his husband, Manases Carpio.

National Bureau of Investigation director Melvin Matibag on Monday held a press conference, wherein he said the bureau is investigating properties linked to Duterte and her family amid allegations of cash deliveries by a dismissed police officer.
Duterte said that she is discussing with her legal team the allegations against her.

“Pinag-uusapan namin ng mga abogado na napakarami naman ng mga legal recourses na ginagawa ni (Ramil) Madriaga, ni (Rodulfo) Gracioso, ni (NBI director Melvin) Matibag, ni (Antonio) Trillanes, kaso we do not expect fairness from the government in general. Pinag-uusapan lang, pero wala naman kaming hakbang.

(My lawyers and I are discussing the fact that Madriaga, Gracioso, Matibag, and Trillanes are pursuing so many legal recourses, but we do not expect fairness from the government in general. We're just discussing it, but we haven't taken any action yet.)
“Ang ginagawa lang namin sa ngayon ay sinasagot na hindi ito totoo, at bakit ginagamit ninyo ang pera ng gobyerno sa paninira?” she added.
(What we are doing right now is simply answering that these allegations are not true, and asking why you are using government funds for smear campaigns?)
When asked for her comment about Matibag’s presser, Duterte said: “'Yung sa press conference niya, ang masasabi ko lang ay hindi makatotohanan ang kanyang sinasabi.”
(Regarding his press conference, all I can say is that what he is saying is untrue.)
Amid the allegations thrown at her, the Vice President said that vote rigging is possible during the 2028 national elections.
“Kung matutuloy man ang 2028 national elections, expect ninyo na 'yung dayaan diyan at expect ninyo na tutuloy-tuloy 'yung tinatawag nilang black propaganda,” said Duterte.
(If the 2028 national elections do push through, expect election fraud there and expect that what they call black propaganda will continue.) —AOL, GMA News

items: The prosecution in Vice President Sara Duterte's impeachment trial has decided to withdraw all but one article, retaining only the unexplained wealth case to expedite proceedings.
Lead prosecutor Gerville Luistro stated that focusing on a single article would narrow the court's considerations and benefit all parties involved.
The defense team expressed concerns about the implications of dropping charges, emphasizing the importance of due process and the right to fully present their case.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – The prosecution team in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte has moved to withdraw all but one of the articles of impeachment to expedite the proceedings.

In an open court manifestation on Tuesday, October 13, lead prosecutor Gerville “Jinky” Luistro said they would retain only the unexplained wealth case against the Vice President, dropping the impeachment articles against Duterte on alleged confidential fund misuse, bribery, and threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.

“The prosecution believes it has presented sufficient evidence for Article 2 to stand on its own. We are all in here. We believe that evidence is substantial and compelling, and warrants the respondent’s removal from office for culpable violation of Constitution and betrayal of public trust,” Luistro said.

“Had we proceeded on all four articles, the impeachment court will have had to consider the evidence offered for each together with the corresponding objections and arguments. By focusing on one article, the matters requiring the impeachment court’s consideration are correspondingly narrow, with practical benefits, for the Senate, for the respondent, and even the public,” Luistro added.
Responding to the move, the defense team said that while the prosecution has the prerogative to drop cases, it cannot dictate the defense on how the Duterte camp would proceed.
“The prosecution cannot be allowed to have the benefit of its accusations without bearing the burden of having those accusations tested,” said defense lawyer Sheila Sison.
Sison also warned of a mistrial, should the prosecution’s dropping of cases force the defense team to shorten its presentation of evidence.

“That prerogative to withdraw an accusation is not the power to suppress its rebuttal on the part of the respondent,” Sison said. “The authority to streamline or to achieve speed in a trial is not the authority to diminish due process or to altogether disregard fundamental rules of fairness and the desire to reach a verdict.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: Card surcharge ban used as ‘cover’ for larger price increases by Australian businesses, experts say
articles.summary: ‘Round-up’ pricing in items such as coffee suggests increases are exceeding the typical 1.5% surcharge fee

blocks.text: Businesses are using the recent ban on credit card surcharges as “cover” to pass along much larger price increases to customers, experts say, as cafes and restaurants struggle to cope with climbing costs and rising interest rates.

Credit card surcharges, typically worth about 1.5% of the transaction, were banned from 1 October, as part of a Reserve Bank-led reform aimed at improving transparency for customers and, ultimately, lowering bank fees.
Small Flat White, an online coffee price tracker, has reported that 17% of cafes have increased their prices since the start of the surcharge ban.
Of those who raised coffee prices, the average increase was 50c, or more than 10%, according to the survey of more than 1,500 cafes.
That is multiples of the typical 1.5% card surcharge fee.

Stephen Wu, an economist at investment bank UBS, said resilient consumer demand and a high inflation environment “may be allowing merchants to use the change as ‘cover’ to pass through broader cost pressures”.
“Following years of above-target inflation, consumers may be more accepting of price rises,” Wu said.
“Evidence of ‘round-up’ pricing in items such as coffee suggests pass-through could exceed the surcharge itself.”

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) has warned businesses that they must not “mislead consumers” by claiming a price rise is due to the surcharge ban when the increase also reflects other costs.
The ACCC has also said that businesses who try to avoid the ban by describing the surcharge as another type of fee or charge “may be engaging in misleading conduct”.
Wes Lambert, chief executive of the Australian Restaurant & Cafe Association, said business costs were rising rapidly while coffee prices in Australia were among the cheapest in the world.
Lambert said businesses change their prices for many reasons, and that the surcharge ban could have been the impetus for company owners to build up the courage to pass on costs to customers.
“Maybe this is the catalyst that has caused cafes and restaurateurs around the country to wake up.”
Lambert said restaurants were blaming the need for price hikes on rising produce costs, steep rents, and recent adjustments to junior pay rates and awards.
Many business owners are also affected by the four interest rate hikes in 2026, which have driven up repayments on variable-rate loans and equipment financing.
after newsletter promotion
“It should be no surprise that in a high inflation, high interest rate environment that businesses are going to raise their prices,” he said.
Despite being telegraphed well in advance, the surcharge ban has triggered a furious response from small business groups.
Jim Chalmers, the treasurer, was forced to intervene after the Australian Taxation Office announced it would no longer accept credit card payments for tax owing.
Chalmers said the government would provide additional funding to the ATO to cover the cost of the surcharge until the middle of next year.
Despite the furore, Morgan Campbell, the head of policy at consumer advocate group Choice, said: “I don’t think there’s any shock in the way this is working”.
“There was always an acknowledgement that some businesses would put up their prices. But consumers are better off knowing the price up front,” Campbell said.
He said it was too early for Choice to begin its own research on how the surcharge ban was working.
“Some of this will take some time to wash through the system,” he said, noting the RBA expected businesses to put more effort into finding lower cost bank providers.
If some businesses are putting up their prices by much more than the surcharge, Campbell suggested it was up to customers to decide how to respond.
