articles.title: Death threats and isolation - the cost of fighting sexual violence in Iraq
articles.summary: Women say they share stories of abuse to highlight the issue, despite social pressure and safety fears.

blocks.text: "Your camera is your weapon," says Sarah Jassim, who says the videos she posts help document evidence of harassment
BySally Nabil
BBC News ArabicReporting fromBaghdad
This story contains details of sexual violence which some readers may find upsetting

"Get out of the car!" screams a woman, accusing a driver of exposing himself and making obscene comments as she walked by. She is filming the scene in a busy Baghdad street on her phone, and the camera captures him resisting her attempts to open the door as she confronts him.

The video can be seen, with others like it, on the Instagram page of Iraqi women's rights activist Sarah Jassim. She posts them on behalf of women who complain about sexual abuse and harassment by Iraqi men and boys.
"Your camera is your weapon," she tells the BBC. "It's a way to document evidence in case a woman decides to sue her harasser, or at least it is a means to shame him."
One of the videos she posted led to the arrest of the alleged perpetrator, a policeman accused of harassing schoolgirls, she says.

blocks.caption: Image caption, A video posted by Jassim shows a woman shouting at a man she accuses of exposing himself, then trying to open his car door

blocks.text: Image source, Instagram
A video posted by Jassim shows a woman shouting at a man she accuses of exposing himself, then trying to open his car door
Jassim says posting the videos is risky both for herself and for the women concerned. We have spoken to numerous victims of sexual abuse in Iraq who say that society often blames the victim.

"I have received death threats, and I have also been threatened with acid attacks," Jassim says. "I have been accused of inciting public indecency, because I encourage women to speak in a society that expects us to be silent."
She now barely leaves home, for her own safety, and instead spends hours playing with her dog.
There is a need for stricter laws, she argues, including laws that explicitly criminalise "harassment" and "gender-based violence" - terms that are currently absent from the penal code.
"Recognising the problem is the best way to address it," she says. "We need protection, abusers have to be deterred."
'No-one will hear if I kill you'

Many Iraqi women have told the BBC they felt failed by the justice and police systems. Pursuing legal action against a harasser or a rapist is a long path in Iraq, with complicated procedures, and uncertain results, according to a number of activists and lawyers we have spoken to.
Violence against women and girls in Iraq is "widespread and under-reported," according to a report in May by a UN committee on discrimination against women, which called for stronger legislation.

Among dozens of recommendations, it urged the authorities to repeal "discriminatory" laws that exonerate rapists if they marry their victims, and allow reduced sentences for murder in cases where a perpetrator was carrying out a so-called "honour killing".
Amal - not her real name - has been battling in court for about five years. She accuses her ex-husband of repeatedly raping their daughter - who was under 18 at the time - at gunpoint.

She recalls her daughter's harrowing account of the incident, when she says the father walked into the girl's room and laid his weapon on her bed. She says he told her: "No-one will hear you if I kill you."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Amal accuses her ex-husband of repeatedly raping their daughter, who was under 18 at the time

blocks.text: Amal accuses her ex-husband of repeatedly raping their daughter, who was under 18 at the time

Sexual abuse has long been seen as a taboo subject in Iraq. I have been in touch with many survivors who say that they prefer to hush it up, because of a potential family backlash. Others told us they were afraid to go to the police, for fear of social stigma and possible harassment. But Amal was determined to seek justice and rushed to police to report the incident.
"She had lots of bruises around her wrists, as he held her hands tight. Whenever she tried to scream, he would cover her mouth with his hands," Amal says.
Amal showed me medical documents, including DNA evidence, which support her account.

A further demonstration of her ex-husband's cruelty came, Amal says, when she heard him tell a family member to "wash off our disgrace" if he was arrested. The expression is used in Iraq to refer to so-called honour killings - carried out in the belief that a woman has compromised a family's reputation.
Amal says she believes the father threatened to put an end to his daughter's life "so the medical report would not be released and the assault would not be proven".
She says her ex-husband is on the run and the court case remains open.

"I fought all alone," says Amal, bursting into tears as she says her ex-husband hired several lawyers but she could not afford legal representation, and her family turned a blind eye to the situation.
She no longer has any faith that a court ruling will come in her favour. "I just want him to stay out of my way forever," she says, with a sigh of despair.
Activist killed
Amal's daughter is more fortunate than some women who have experienced domestic sexual abuse in Iraq, as she has a safe place to live.
Many survivors have no independent income and nowhere to go. Iraq has very few shelters for abused women.

Those we know of were established by an organisation co-founded by Yanar Mohammed, an internationally recognised women's rights advocate. Last March she was murdered outside her house in Baghdad by armed men. The perpetrators are still unknown.

Experts working for the UN Human Rights Council wrote in April that Mohammed had been receiving death threats and online abuse for years, which were "believed to come from extremist religious militia".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Hanaa Edwar (left) shared a photo of her with Yanar Mohammed, taken, she recalls, just two days before the activist was killed

blocks.text: Image source, Supplied by Hanaa Edwar
Hanaa Edwar (left) shared a photo of her with Yanar Mohammed, taken, she recalls, just two days before the activist was killed
Activists repeatedly told us that targeted attacks on their colleagues have been on the rise in recent years.
Hanaa Edwar, another prominent women's rights activist, says she saw Mohammed just two days before she was killed. She says she has also been threatened.
"There are no laws, no protection, and no justice for women in Iraq," she tells me.

"The problem in Iraq is not that women stay silent. It is that when they speak, very little in the system is built to listen, Mustafa Saadoon, head of the Iraqi Observatory for Human Rights, tells the BBC.
"A woman who reports sexual violence has to get past her family first, then a police station, then a court, and at every one of those doors someone is likely to tell her to settle it quietly."
'Followed in a car'
Among the Iraqi women who say they feel failed by the system is Samira - not her real name.
She tells the BBC that walking in the street puts her on the edge, after repeated harassments.
Once, she says a man "was watching a porn movie on his phone and put it in my face" on public transport.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Samira says she has been harassed on public transport and followed by a man in a car on her way to work

blocks.text: Samira says she has been harassed on public transport and followed by a man in a car on her way to work

In another incident in Baghdad, she says a man once followed her in his car for over 10 minutes. "It was extremely upsetting... I saw a police car. I went over and told them what had happened. They said they didn't have the authority to do anything."

Although her mother is loving and supportive, Samira does not share any stories of sexual harassment with her. "If I tell my family, they will immediately ask me not to leave home in order to stay safe," she says.

She has lost faith in state institutions: "Many men, including police officers, find nothing wrong with sexual harassment. If you are not a harasser, you are not a man, this is how they see it," she adds.
Many women I spoke to in Iraq even accused police of sexual harassment. I put the accusation to Muqdad Miri, a spokesman for Iraq's interior ministry.
"Cases of harassment involving police personnel happen but they are very few. They get a very harsh punishment, up to 10 years in prison and are dismissed," says Miri.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Interior Ministry spokesman Muqdad Miri says some sexual violence is not reported because of "society, customs and traditions"

blocks.text: Interior Ministry spokesman Muqdad Miri says some sexual violence is not reported because of "society, customs and traditions"

I put it to him that some women were now documenting harassment on social media because they were afraid to report it to police. He said they were posting on social media because it was easier than filing an official report, and because doing so has become a common way to draw attention to a cause.
I also put to him Samira's experience, in which she says an officer told her that he had no authority to stop harassment. Miri said Samira could have filed a complaint against this officer.

There are no reliable statistics for sexual violence or harassment in Iraq. Miri told me that police have received about 300 reports of sexual violence since the beginning of the year. However, he accepts that the real number of cases is higher: "Many cases never reach the police because of society, customs and traditions."

The stories of the women the BBC spoke to draw a picture of their battle not just against sexual violence itself, but against deeply entrenched mentalities and social beliefs that allow it to persist.

Edwar has been advocating for women's causes for over 50 years and her assessment is gloomy: "Twenty-three years after Saddam Hussein's regime was brought down, it seems we are going backwards regarding women's rights."
But both she and Jassim say they refuse to give up: "If all of us are going to get scared, no-one will change anything," says Sarah.
Additional reporting by Salma Khattab

If you have been affected by issues involving sexual abuse and violence, you could speak to a health professional or an organisation that offers support. Details of organisations offering advice and support for people in the UK are available from BBC Action Line.

articles.title: Where the US midterm elections will be won and lost
articles.summary: An in-depth look at the key polling, races and issues ahead of an election that will define Trump’s final two years as president.

blocks.text: ByMike Hills
Visual Journalism team
Americans head to the polls on 3 November to decide how the rest of Donald Trump's presidency will play out.

Thousands of races are taking place across the US, at different levels of government. But the main event for voters will be electing members of the House of Representatives and the Senate, the two chambers that make up Congress.
Both of them are currently controlled by the Republicans, the president's party. The success or failure of Trump's final two years in office could rest on the outcome.
Here's our visual guide to where the battle for power will be won and lost - from approval ratings, to key races and issues and the huge amount of money being spent.
Midterms come at bad time for Trump
One of the reasons the opposition Democrats have a chance to take back Congress is the president's low approval rating, which is a good indicator for how well his party could perform.
He began his second term as president with an approval rating of just over 50%, according to polling resource website Silver Bulletin, but it quickly fell into the 40s.

It was hovering around 42% when Trump decided to launch air strikes with Israel against Iran at the end of February this year but it fell below 40% shortly afterwards. It is currently sitting at about 37%.

Eight years ago, Trump's approval rating was significantly higher at this point in his first term, at 43%. Joe Biden's at the same point in his term was at 40%. In both cases, the sitting president lost control of the House in the midterms but kept hold of the Senate.

But Trump's poor ratings help explain why Democrats are hopeful of winning both chambers of Congress and why they are setting their sights on states that Republicans have won consistently in recent years.
The battle for the House

The current Republican majority in the House of Representatives, the lower chamber, is as thin as it gets - they have 218 representatives, which is the exact number needed to have control, plus one independent who votes with them.
Members of the House serve a two-year term so all 435 seats are up for election in November.
But most districts are not considered competitive because the party that holds them has such solid support that there is only one likely winner.
The Cook Political Report, which analyses campaigns and elections, suggests that just 21 districts are "toss-ups" that could be won by either party.

Of those 21 toss-ups, 15 are currently held by Republicans and six by Democrats. If the Democrats win five of those on top of 28 districts classed as likely or leaning Democratic, they will win the House.

Historically, the midterms see a high number of seats changing hands in the House, usually in a protest against the White House. The average number lost by the president's party is 27, according to data, external going back to 1934. Of those 23 elections, the president's party has only made gains in three.
The battle for the Senate
The Republicans have a slightly stronger hold on the Senate. They hold 53 of the 100 seats while the Democrats have 45 and two independents who also vote with them.
Members of the Senate serve six-year terms so roughly a third are up for election every two years.
Thirty-five seats are up for grabs in November but analysis by the Cook Political Report suggests that only seven of them are toss-ups that could go either way.

Of those toss-ups, six are currently held by Republicans and one by Democrats. The Democrats would need to win four of those seats, plus the four classed as likely or leaning Democratic, to hit 51 and take control of the Senate.
But winning a majority is no easy task for the Democrats.

They need to keep hold of their seat in Michigan, where polls suggest the race is tighter than Democrats would like between Abdul El-Sayed, a left-wing political outsider, and his Republican rival Mike Rogers, a Trump ally and former FBI agent.
And they would also need to pick up seats in states that Trump won by double-digits in 2024, including Alaska, Iowa and Ohio.

But polls suggest they have a chance, even in Texas where former teacher James Talarico could become the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in the state since 1988 if he defeats Ken Paxton, the current state attorney general and close Trump ally.

items: What would Democratic control of Congress mean for Trump?
Anthony Zurcher: The Republican candidates walking a Trump tightrope

blocks.text: What are the key issues for voters?
Trump pledged to "end inflation and make America affordable again" in his 2024 election campaign but the cost of living crisis is proving to be the key issue for voters.

The president proudly declared that gas was "now below $2.30 [£1.74] a gallon in most states" in his State of the Union address on 24 February. But the war with Iran began four days later, disrupting Middle Eastern energy supplies and causing gas to hit $4 (£3.03) in the US.

The war became increasingly unpopular as its consequences reverberated around the world and ultimately hit American consumers in the pocket. One poll carried out in August found 63% of respondents disapproved of Trump's handling of the situation.
Other issues that voters say are important to them include healthcare and immigration.
Trump has recently touted his policies around immigration as a big success, citing significantly lower border-crossing figures than in recent years.
Many Democratic candidates are focusing on the high costs of US health insurance and the impact of Trump's legislation on access to the healthcare system.

items: Trump wants to reduce the cost of fuel as the midterms loom - will it work?

blocks.text: Can Trump defy political gravity?
Most signs point towards a successful midterms for the Democrats, but it wouldn't be the first time that Trump and his party have outperformed polls if they do win more seats than expected.
One of the few things in their favour is their huge financial advantage.
At the end of August, the Republican National Committee and its allied groups had more than $600m (£455m) cash on hand, while the Democrats had just under $400m (£303m).
On top of that, the Republicans also had more than $400m held by Trump's MAGA Inc group, the main fundraising and spending arm of the "Make America Great Again" political movement.
The Republicans are using that financial advantage to buy advertising.

More than $1bn worth of political ads were broadcast to US voters in September, according to research firm AdImpact, external. Republicans spent $200m more than the Democrats and outspent them in nearly all of the Senate races classed as toss-ups.
Trump will be hoping this late messaging blitz can help convince Republicans to get out and vote in November, boosting turnout and limiting the damage done to him and his party.

Whatever the result, attention will quickly turn to the next presidential election in 2028. Trump's unpopularity has dominated the midterms, but with him constitutionally unable to run for a third term the focus will shift to what the Democrats stand for, not just what they stand against.

articles.title: Russia's offensive ability is broken, Kyiv's former top general tells BBC
articles.summary: In his first interview since being forced from his post, Gen Syrskyi speaks about Ukraine's future in the war.

blocks.text: Ukraine has stabilised the front line and "broken Russia's ability to advance" by killing so many of its men, Ukraine's former commander-in-chief has claimed in an interview with the BBC.
Gen Oleksandr Syrskyi made the comments in an exclusive interview, his first since he was dramatically forced from his post in the summer.
He addressed his sacking, disagreeing with his critics who declared him too "old school" to command Ukraine's new, technologically advanced forces.

He also pushed back against allegations made by soldiers who previously served under him, who told the BBC they were ordered to remain at their positions even when they were almost surrounded by Russians, leading to high losses.
Syrskyi said that Moscow's overall losses in the war were six times higher than Ukraine's. "If you count only dead, then it's up to 11 times," he added.

Neither Russia nor Ukraine officially release the numbers of their dead. Ukraine's military says it inflicted record losses this year on Russian soldiers in September, although that cannot be verified.

UK intelligence chiefs estimate Russia has lost around half a million men killed in Ukraine since launching its full-scale invasion in 2022. The US-based Center for Strategic and International Studies meanwhile believes, external Ukraine has lost up to 150,000 troops killed by June 2026.

He says this difference in death toll – as well as technological advances, and a strategy of attacking weak points in Russia's lines while containing their advances in other parts – accounts for the current stalemate at the front.
In the first six months of 2026, Russia managed overall to seize 61 sq km, the general said. "It's an indication that the front line has been stabilised."
The Institute for Study of War (ISW) has also confirmed this trend. One of its recent reports, external says that in September 2026, Moscow lost more territory than it took.

Syrskyi was appointed Ukraine's commander-in-chief in 2024. He had previously won praise for defending Kyiv at the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, and for leading the successful counteroffensive east of Kharkiv in the autumn of that year.
But President Volodymyr Zelensky fired Syrskyi this summer, amid a major disagreement with then-defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov.
Fedorov had said that instead of adapting to the realities of the changing war, the army under Syrskyi had blocked his initiatives.

Zelensky initially fired Fedorov, as tensions burst into the open between the two men. But mass street protests then forced the president to also fire Syrskyi, replacing him with Maj Gen Mykhailo Drapatyi, 43.
Syrskyi told the BBC that he had "disagreements" with Fedorov because the latter "didn't take into consideration the interests of the army" when procuring weapons and supplies.

Fedorov had created an "imbalance" in supplies, Syrskyi said. He had prioritised drones while overlooking key front-line kit such as unmanned ground vehicles, pick-up trucks and motorbikes. Even with drones, Syrskyi said, there were shortages as the army got only half of what they needed.

Fedorov was a popular young minister who was known for his digital and technological initiatives. Many contrasted him with Syrskyi, who critics thought was not fit to lead the new technological arms race with Russia.

But Syrskyi disagrees with such criticism. It was during his time the use of drones reached this new, unprecedented level, including deep strikes more than 2,000km (1,200 miles) behind enemy lines, he said. Ukraine was the first country to create the Unmanned Systems Forces as a separate branch of armed forces, under his command: now, he said, drones account for 80% of Russia's losses.
Under his military leadership, however, Ukrainian troops undertook chaotic withdrawals from the eastern cities of Avdiivka and Vuhledar, and from around Pokrovsk.

Soldiers who spoke to the BBC in the past complained that they were ordered to remain at their positions at any costs. By the time they were told to pull back, it was often too late as they were almost surrounded by Russian troops.
Syrskyi does not deny that such situations occur on the front line. But he told the BBC that Ukraine was fighting against a far more powerful army.

In 2025, the ratio of jets and bombs was 18 to one in Moscow's favour, he said. In the same year, Russia had two-and-a-half times more artillery pieces and shells than Ukraine. And with four million militarily trained men who they can mobilise, Russian forces can create chances to push through, he argued.

One of Syrskyi's most famous operations was an incursion into Russia's Kursk region that started in August 2024. It ended with a dramatic retreat the following spring, which some soldiers described as "catastrophic". Syrskyi, however, insisted that the Kursk operation was "a necessity".
"In the summer 2024, Russian forces were pushing along all main directions on the front line with up to six times more troops than we had," he explained.
The Kursk incursion disrupted Russia's offensive and forced Moscow to redirect troops, giving Ukraine a respite and a chance for its stretched brigades in the east and south to recover, Syrskyi said.

He also had strong words for European allies who doubt that Russia may have territorial ambitions beyond Ukraine. He advised European partners to start preparing for the war now and "drop all illusions that [it] will not come".

He also said he believed Ukraine's war was going to become even more technological. There will be more robots, automated systems and artificial intelligence (AI). "Even ordinary weapons now get an AI-based control system to enhance their capabilities," he said.
Such technologies can give a new life to conventional weapons like tanks. Both Russia and Ukraine were now racing to develop "active systems of defence" to protect armoured vehicles, Syrskyi said.
But he insisted that "the human role will remain definitive [on the battlefield] because [people] will need to control those systems".

articles.title: DENR deploys early warning systems to monitor El Niño impact
articles.summary: The Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) on Tuesday said it has deployed early warning systems in several regions to monitor the potential effects of a strong El Niño and help…

blocks.text: Published October 13, 2026 12:58pm

The Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) on Tuesday said it has deployed early warning systems in several regions to monitor the potential effects of a strong El Niño and help authorities respond before severe environmental damage occurs.

In a statement, DENR Secretary Juan Miguel Cuna said the systems use automated weather stations (AWS), satellite-based heat stress monitoring and Geographic Information System (GIS)-based risk modeling to track environmental conditions and identify areas at risk.

"By deploying satellite-based heat stress tracking for coral reefs in Aurora, processing Automated Weather Station data to map fire hazards in the Agusan Marsh, and running Red Flag alert systems in Region 1, the DENR is replacing reactive measures with precision early warning," he said.
In the Ilocos Region, the DENR has established a Red Flag Alert system to detect potential wildland fires and enable authorities to respond early.
In Central Luzon, authorities are monitoring sea surface temperatures and issuing coral bleaching alerts in Aurora province to track threats to marine ecosystems.
In the Caraga Region, data from automated weather stations are being used to monitor localized heat indices, rainfall deficits and changes in water levels in the Agusan Marsh.
Similar monitoring systems are being used in the Bicol Region to identify drying creeks, dry forests and shallow reefs in Catanduanes and Masbate.

"We are equipping our field teams and local chief executives with real-time environmental intelligence to safeguard our forests, coral reefs, water resources, and coastal communities before severe damage occurs," Cuna said.
State weather bureau PAGASA earlier warned that the upcoming El Niño could persist until March or even June, potentially bringing below-normal rainfall to several parts of the country.

Around 40 provinces are expected to experience reduced rainfall, with some areas potentially facing dry spells or drought. The number of affected provinces could double by January, according to PAGASA.
Aside from reduced rainfall, the potentially strong El Niño could bring higher temperatures, with PAGASA warning that air temperatures could reach 38.7 degrees Celsius by March 2027.
The heat index, which factors in humidity, could climb to between 45 and 52 degrees Celsius.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Hurricane Simon and Tropical Storm Rachel kill five people on Mexico’s Pacific coast
articles.summary:
Security forces use helicopters to rescue dozens of people as the two storms damage infrastructure and cause flash flooding

At least five people have died after Hurricane Simon and Tropical…

blocks.text: At least five people have died after Hurricane Simon and Tropical Storm Rachel pummelled Mexico’s Pacific coast, causing flooding that downed trees and electricity poles, blocked roads and inundated homes.
Simon claimed the life of a 71-year-old man who died when a wall collapsed in Chilpancingo in the southern state of Guerrero, governor Evelyn Salgado said at a press conference.
The storm also damaged infrastructure and homes in the state’s coastal towns, including the major seaport of Acapulco, she said.

Tropical Storm Rachel is blamed for the deaths of four members of one family, including two children, whose bodies were found on the outskirts of the city of Ensenada in Baja California, the state’s prosecutor’s office reported.

Five more people remained missing, while security forces used helicopters to rescue 32 people, prosecutors said. Baja governor Marina del Pilar said officials were helping more than 50 people in temporary shelters.

blocks.caption: Hurricane Simon has flooded streets in towns along Mexico’s Pacific coast. Photograph: Christian Ruano/Reuters

blocks.text: Simon did not make landfall and, after weakening to category two on the five-point Saffir-Simpson scale, was moving away from the coast, authorities said. A rain alert remained in place.
The National Hurricane Center in Miami said heavy rainfall associated with Simon in west-central Mexico over the next few days might still produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides.

Officials warned waves of up to five metres high were still expected in some coastal areas. Flooding and landslides had already hit communities close to rivers and streams in the states of Michoacan and Colima.

blocks.caption: A man walks past a boarded-up business in Puerto Vallarta bearing the message ‘Simon, be brief, be peaceful’. Photograph: Christian Ruano/Reuters

blocks.text: The El Niño phenomenon, characterised by rising water temperatures in the Pacific, is fuelling a more intense hurricanes this season in the region.

Meteorologists say the 2026-27 El Niño, which causes global changes in winds and rainfall as well as erratic weather conditions, is certain to be the biggest ever recorded. Scientists now also think human-caused global heating is making El Niños more intense.
With Agence France-Presse and Associated Press

articles.title: 27 Chinese vessels monitored in West Philippine Sea in past 6 days
articles.summary: The Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) on Tuesday said that there were at least 27 Chinese vessels monitored across several West Philippine Sea (WPS) features from October 6 to October 12.

blocks.text: Published October 13, 2026 12:11pm
At least 27 Chinese vessels were monitored in parts of the West Philippine Sea (WPS) from October 6 to October 12, according to the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP).

According to spokesperson for the WPS Rear Admiral Roy Vincent Trinidad, their weekly monitoring of Chinese vessels revealed a mix of boats belonging to the Chinese Coast Guard (CCGV) and People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) across the flashpoint waters.
In Ayungin Shoal, there were five CCG and four PLAN vessels, while in Bajo de Masinloc, there were eight CCG and four PLAN boats roaming around.
Meanwhile, Escoda Shoal had one PLAN boat in its waters, while the Pag-asa Islands had three CCG boats and two PLAN vessels.

The West Philippine Sea refers to the maritime areas on the western side of the Philippine archipelago, including the Luzon Sea and the waters around, within, and adjacent to the Kalayaan Island Group and Bajo de Masinloc.
In 2016, the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague ruled in favor of the Philippines over China's claims in the South China Sea, saying that it had "no legal basis."
China has refused to recognize the decision. —VAL, GMA News

blocks.text: The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.
On this page, we bring you the latest updates, analyses, videos, and photos as the trial of the Vice President unfolds.

articles.title: ‘Universal appeal’: Celebrity Traitors producer reveals secrets to its success
articles.summary:
Over 10m people have tuned in for episodes of new season of BBC hit as mass TV audiences become increasingly rare

For the celebrities chosen as traitors in the BBC’s juggernaut reality show,…

blocks.text: For the celebrities chosen as traitors in the BBC’s juggernaut reality show, the task is simple – kill off fellow contestants without getting caught.

Yet with the new series of Celebrity Traitors once again attracting huge audiences, its UK producers are delighting in one of the show’s more wholesome qualities – its popularity is staving off the death of television’s ability to unite the nation.

“It’s very difficult to get people to watch programmes, and there is a huge joy coming up with something that a very large amount of people watch,” Stephen Lambert, head of the Celebrity Traitors producer Studio Lambert, told the Radio Times.
“The show has universal appeal … It has established itself as ‘appointment-to-view TV’,” he added.
Despite its appeal, however, Lambert may still struggle to attract the man he revealed to be his dream contestant: Tom Cruise.

More than 10 million people have tuned in to watch some episodes, well in excess of half the viewers watching TV during the show’s time slot. It is also pulling younger viewers away from other devices and on to the sofa, with 1.6 million people aged between 16 and 34 tuning in for this series’ premiere.

blocks.caption: ‘We get that wonderful extra sneaky peak behind the facade of celebrity’. Photograph: Euan Cherry/BBC/Studio Lambert

blocks.text: In doing so, it has bucked a long-running trend that has seen mass TV audiences become increasingly rare. The arrival of streamers, digital platforms and smartphones have ensured such viewing figures have become the preserve of the Olympics, England World Cup matches and the odd breakthrough hit.

The success of The Traitors has inevitably spawned similar formats based on deceit and questionable detective skills, as producers attempt to replicate its allure. Lambert said that whether it was the celebrity edition or the regular series of The Traitors, the secret to its success came down to two words: “Dramatic irony.”
“It’s the engine of The Traitors,” he said. “It’s about the pleasure that we know more than the protagonists – we know who is lying. And it’s fun to try and watch people work out who the liars are.”

When it comes to the celebrity edition, he said viewers delighted in seeing famous faces uncomfortable as they “have so little control” over events. “It’s such an immersive game that people get caught up in it, and show how they really are,” he said.

Lambert confirmed that casting for Celebrity Traitors was not difficult because its popularity meant that the names who agreed to go into the traitors’ castle were also fans. Producers have previously noted the show does not face the usual challenges of attracting names to formats that ask them to eat bugs or train for weeks on end.

Not only would Cruise be a tough man to pin down, Lambert also said securing sports stars continues to be a perennial problem for casting directors. Sports men and women not only have gruelling schedules, but their media activities are guarded closely by personal agents and their clubs.
When asked about dream contestants, Lambert said: “Tom Cruise, maybe? And we would like to have a big sports star. But if they are an active one, they have commitments.”

Shows similar in style to The Traitors have been attempted, such as Channel 4’s The Inheritance or ITV’s The Neighbourhood, though both networks and production companies usually bridle at any suggestion that their latest reality format amounts to their new spin on The Traitors.
Even the most experienced TV insiders freely admit that productions that were fun to make and have found audiences overseas come with no guarantee of success.

“If anyone tells you what the secret is, they are not in full command of reality,” said Jonathan Glazier, a former head of BBC light entertainment. “Don’t you think if we knew, every show would be a Traitors?

“It’s just a joy to sit back and marvel at the duplicity and wonder why the faithful can’t see the traitors for who they are! That said, the cliffhangers are so brilliantly executed … and with the celeb version we get that wonderful extra sneaky peak behind the facade of celebrity.
“It’s a joy to watch and any team that tries to imitate that kind of simplistic perfection is going to come a cropper.”

articles.title: Women ‘more likely to be told autoimmune conditions are psychological’
articles.summary:
Cambridge University study suggests stark gender divide in misdiagnosis, with women also waiting longer for treatment

Women with autoimmune conditions are up to 74% more likely than men to…

blocks.text: Women with autoimmune conditions are up to 74% more likely than men to be told their symptoms are psychological or psychosomatic, and face much longer waits for a diagnosis and treatment, a study suggests.
Hundreds of millions of people – about one in 10 globally – are affected by autoimmune conditions, which can cause a range of health issues including fatigue, muscle pain and rashes.
But research by the University of Cambridge and University of East Anglia suggests a stark gender divide when it comes to how signs of the conditions are handled by doctors.

Women are more likely to have their conditions wrongly attributed to psychiatric causes, more likely to have symptoms misdiagnosed as psychosomatic, and more likely to experience delays in getting a diagnosis, according to the study.
The lead author, Melanie Sloan, said: “The damage caused to women by these types of misdiagnosis can be very long lasting in terms of trusting doctors and their own self-esteem.”

Sloan, a researcher in the department of public health and primary care at Cambridge and UEA, said some women were forced to wait years before finally getting a diagnosis, causing long delays to treatment for their condition.
The study, published in the Lancet eClinicalMedicine journal, included more than 6,600 people with autoimmune conditions. Most were female and from the UK.

Patients listed their main condition, with almost a quarter of the women having autoimmune thyroid disease, which can cause the gland to become underactive – known as Hashimoto’s disease – or overactive, known as Graves’ disease. Hashimoto’s disease can cause weight gain, hair loss, fatigue and joint pain, while the symptoms of Graves’ disease include bulging eyes, palpitations and weight loss.
One in seven women in the study had systemic lupus, which can cause tiredness, rashes and muscle pain.
Among male patients, rheumatoid arthritis, vasculitis and antiphospholipid syndrome (APS), also known as “sticky blood” syndrome, were the most common conditions.

blocks.caption: Women were almost 46% more likely to report having received a psychiatric misdiagnosis, and nearly 74% more likely to have a psychosomatic misdiagnosis.  Photograph: MBI/Alamy

blocks.text: Researchers found 43% of women reported being told their condition was down to a psychiatric cause compared with a third of men (33%).
A third (34%) of women also reported having symptoms misdiagnosed as psychosomatic – meaning they were triggered or worsened by stress or anxiety – compared with 22% of men.

Overall, after accounting for factors including age, disease group, continent and household finances, researchers said women were 46% more likely to report having received a psychiatric misdiagnosis, and 74% more likely to report a psychosomatic misdiagnosis than men.

Researchers also found women reported much longer periods between the onset of symptoms and receiving a diagnosis, as well as more healthcare consultations. Among men, the most frequently reported time to diagnosis was less than three months. Among women, it was one to two years.
Autoimmune conditions, which happen when the immune system attacks the body by mistake, can be complex to diagnose as they often present with symptoms common in the wider population.
after newsletter promotion
The study team said “broader diagnostic challenges affect both sexes” but “females may face additional disadvantages”.
They added: “Historical biases in medicine may persist, including positioning females as less credible and emotional reporters of symptoms than males.”
Sloan said the findings “highlight that psychological or mental health explanations can be given too soon”.
She added: “This is true for both sexes, but our study suggests that females may be particularly vulnerable to these types of misdiagnoses.
“It is really important that symptoms are not automatically assumed to be psychological and for doctors to just say, ‘I believe you,’ to patients with symptoms that the doctors cannot see.”

Shaista Tayabali, a patient affected by an autoimmune condition who was part of the research team and a co-author of the study, said: “The differences between the sexes in misdiagnoses for people with autoimmune diseases is stark.
“The fact that females reported higher rates of psychiatric and psychosomatic misdiagnoses than males … suggests that historical gender biases remain a challenging aspect of the diagnostic journey.
“Although labels such as hysteria are outdated, and fortunately rarely used nowadays, as women we still often have a harder time having our symptoms believed and therefore addressed accurately.”

articles.title: ASEAN to discuss tackling transboundary haze ahead of November summit
articles.summary: Southeast Asian foreign ministers will during a meeting next month seek to tackle the transboundary haze blanketing parts of the region, ASEAN chair the Philippines said on Tuesday.

blocks.text: Published October 13, 2026 11:45am
A drone view shows St. Joseph's Cathedral shrouded in haze from wildfires, in Pontianak, West Kalimantan province, Indonesia, September 15, 2026. REUTERS/Ajeng Dinar Ulfiana/File

MANILA/KUALA LUMPUR - Southeast Asian foreign ministers will during a meeting next month seek to tackle the transboundary haze blanketing parts of the region, ASEAN chair the Philippines said on Tuesday.

Forest and land fires that have raged for months in Indonesia have in recent weeks caused thick haze in Singapore and in Malaysia, which closed schools in several states last week after air pollution hit unhealthy levels.
The wildfires, mainly on the islands of Sumatra and Borneo, are Indonesia's most intense in 11 years.

"It's in the agenda," Philippine Department of Foreign Affairs spokesperson on ASEAN Dominic Xavier Imperial said on Tuesday, referring to the preparatory foreign ministers' meetings in November ahead of the summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations
Malaysian Foreign Minister Mohamad Hasan on Monday said he would raise the haze issue with ASEAN, noting that the bloc's existing mechanisms to deal with natural disasters did not include haze.
Malaysia has previously offered assistance to Indonesia to combat fires.

Firefighting attempts in many areas were complicated by poor visibility, accessibility issues and a lack of suitable conditions for cloud seeding, Mohamad said, citing discussions with his Indonesian counterpart. —Reuters

articles.title: Sara Duterte denies owning lot NBI tied to her asset declarations
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte has denied owning a lot that the National Bureau of Investigation claims to be one of the properties in her statement of assets, liabilities and net worth (SALN), and…

blocks.text: October 13, 2026 | 11:45am
Images show footage of properties linked to the Vice President and Davao City Rep. Paolo Duterte during a presentation by the National Bureau of Investigation.
NBI images

MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte has denied owning a lot that the National Bureau of Investigation claims to be one of the properties in her statement of assets, liabilities and net worth (SALN), and accused the bureau of misleading the public.

The denial came a day after NBI Director Melvin Matibag presented the agency’s initial findings on alleged discrepancies in the declared property values of Duterte and her brother Rep. Paolo Duterte (Davao City, 1st District), based on on-the-ground inspections by NBI agents in Davao City.

Duterte’s SALN declarations are also currently at issue in the Senate impeachment trial, where the court has been shown stacks of financial and corporate records that prosecutors claim is proof of her unexplained, undeclared and disproportionate wealth.

“The lot in the photo that he said is in my Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth is not mine,” Duterte said in a statement in Filipino. She did not identify the specific property she was alluding to.
Duterte said it was alarming that the NBI was using its operations “for activities with no clear benefit to the public.”

She said such “deception of the public” was the reason the NBI was removed from the list of witnesses the prosecution would present in the impeachment proceedings. She cited what she described as allegations that the bureau had again put forward questionable evidence, as with the affidavit of dismissed police officer Rodulfo Gracioso Jr.
The prosecution has confirmed that it would be presenting no more witnesses after forensic financial analyst Alexander Cabrera, who is the prosecution's last witness for its case-in-chief.

Citing a need to speed up proceedings, prosecutors have trimmed their witness list several times, including forgoing 15 of 27 witnesses originally planned for the confidential funds charge, and last week dropped the Article III or bribery charge.
NBI claims Duterte property worth up to P60 million

At a briefing on Monday, October 12, Matibag claimed a property in Catigan, Davao City, declared as agricultural land worth P890,000, was estimated at P50 million to P60 million after it was inspected.
Matibag said the Duterte family has 121 properties in Davao City and Davao del Norte, 24 of which belong to the vice president and are under investigation.
About 14 properties had been identified from the vice president's SALNs for field inspection, according to the NBI.

The probe, Matibag said, follows a pattern the bureau established from Gracioso’s affidavit, in which money was allegedly put into land banking, as he said was the practice with former House Speaker Lord Allan Velasco.
Matibag said the NBI would submit initial findings to the Ombudsman and the Department of Justice, possibly within the week, and denied the investigation was politically motivated.

Gracioso, whom the national police confirmed served on Velasco’s security detail, has alleged that he delivered more than P2 billion in cash to Duterte in more than 20 transactions, ranging from P20 million to P50 million each. He also claimed deliveries to Paolo Duterte and former President Rodrigo Duterte between 2018 and 2020.
Duterte has denied knowing Gracioso or receiving money from him.

articles.title: Chel Diokno: Evidence vs. Sara Duterte based on independent, verifiable facts
articles.summary: House prosecutor and Akbayan party-list Rep. Chel Diokno on Monday said the prosecution's evidence against Vice President Sara Duterte was based on independent and verifiable facts, rejecting claims…

blocks.text: Published October 13, 2026 11:37am

House prosecutor and Akbayan party-list Rep. Chel Diokno on Monday said the prosecution's evidence against Vice President Sara Duterte was based on independent and verifiable facts, rejecting claims that the allegations against her were fabricated.

Diokno made the statement when Senator Lito Lapid asked what the public should make of the extensive evidence presented by the prosecution, including Duterte's Statements of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALNs), bank transactions and deposits, insurance policies, business interests and income records involving her and her husband.

“Madali po kasi ang magpanggap ang isang official na simpleng tao lang siya, kumakain lang sa carinderia, malinis, wala naman na tinatago sa SALN. Pero pag titignan po sa isyu ng Article 2 on unexplained wealth, doon po tayo magkakaalaman,” Diokno said.

(It is easy for a public official to pretend to be an ordinary person who eats at carinderias, has nothing to hide and has a clean SALN. But when we examine Article II on unexplained wealth, that is when the truth will come out.)
Diokno stressed that the prosecution's case did not rely solely on witness testimonies but was also supported by financial documents obtained from independent sources.

“Because we are not just looking at the witnesses here. We are looking at the documents and numbers. Attorney Cabrera looked at bank records from the Anti-Money Laundering Council, Bureau of Internal Revenue, Securities and Exchange Commission," Diokno said.
"And the bank documents were submitted by the banks to the Senate court, not the prosecution. That is why we can say that these are independent facts verifiable by everybody,” he added.
He was referring to the testimony of lawyer and accountant Alex Cabrera, who conducted a forensic examination of the financial records of Duterte and her husband, lawyer Manases Carpio.

Cabrera concluded that based on a "conservative" assessment, the couple had at least P817 million in alleged unexplained wealth, with the amount potentially reaching P1.5 billion due to assets purportedly left undeclared in their joint SALNs.

Earlier on Monday, October 12, the 38th day of her impeachment trial, Duterte claimed during a press conference that the evidence against her had been fabricated and that the impeachment case was falling apart.

Meanwhile, House prosecutor and Manila Rep. Joel Chua challenged Duterte's defense team to seek the dismissal of the impeachment charges through a demurrer to evidence if it believed the prosecution had failed to establish its case.

“If they believe that our evidence is weak and we haven’t proven anything, then I challenge them to file demurrer to evidence. That is being done in a regular court. They can file that so this will be resolved earlier,” Chua said in an interview on Super Radyo dzBB.

A demurrer to evidence is a legal remedy through which an accused may seek the dismissal of a case after the prosecution rests, arguing that the evidence presented is insufficient to sustain a conviction.
Chua maintained that the prosecution's allegations were supported by Duterte's own declarations, including information she disclosed or allegedly failed to disclose in her SALNs.

“Our Constitution clearly states that the Vice President, President and Cabinet Secretaries are not allowed to have business interest, either directly or indirectly. But she declared business interests in her SALN [while she was] already the Vice President,” Chua said.
He was referring to GenCorp Foods Corporation, which Duterte listed among her business interests.
“Maliwanag na po yun na paglabag, not just an ordinary law, but the Constitution at that,” Chua added.
(That is clearly a violation, not just of an ordinary law but of the Constitution itself.)— MCG, GMA News
Follow GMA News Online on Facebook for real-time news and developments in the Philippines and around the world.

articles.title: US: Man killed in Six Flags roller coaster incident
articles.summary: Local media showed passengers being evacuated from the Goliath coaster, which reaches a maximum height of 61 meters and speeds of up to 113 km/h.

image.caption: People were seein being evacuated from the Goliath roller coasterImage: Emilie Megnien/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: One person has died and several others were injured in an incident on Monday involving a roller coaster at a Six Flags theme park in the United States.
The incident occurred at Six Flags Over Georgia, about 15 miles (24 kilometers) northwest of Atlanta.
Witnesses told local media outlets that they saw a man fall from the ride.
"I cannot imagine the horror the patrons and employees witnessed today, and my heart aches for the family who lost a loved one," said Lisa Cupid, chair of the Cobb County Board of Commissioners.
Six Flags temporary closes 9 roller coasters
Following the incident in Georgia, Six Flags temporarily closed nine roller coasters across six amusement parks.
According to a park spokesperson, similar attractions were closed across their parks "out of an abundance of caution" following the incident at Six Flags Over Georgia.

This comes less than two weeks after Six Flags Magic Mountain in Southern California announced it would retire its famous X2 roller coaster amid lawsuits alleging the ride caused serious brain injuries.
What do we know about the roller coaster?
Althought the park did not identify the ride involved in Monday's incident, local media showed passengers being evacuated from the Goliath coaster.
Built in 2006, Goliath can reach speeds of 113 km/h (70 mph) and a maximum height of 61 meters (200 feet).
According to the theme park's website, riders "navigate through razor-sharp turns and soar over colossal hills."
Monday's death would be at least the seventh to occur at the Georgia theme park, according to the Doan Law Firm, which focuses on amusement park accidents.
That includes one 2006 incident when a man had a likely heart attack while riding the same roller coaster, Goliath.

articles.title: Argentina temporarily closes Iguazu Falls after El Niño-fuelled surge in water levels
articles.summary:
National park officials took the precautionary measure to limit tourist access after heavy rain caused the Iguazu River to flow at six times the normal rate

Heavy rainfall fuelled by a

blocks.text: Heavy rainfall fuelled by a supersized El Niño weather pattern briefly forced Argentinian authorities to close tourist access to the famed Iguazu Falls, amid fears that rapidly rising water levels would cause the river to burst its banks.
National park officials took the precautionary measure on Monday when the Iguazu River’s flow exceeded 12,000 cubic metres per second – more than six times its average rate.
It later said the area would reopen to tourists on Tuesday, citing a “gradual decline” in the river’s flow.

José María Hervás, the director of the Iguazu national park, said access was closed because “it just keeps raining” and the volume of water being released from dams upstream on the Iguazu River was not falling, reported the Buenos Aires Times.

blocks.caption: A view of the Iguazu Falls from the Argentinian side of the border.  Photograph: Sinan Dogan/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: The Iguazu Falls, recognised by Unesco as one of the world’s largest and most impressive waterfalls, sits on the border of Argenina and Brazil and spans approximately 2,700 metres.
In 2023 and 2024, Argentinian officials closed the park on its side of the border over flooding caused by a previous El Niño cycle.

Meteorologists say the 2026-2027 El Niño, which causes global changes in winds and rainfall as well as erratic weather conditions, is certain to be the biggest ever recorded. Scientists now also think human-caused global heating is making El Niño’s more intense.

blocks.caption: Aerial view of Iguazu falls. Photograph: Travel Pix/Alamy

blocks.text: El Niño begins in the equatorial Pacific where changes in winds allow huge amounts of heat to escape the oceans and heat the atmosphere. It grows in the northern hemisphere autumn and peaks in December but has impacts well into the following year.
Last month, Argentina’s coastal region experienced above-average rainfall “similar to that seen during strong El Niño events,” the national meteorological service said.

articles.title: One person dead, several injured in roller-coaster accident near Atlanta
articles.summary: One person has died and several others were injured in an incident involving a Six Flags roller-coaster on Monday afternoon in Georgia, according to police.

image.caption: A roller-coaster is shown at Six Flags Over Georgia on Monday. One person died and several others were injured in an incident involving a roller-coaster at the park. (Emilie Megnien/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New
One person has died and several others were injured in an incident involving a Six Flags roller-coaster on Monday afternoon in Georgia, according to police.
Officials haven't yet given details about what happened on Six Flags Over Georgia ride

Officials did not confirm how the person died or what caused the others to be injured at Six Flags Over Georgia, about 25 kilometres northwest of Atlanta. Detectives with the Cobb County Police Department's major crimes unit are investigating.
A Six Flags spokesperson said the park and local authorities responded immediately and that they are fully co-operating with local authorities as they investigate.
"We are deeply saddened by the guest incident at our park today," the spokesperson said.
Authorities and Six Flags did not identify the roller-coaster. However, local TV stations showed video of passengers being evacuated from the Goliath coaster.
One dead, several injured after incident on a Six Flags roller-coaster in Georgia | Hanomansing Live

The roller-coaster, which was opened in 2006, reaches top speeds of about 113 km/h and heights of 61 metres, the park's website reports. During about 3-1/2 minutes, riders "navigate through razor-sharp turns and soar over colossal hills," according to the website.

"I cannot imagine the horror the patrons and employees witnessed today, and my heart aches for the family who lost a loved one," Lisa Cupid, chair of the Cobb County Board of Commissioners, said in a statement. She added that next of kin have been notified.
The amusement park is a major part of the county's tourism and brings in visitors from across the southeast, Cupid said.
"We are all grappling with how something so devastating could happen at a place that has given generations of families such happy memories," she said.

This death would be at least the seventh at the Georgia park, including one in 2006 in which a man had a likely heart attack on the Goliath coaster, according to the Doan Law Firm, which focuses on amusement park accidents.

It also comes less than two weeks after Six Flags Magic Mountain, in Southern California, announced that it is retiring its famous X2 roller-coaster amid lawsuits alleging serious brain injury caused by the ride. The park had settled one wrongful-death lawsuit from the family of a 22-year-old man who died after riding the coaster in 2022.

Last year, a 32-year-old man died after riding a high-speed roller-coaster at the Universal Epic Universe theme park in Florida. He died from blunt impact injuries, and his death was ruled accidental.

articles.summary: Aerial footage at the park after the incident shows a stuck rollercoaster with riders being helped off.

blocks.text: One person has died and several others were injured after an incident on a rollercoaster at Six Flags Over Georgia, an amusement park in the US state of Georgia.
The Cobb County Police Department said it was investigating the fatality at the park, about 15 miles (24km) from Atlanta, according to the BBC's news partner CBS.
Police did not specify what ride was involved, but aerial footage from news helicopters showed the Goliath rollercoaster stopped midway, with riders being helped off by workers.
Six Flags Over Georgia said it was "deeply saddened by the guest incident at our park today. Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with the guest's family, friends, and loved ones."
Officials have not said how the person was killed. The BBC has contacted local police and fire authorities, as well as park officials.
Witnesses told local media they saw a man ejected from the ride, accounts that the BBC has not verified.
Local outlet 11Alive quoted, external a witness saying the man fell from the rollercoaster on to the roof of a haunted house attraction.
A park spokesperson said in a statement that its team and local authorities had responded immediately, and they were co-operating on an investigation into the incident.
Mableton Mayor Michael Owens said the city's public safety director was co-ordinating with local police and park security on the situation.

The Goliath ride opened in 2006, and it has an elevation of 200ft (60m), a 170ft plunge, a 540-degree spiral, and a speed of up to 70mph (112km/h), according to the park website. On its "thrill scale", Six Flags ranks Goliath at level four out of five.
Six Flags is the largest amusement park operator in North America, with 20 amusement parks, 14 water parks and nine resorts across Canada, the US and Mexico.
The incident comes just weeks after one of its parks in southern California announced it would close the popular X2 roller coaster after more than 100 people alleged brain injuries from the ride.
Six Flags said the ride had passed a range of safety tests, but that it had decided to retire it because it was "the right thing to do".

articles.title: Sara Duterte’s unexplained wealth could reach P1.5 billion, witness says
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte’s unexplained wealth could reach P1.5 billion from 2022 to 2025, forensic financial analyst Alexander Cabrera told the impeachment court on Monday, October 12,…

blocks.text: October 13, 2026 | 10:21am

MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte’s unexplained wealth could reach P1.5 billion from 2022 to 2025, forensic financial analyst Alexander Cabrera told the impeachment court on Monday, October 12, citing potential discrepancies in financial records and income from business interests.
The estimate is nearly double the P817.87 million in unexplained wealth Cabrera had previously calculated, based on his review of Duterte’s financial records.
Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero asked Cabrera how much Duterte’s undeclared wealth could reach if he had not used conservative assumptions in his analysis.

“Kung hindi po kayo conservative, kung ito po 'yung bare minimum, in your expertise and based on your review of the documents, ano po ba 'yung sukdulang hangganan? Kung ito po 'yung bare minimum niyo, ano po 'yung inyong maximum?” Escudero asked.

(If you were not being conservative and this is the bare minimum, based on your expertise and review of the documents, what would be the upper limit? If this is your bare minimum, what would be your maximum?)
(Based lang po sa mga documents po na nakita namin, hindi ko po sinama ang confidential funds po. So 475 (million) po ’yun,” Cabrera said.
(Based only on the documents we reviewed, I did not include the confidential funds. So that would be P475 million.)

He added that discrepancies involving the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) could amount to P100 million if he did not use conservative assumptions. Applying a 45% assumption used for GenCorp Industries Inc. to undeclared sales could also increase the estimated amount by around P250 million.
Cabrera said these adjustments could nearly double his initial estimate.
“Mga 1.5 po,” he told Escudero when asked to compute the maximum estimate.
“1.5 billion?” Escudero asked.
“1.5 billion po,” Cabrera replied, clarifying that the amount was less than P1.6 billion.
Escudero then confirmed whether the P1.5-billion figure represented the maximum estimate of Duterte’s undeclared wealth from 2022 to 2025, without double-counting amounts across different years.
“Tama po,” Cabrera said. (That’s correct.)
Business interests account for part of estimate

During the hearing, Escudero also examined how much of Cabrera’s initial P817.87-million estimate would remain if income attributed to Duterte and her husband, lawyer Manases Carpio, from their business interests were excluded.
These included GenCorp Industries Inc., Metro Chow King Foods and Cale 88 Food Corp.
Escudero cited Cabrera’s computation that GenCorp accounted for approximately 25.9% of the total, equivalent to P212.63 million.
He also cited the combined P142.2 million attributed to Metro Chow King Foods and Cale 88 Food Corp., equivalent to 17.3% of the estimated unexplained wealth.

Escudero said that excluding the amounts attributed to GenCorp Industries Inc., Metro City Chow Foods Corp. and Cale 88 Foods Corp. would leave P463.05 million in unexplained wealth, based on Cabrera’s review of bank accounts and insurance policies.
The amount represents 56.6% of his initial P817.87-million estimate, which Cabrera affirmed.
Tax liabilities may reduce total
Escudero also asked whether taxes that should have been paid on the wealth would have to be deducted from the estimate.
Cabrera said this was possible, explaining that any outstanding tax liability could be subtracted when calculating the amount.
“Whether it's the low of 817 (million) or the high of 1.5 (billion), any liability would have to be subtracted or deducted from that?” Escudero asked
“Tama po,” Cabrera replied. (That’s correct.)
Cabrera explained that the classification of wealth as unexplained depended not only on whether its source was known but also on whether the source was legal.
“Pero ’pag ang pinanggalingan po ay hindi po legal, nagiging unexplained din po siya kahit alam niyo po kung saan nanggaling,” he said
(But if the source is illegal, it also becomes unexplained wealth, even if you know where it came from.)

Cabrera was presented by the prosecution as an expert witness on Article II of the impeachment complaint against Duterte, which accuses the vice president of amassing unexplained wealth disproportionate to her lawful income, failing to fully disclose her assets in her Statements of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALNs), and maintaining prohibited business interests while in office.

articles.title: IMF warns global economy ‘could soon test the limits of resilience’
articles.summary: World Economic Outlook says states’ oil stocks are low and budgets are overstretched, as it upgrades UK GDP growth forecast for 2026

blocks.text: The global economy “could soon test the limits of resilience”, as emergency oil stocks run low and government budgets become overstretched, the International Monetary Fund has warned.
In its twice-yearly World Economic Outlook, the IMF said global growth had withstood the Middle East conflict better than feared over the past six months.
It said the rerouting of oil supplies away from the strait of Hormuz, and the release of strategic energy stocks, had helped to contain the impact on oil prices from the US-Iran war.

However, it warned that emergency stocks are now depleted, and high debt levels and deficits in many countries could leave governments with little capacity to protect consumers from any future jump in prices.

“Without shoring up supply capacity and replenishing policy buffers, the global economy could soon test the limits of resilience,” it said. “Inventories in energy markets are dwindling and additional geopolitical shocks could still transmit rapidly through prices and supply disruptions.”

The International Energy Agency announced the largest-ever emergency releases of oil stocks on to the market in March this year, and promised to accelerate it after a meeting of oil ministers last month.
But in a sign of the system’s vulnerability, the US strategic petroleum reserve was recently reported to have fallen to its lowest level since 1982.

Last week, Donald Trump agreed a deal with Vladimir Putin to temporarily lift sanctions on US imports of Russian diesel in an attempt to bring down prices at the pumps, which analysts said would have little “meaningful” effect.

The World Economic Report was published on Tuesday in Bangkok, where the IMF and World Bank are holding their annual meetings this week, with finance ministers and central bankers scheduled to attend.

Ahead of the gathering, the IMF managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, urged governments to tighten their belts, amid rising global debt levels. “We cannot keep delaying necessary policy action – you have the tools, now have the wisdom to use them,” she said.
In the report, the IMF revised up its forecast for global economic growth this year marginally, to 3.1% – against 3% in its last update in July. Next year’s forecast is unchanged, at 3.4%.
US growth remains unchanged at 2.3% this year and revised up to the same pace, 2.3%, for 2027 – from 2.2% at the last update.

The IMF predicted GDP growth of 1.3% for the UK this year – up 0.3 percentage points from its most recent update in July – in welcome news for the chancellor, John Healey, who is set to arrive in Bangkok later this week.

However, the IMF also warned that prolonged high oil prices and rising interest rates meant growth was likely to “edge down” in 2027, “as higher energy prices and long-term interest rates weigh on consumption and investment”. It cut its UK growth forecast for next year modestly to 1.2%, from 1.3%.
after newsletter promotion

However, the IMF warned that “risks are skewed to the downside” for the global economy. In particular, it pointed to the threat of “a prolonged stalemate or further escalation in the Middle East”, which would lead to higher energy and food prices.
“Further disruptions to energy infrastructure, cyber-attacks, or extreme weather events could amplify these effects,” the IMF added.
Trump has continued to insist that he could launch another wave of attacks on Iran in the coming weeks, with little sign of a peace agreement being negotiated.
The persistence of elevated oil prices means the spike in inflation is now expected to last longer than previously forecast.
Global inflation is expected to be 4.7% this year – the same level as forecast in July – and to decline to 4.1% in 2027 – up from 4% in the last update.

The IMF urged the world’s central banks not to overreact to short-term jumps in inflation, but to be ready to respond quickly if it appears to be becoming entrenched. “With economic conditions in flux, agility is at a premium,” it said.
As well as fresh turmoil in energy markets, the IMF pointed to the continuing risk to the global economy of an AI-driven market crash.

articles.title: Bumble shares soar after report dating firm in $1bn takeover talks
articles.summary: The jump pushed Bumble's stock market valuation to more than $580m but that is still far below their peak of more than $14bn.

blocks.text: Shares in dating app company Bumble soared by almost 50% on Monday after a report that it is in advanced talks to be bought for around $1bn (£757m).
Technology holding company Ithaca could announce a deal to buy the Texas-based firm as early as this week, according to the Wall Street Journal.
The jump in Bumble's shares pushed its stock market valuation to over $580m but that is still far below a peak of more than $14bn it reached after listing on the Nasdaq in 2021.
Bumble is one of the world's most downloaded dating apps, operating in a crowded market where growth has slowed. The BBC has contacted Bumble and Ithaca for comment.
Bumble was launched in 2014 by Whitney Wolfe Herd, who was also a co-founder of dating app giant Tinder.
Wolfe Herd built Bumble's brand around a distinctive feature that only allowed women to initiate conversations with matches.
It recently abandoned that rule, prompting debate among users over whether the app had lost what set it apart from rivals.

"Today, our community is asking for more flexibility, less pressure, and more opportunities to create real, meaningful connections and that is what this new experience provides," Wolfe Herd said in August.
Dating apps like Bumble have come under pressure in recent years as some younger users have grown disillusioned with browsing for dates.
Bumble said in 2025 that it would cut almost a third of its workforce as the industry grappled with what Wolfe Herd described as an "inflection point" in online dating.
Investments in other dating companies have also soured as apps have struggled to convince users to pay for their services.
Match Group - which owns apps including Tinder, OkCupid and Hinge - has also seen its shares fall sharply from their peak in 2021.
According a report by media watchdog Ofcom in 2025, adults in the UK were spending less time on dating apps compared to three years earlier.
Some single people are instead turning to board game get-togethers, book clubs and other group activities in the hope of finding a partner.

articles.title: P41-million withdrawal from Mans Carpio’s accounts in 73 minutes ‘unusual' — witness
articles.summary: A forensic accountant has described as “unusual” the withdrawal of P41 million in cash from the bank accounts of Vice President Sara Duterte's husband, Mans Carpio, within an hour and 13…

blocks.text: October 13, 2026 | 9:13am

MANILA, Philippines — A forensic accountant has described as “unusual” the withdrawal of P41 million in cash from the bank accounts of Vice President Sara Duterte's husband, Mans Carpio, within an hour and 13 minutes on Aug. 6, 2024, saying the closely timed transactions appeared rushed.

Responding to Sen. Risa Hontiveros’ questions during the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on Monday, October 12, forensic accountant Alexander Cabrera said the amount and timing of the withdrawals raised questions.
“Sa ordinaryong tao po, unusual po. Eh 41 million in cash, kailangan n'yo po siyempre ng bag po doon. And parang may hinahabol po eh, kasi lahat po ginawa within the hour po,” he said.
(For an ordinary person, that would be unusual. P41 million in cash would, of course, require a bag to carry. And it seemed like they were in a hurry because everything was done within an hour.)
Hontiveros cited Table 24, page 18 of Cabrera’s forensic report, which recorded the total cash withdrawals of P41 million on Aug. 6, 2024.

Cabrera confirmed that both accounts involved in the transactions belonged to Carpio. He questioned why such a large amount was withdrawn in cash instead of being transferred to another bank account or obtained through a manager’s check.
He said the absence of supporting documents could also serve as evidence in a forensic investigation, particularly when a transaction took place without a clear paper trail.

“Pagka po ‘yung mga transactions po kulang sa trail, kulang sa record, wala pong document evidencing it pero nangyari po yung transaction, yung pong walang document nangyari yung transaction, evidence din po ‘yun eh,” Cabrera said.
(When transactions lack a trail, lack records and have no documents to support them, but the transactions still took place, the absence of documentation is also evidence.)
His team also examined the timestamps of the withdrawals and found that the transactions were closely spaced, with the final withdrawal taking place after a lunch break.
“Nag-lunch muna, tapos kinuha po ‘yun. Kaya sabi namin parang may hinahabol kasi right after lunch tuloy ‘yung transaction. Matagal din po kasi magbilang ng 41 million,” he said.

(They [Carpio's camp] had lunch first, then withdrew the money. That’s why we said it seemed like they were in a hurry because the transaction continued right after lunch. It also takes a long time to count P41 million.)
Sen. Kiko Pangilinan, meanwhile, questioned the timing of the withdrawals in relation to developments involving Duterte and Carpio.

"'Yung August 6, 2024, sabi ninyo 41 million ang winithdraw sa isang araw at parang may hinahabol. So ako rin naging curious dito, kaya iniisip ko, ano ba nangyari noong August 6 o kaya thereabouts, no?" Pangilinan said.

(On August 6, 2024, you said P41 million was withdrawn in a single day and that it seemed like someone was in a hurry. I became curious about this too so I wondered what happened on August 6 or around that time.)
He noted that Duterte resigned as education secretary on July 19, 2024, before drug charges were filed against Carpio on July 30 in connection with the so-called magnetic lifter case.

Just to place on record, uh, Vice President Sara Duterte resigned as DepEd chairperson July 19, 2024. And then on July 30, uh, it's in the news and we can Google it because that's what we did, uh, drug charges were filed against Attorney Mans Carpio doon sa, um, 'yong tawag dito, magnetic lifter," Pangilinan said.
"So July 30 'yun. So that was, uh, the filing was July 30, and then six days later nangyari ito," he added, referring to the August 6 withdrawals.
(So that was on July 30. The charges were filed on July 30, and then this happened six days later.)

Carpio has maintained that the credit card expenses discussed during the impeachment trial were personal expenditures paid for with his own money. He has also denied Duterte's involvement in the transactions and said no public funds were used.

Cabrera was presented by the prosecution as an expert witness on Article II of the impeachment complaint against Duterte, which accuses the vice president of amassing unexplained wealth disproportionate to her lawful income, failing to fully disclose her assets in her Statements of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALNs), and maintaining prohibited business interests while in office.
