articles.title: 'Breaking Bad' actor and disability advocate RJ Mitte dies
articles.summary: RJ Mitte said his lived experience with cerebral palsy was an asset for his role as Walter White's son Flynn on "Breaking Bad."

image.caption: RJ Mitte had key roles in 'Breaking Bad,' 'Switched at Birth' and 'Guardians of Justice'Image: Gage Skidmore/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: American actor RJ Mitte, whose lived experience with cerebral palsy was channeled into a key role in "Breaking Bad," died on Monday at the age of 34.
"It is with profound ​sadness that we share the tragic passing of beloved actor, philanthropist, and passionate disability rights ​advocate RJ Mitte," his management agency said in a statement.
No other details about the circumstances of his death were given.

In addition to his breakout role in in "Breaking Bad" and later credits including "Switched at Birth" and "Guardians of Justice," Mitte also served as an ambassador for United Cerebral Palsy and Shriners Hospitals for Children.
An 'authentic' breakout role

In "Breaking Bad," Mitte played Walter White Jr., the son of Bryan Cranston's character, chemistry teacher-turned-meth dealer Walter White. Mitte's character used crutches and spoke with a slur, and gained greater prominence as the series progressed.
"Mitte brought authenticity to the role and built ​a platform on disability awareness and inclusion," the statement said.
"Breaking Bad" ran from 2008 until 2023. With 16 Emmy awards, it's often cited by critics as one of the best television dramas of all time.

Shortly after the series wrapped up, Mitte told the Associated Press that his disability and the surrounding struggles with physical therapy, family problems and exorbitant medical bills — all of which featured in the show — made him better in his role.
"You develop a different mentality and you develop a different look at how the world sees you and how you see the world," he said in 2024.
"You're able to use that. And I think it's an asset instead of something that would hinder," Mitte added.

articles.title: Supreme Court orders release of mining tycoon Joseph Sy amid citizenship dispute
articles.summary: The Supreme Court has ordered the release of Globe-Ferronickel chairman Joseph Sy.

blocks.text: October 13, 2026 | 8:22am
Joseph Sy attends the Senate inquiry on Dec. 15, 2025 which tackled the alleged abuse of identity documents reserved to Filipino citizens by foreign nationals.
Senate of the Philippines - Social Media Unit
MANILA, Philippines — The Supreme Court has ordered the release of Globe-Ferronickel chairman Joseph Sy.
In a resolution dated October 7, the high court granted a writ of preliminary mandatory injunction.
According to a copy of the order obtained by Philstar.com, the order took effect upon the posting of a P900,000.00 cash bond.
On Aug. 21, 2025, Sy was intercepted and detained by Bureau of Immigration personnel at the Ninoy Aquino International Airport (NAIA) upon his arrival from Hong Kong.

The bureau acted on a mission order issued by Immigration Commissioner Joel Viado, claiming that Sy was an alias for Zhong Zhen Chen, a Chinese national who had allegedly misrepresented himself as a Filipino.

To support their claim, immigration officials presented fingerprint evidence from an Alien Certificate of Registration issued 29 years ago, which they said matched the fingerprints on Sy's Philippine passport.
However, Sy’s representative, Dante Bravo, filed a petition for habeas corpus, arguing that Sy is a Filipino citizen.
Bravo provided Sy's Certificate of Live Birth, issued through late registration in 2007, which identifies him as a Filipino born in Quezon City to Filipino parents.
Sy also holds a Philippine passport valid until 2031 and various other government identification cards.

On February 20, the Court of Appeals ruled that Sy’s continued detention was unlawful, finding that the Bureau of Immigration cannot institute summary deportation proceedings against someone with a valid birth certificate.
In a statement, the Bureau of Immigration said that it would respect the Supreme Court’s decision.
However, the bureau emphasized that Sy's release from custody does not “constitute a final determination of the questions surrounding his citizenship and identity.”

“It is also noted that the case before the Supreme Court is an appeal in the Habeas Corpus Petition involving Mr. Sy, which only involves questions on legality of his detention, and not a determination on his citizenship,” the Bureau of Immigration’s statement read.
“The Bureau acted in the exercise of its statutory mandate to investigate questions concerning immigration status, identity, and citizenship documentation,” it added.

articles.title: Shock and surprise after FBI arrests Canadian cybersecurity expert in ShinyHunters hacking case

image.caption: The FBI arrested a 'suspected co-conspirator' in the recent ShinyHunters cyberattack on FBIjobs.gov, who Reuters and court records have identified as Canadian cybersecurity expert Ed Dubrovsky. (Jenny Kane/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Canada
Canadians in the cybersecurity world say they were shocked to hear a prominent ransomware negotiator was arrested by the FBI over suspected connections to criminal hacking group ShinyHunters.
The prominent ransomware negotiator was arrested last week
· CBC News
· Posted: Oct 12, 2026 8:10 PM EDT | Last Updated: 21 minutes ago

Canadians in the cybersecurity world say they were shocked to hear that a prominent ransomware negotiator had been arrested by the FBI over suspected connections to criminal hacking group ShinyHunters.
FBI Director Kash Patel on Friday confirmed the arrest of a "suspected co-conspirator" in the recent ShinyHunters cyberattack on FBIjobs.gov which exposed a trove of sensitive data about FBI staff.
"We will continue to work closely with our partners to disrupt what's left of the ShinyHunters group and their associates, no matter where they operate," Patel said on social media.

Reuters reported Sunday that sources familiar with the matter identified the arrested suspect as Ed Dubrovsky, a Canadian cybersecurity executive whose career has focused on helping clients negotiate with ransomware attackers.

Court documents from the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania show Dubrovsky is facing two criminal charges: conspiracy to threaten to impair the confidentiality of information with the intent to extort money, and interference with commerce by threats.
The allegations have not been proven in court.

FBI Director Kash Patel testifies during a Senate Judiciary hearing on Oversight of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, in September 2026 in Washington. Patel confirmed the arrest of a suspected co-conspirator in the ShinyHunters investigation. (Manuel Balce Ceneta/The Associated Press)
'A sense of shock'
"For the cybersecurity community in general, I think that there's a sense of shock," Toronto-based tech and cybersecurity analyst Ritesh Kotak told CBC News on Monday.
Kotak says Dubrovsky is "very popular" and has spoken at numerous conferences, but stressed that the charges "are clearly just allegations" and that it is not yet known "what exactly has happened."
"This is an individual that was for the most part respected when it came to ransomware negotiations," he said. "A lot of people are familiar with his work as well."

items: ShinyHunters hackers say they won't leak sensitive FBI data
Dutch police arrest security professional in ShinyHunters investigation

blocks.text: The ​court records, which are partially sealed, provide conflicting spellings of the suspect's last ⁠name — "Dobrovsky" or "Dobrosky" — and do not identify his age, profession or employer.
Prison records show a 54-year-old named Edward Dubrovsky is being held at a federal detention centre in Philadelphia.

Reuters reported that electronic wallet records leaked in 2010 and preserved by dark-web intelligence firm District 4 Labs identify Dubrovsky as a 54-year-old resident of Richmond Hill, a suburb of Toronto.
Long history in cybersecurity

Dubrovsky's LinkedIn profile describes him as a specialist in ‌negotiating with cybercriminals over ransom payments, as well as a "globally recognized cybersecurity expert, business leader, speaker, author and educator."
According to his profile, Dubrovsky has held senior positions in cybersecurity for decades.

He wrote on LinkedIn last month that he would be attending the NetDilligence conference in Philadelphia in October with cybersecurity firm CyberSteward. The company posted photos of Dubrovsky at the conference a week ago and said he was signing copies of a book he recently published about handling cyber extortion.
AI can make cyberattacks faster and smarter

In the book's introduction, Dubrovsky writes: "I have negotiated with criminals who viewed themselves as martyrs, criminal masterminds, and patriots of their own countries even after deploying malware against critical infrastructure and causing billions of dollars in damage. Such people could still look in the mirror and see goodness."
CBC News reached out to CyberSteward by phone, email and in person at its Toronto address, but did not get a response Monday.
The FBI's national press office declined to comment directly on Dubrovsky's arrest and referred CBC News to Patel's statement.

RCMP spokesperson Ian Lordon told The Canadian Press on Friday that "the RCMP is aware of the arrest of a Canadian in the U.S. in connection with the ShinyHunters hack," but directed all further questions to the FBI.
ShinyHunters 'poked the bear': expert
ShinyHunters is known as one of the world's most prolific data theft and extortion groups, typically demanding ransom payments in exchange for not releasing the sensitive data it has obtained.

The hacking group caused chaos at universities around the world in May, including in Canada, with a cyberattack on Canvas, an online learning-management system that connects millions of students with their instructors.
ShinyHunters has also been associated with high-profile cyberattacks affecting companies including Telus, Microsoft, Ticketmaster, Pornhub and Rockstar Games.

items: What drives ShinyHunters, the group that claimed responsibility for hacking the FBI?

blocks.text: Last month, the group claimed responsibility for stealing a massive trove of data from the FBI — including officials' job assignments, addresses and social security numbers — in what it said was retaliation for the law enforcement agency making false claims about the group.
ShinyHunters later told CBC News they would not release the data.

David Shipley, a cybersecurity expert and CEO of Fredericton-based Beauceron Security, said the stunt "poked the bear" and has "literally unleashed the most powerful law enforcement agency in the world on them."
Online learning platform strikes deal with hackers that targeted schools | Hanomansing Tonight
Shipley said surprise was the first thing that came to mind when he heard of the latest arrest.
"I knew the ShinyHunters investigation was going to go in interesting places because it's already the stuff of Hollywood movies," he told CBC News.
"I don't think anyone saw this twist coming."
Shipley said Dubrovsky was well regarded and worked for "top-tier" cybersecurity firms.
"I feel terrible for his former colleagues, both at his current firm and his past firms, who have been dragged through these awful headlines," he said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Kevin Maimann is a senior writer for CBC News based in Edmonton. He has covered a wide range of topics for publications including VICE, the Toronto Star, Xtra Magazine and the Edmonton Journal. You can reach Kevin by email at kevin.maimann@cbc.ca.
With files from Reuters and The Canadian Press

blocks.text: One person has died and several others were injured in an incident involving a Six Flags rollercoaster on Monday afternoon in Georgia, according to police.
The incident took place a Six Flags Over Georgia, about 15 miles (25km) north-west of Atlanta, according to the Cobb county police department.

Officials did not confirm how the person died or what caused the others to be injured. However, multiple outlets reported a person had fallen from the park’s Goliath rollercoaster, citing eyewitnesses and anonymous local officials.

A Six Flags spokesperson said the park and local authorities responded immediately and that they are fully cooperating with local authorities as they investigate the incident.
“We are deeply saddened by the guest incident at our park today,” the spokesperson said.

Late last month, Six Flags Magic Mountain, in southern California, announced that it was retiring its famous X2 rollercoaster amid lawsuits alleging serious brain injury caused by the ride. Six Flags recently settled a wrongful-death lawsuit from the family of a 22-year-old man who died after riding the coaster in 2022, and three more lawsuits alleging traumatic brain injuries were filed last week.

articles.title: Boardroom feud tests trusted Indian business empire
articles.summary: The dispute raises questions about the Indian conglomerate's governance, succession plans and future.

blocks.text: Before dawn breaks over Mumbai, Mansi Kadam begins preparing vada pav, a savoury snack synonymous with the western Indian city, for the day's customers. One ingredient is non-negotiable: Tata salt.
When asked whether she would ever consider switching brands, her reply is a reminder of an old Hindi ad jingle, "If it's salt, it has to be Tata."
She knows little about the developments unfolding in the boardroom of the Tata group, one of India's oldest and most influential business empires that makes everything from salt to software.
But her instinctive loyalty points to a question confronting the group: Can one of India's most trusted brands remain insulated from a public battle over power, governance and control?
A recent public disagreement between the board of Tata Sons, the holding company of the Tata group and Tata Trusts, its principal shareholder, has put a spotlight on the conglomerate.

At the centre of the dispute are two issues - the proposed public listing of Tata Sons and the reappointment of chairman N Chandrasekaran. Most of the Tata Sons board, including its biggest minority shareholder SP Group, supported the decisions.

But Noel Tata, chairman of majority shareholder Tata Trusts, has opposed both resolutions. He maintains that a public listing would dilute the group's philanthropic ethos and is likely to get both decisions overturned at its annual general meeting.

"When we say this is a governance crisis, it's a misalignment of interests between the board [of Tata Sons] and the shareholders [Tata Trusts]," Shriram Subramanian, head of independent corporate governance firm InGovern Research, told the BBC.
While he does not expect the brand's image to be affected immediately, he flags concerns over the leadership's ability to navigate the challenges.

Disagreements within the Tata Group have been simmering since the death of former chairman Ratan Tata - Noel Tata's half-brother who designated him successor after his death - in 2024. For many Indians, Ratan Tata's philanthropy and leadership had become inseparable from the brand. His death triggered widespread mourning and experts say it left a leadership void in the group's image with the public.
The Tata group has topped India's most valuable brand list by valuation consultancy Brand Finance since 2018, according to the group's website.
Tata Sons, the business entity, is described by the group as the "fastener keeping the many disparate elements of the whole together".
Tata Trusts, which represents seven philanthropic trusts that own the majority stake in the group, is widely regarded as its moral compass, guiding the businesses on social impact and philanthropy.
For many Indians, both the entities together make up what most companies cannot buy - trust.
Now with these entities in rival corners, that is coming under strain.
"Once upon a time, there was a unified audience which said the Tatas are good people with good governance. Today, the opinion is divided," said Harish Bijoor, business and brand strategy consultant.

While most consumers appear unfazed, the dispute has polarised other stakeholders including business partners, investors and employees. Some view it as corporate power politics, others as a genuine governance debate, but few agree on which side is right, Bijoor said.
"This conflict has brought the Tatas into conversations everywhere, which is not good as they have always liked to be out of it," he says.
The group has been traditionally preferred being low profile about philanthropy and conflict resolution.
The Tata group did not respond to BBC's email with detailed questions.
Founded by Jamsetji Tata in 1868, the Tata group expanded under JRD Tata who transformed it into a professionally managed conglomerate. Ratan Tata drove its global ambitions through acquisitions.
Tata group, which has a combined market value of more than $260bn (£195.6bn) and employs hundreds of thousands of people in more than 100 countries, is not new to controversies.

The conglomerate has faced protests over industrial projects, scrutiny of its Indian telecom business during a spectrum allocation controversy, a high-profile dispute with Japan's Docomo and, more recently, questions over Air India's performance.

Some of its business decisions have also drawn attention, particularly Tata Steel's troubled Corus acquisition, though other overseas bets such as Tetley and Jaguar Land Rover were successful and helped expand the group's global footprint.

Its biggest controversy was in 2016 when the Tata Sons board abruptly removed Cyrus Mistry as chairman and brought back Ratan Tata as interim head. Mistry, heir to the SP Group, was chosen by a team led by Ratan Tata himself. It led to a long battle which ended in 2021 with the Supreme Court ruling in the Tatas' favour.

Last month, journalist Sucheta Dalal wrote in her column for Moneylife magazine that the Tata group has "weathered serious governance storms" and enjoys "special privileges available to no other business group [referring to a tax exemption granted to Tata Trusts for holding shares in Tata Sons]" because of a reputation built over decades.
Most Tata watchers agree.
In an email interview, Morgen Witzel, a fellow at Exeter Centre of Leadership who wrote a book on the brand in 2010, cited several examples on the group's connection with people.

At Jamshedpur in Jharkhand state, where the group set up India's first integrated steel plant and an industrial city, it provides healthcare and education to people in hundreds of villages. Watchmaker Titan supports employees who want to leave and start their own businesses. Tata Motors at Pune has supported thousands of female entrepreneurs, he points out.
"It is the concatenation of all of these things that builds trust because people see that, by and large, Tata is there to serve their needs rather than just take their money," Witzel said.
But while the group has weathered other storms, this time, the divide is within.
The boardroom tussle has increasingly spilled into the public domain, with Tata Sons and Trusts clashing through legal notices and conflicting statements.
Venu Srinivasan, vice-chairman of Tata Trusts and a nominee director on Tata Sons' board, has sought a probe into alleged governance lapses at some trusts. The trusts deny the lapses.
Noel Tata has made two proposals to avoid listing the company.

First, that the Tata Sons board buy back a portion of SP Group's minority stake as a "fair and equitable solution" to the latter's demand to monetise their stake. Secondly, restructure Tata Sons by merging with itself two businesses which would change the way it is classified by India's central bank, helping the group potentially avoid a listing.
It is not clear whether he can pull this off, given that unlike Rata Tata, he had not consolidated power yet.

"Ratan Tata's larger-than-life image is, to some extent, the reason behind the current conflict. Everyone was deferential towards him and his successor was known only after his death through his will," says Subramanian.
Had Ratan Tata overseen the succession himself, the transition would have been smoother, he says.
Brand expert Bijoor calls for the Tata group to put together a "white paper" on how the conflict plays out in the end. "They stood for transparency, and they must never shed that."

How the influential group manages these tensions may offer a glimpse into its future. The outcome will be watched closely across corporate India, where Tata's governance and business practices have long been regarded as a benchmark.

articles.title: 2 Filipinos under probe over Laos shabu haul bound for PH — PDEA
articles.summary: The agency said they are currently building a case against the two Filipinos, noting that some of the information remains confidential amid the probe.

blocks.text: October 13, 2026 | 6:54am
Motorists drive past Laos national flags and Lao People's Revolutionary Party flags ahead of the election in Vientiane on February 19, 2026.
STR / AFP

MANILA, Philippines — Two Filipinos are currently the subjects of an ongoing investigation by the Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency (PDEA) over their alleged link to a recent high-value drug bust in Laos, which authorities also confirmed was bound for the Philippines.

In a press briefing on Monday, October 12, the drug enforcement agency said they have established that the 521 kilograms of suspected methamphetamine, or shabu, that Lao authorities intercepted over a week ago at Luang Prabang International Airport was supposed to be delivered to the Philippines through a private jet.

The pilot of the private jet reportedly refused to load the luggage of the Filipino passenger who was carrying the luggage, which eventually led to the individual’s arrest and the plane’s cancellation of its flight to the Philippines.

“The very clear feature as of today is na-discover iyong droga dahil the pilot refused to load those baggages doon sa airplane papuntang Pilipinas. Kaya nung hindi na natuloy ‘yung ah 'yung pag-load ng baggages doon sa eroplano, ang ginawa ng airline company canceled its flight plan papunta sa Pilipinas,” PDEA Director General Undersecretary Isagani Nerez said.

(The very clear feature as of today is that the drugs were discovered because the pilot refused to load those baggages in the airplane bound for the Philippines. That's why the loading of baggage did not proceed, and the airline company canceled its flight going to the Philippines.)
The agency identified the arrested suspect as “Fajad”, a confirmed Filipino national with alleged current residence in Marawi. Nerez said they also have a list of Fajad’s other addresses.
Authorities are now investigating to identify Fajad’s accomplices while he remains detained in Laos, including another Filipino identified as “Boyet”.
'Boyet'
Nerez said Boyet is among the persons of interest in PDEA’s target list for allegedly being responsible for chartering the private jet that was supposed to be used to transport the suspected drugs.
The authorities said they have established a link between Fajad and Boyet, and found that both of them have residences in Luzon.
“We have a data that si Boyet is taga-rito sa Luzon, at ‘yung si Fajad meron ding address sa Luzon, parehas po. So that links them na or establish 'yung link nila na magkakilala,” Nerez said.
(We have data showing that Boyet is from Luzon, and Fajad also has an address in Luzon. So that links them or establishes a connection between them, suggesting that they know each other.)
Boyet allegedly paid for the private jet through bank transfer, but authorities did not disclose the amount.
PDEA also said they have acquired information saying Boyet had already skipped the country and went to Hong Kong.
The agency said they are currently building a case against both Boyet and Fajad, noting that some of the information remains confidential amid the probe.

articles.title: The island where locals say data centres are taking their water
articles.summary: "Not a single drop has come through our taps for the last three months," a local tells the BBC.

blocks.text: "Water! Water!" the crowd shouted as it stormed a compound with data centres, armed with empty plastic bottles and jerry cans.

There were about 300 of them, all residents on the Indonesian island of Batam, and they were furious that the taps at home had run dry, while the data centres in the new Nongsa Digital Park seemed to have enough water to protect their machines from overheating.
"Not a single drop has come through our taps for the last three months... Our water supply had been reliable until the data centres came," Dewi Susanti, one of the protesters, told the BBC.
People in her village, Bakau Serip, were now depending on tanker trucks that dispensed "dirty, cloudy and smelly" water, she said.
Batam's water utility told the BBC it was working to improve supply, but did not comment on whether the disruption was linked to demand from the data centres.
But BP Batam, the agency overseeing trade and industry, blamed it on a prolonged dry spell and denied allegations from locals that water meant for homes was being channelled to data centres.
This is not the first such protest in Batam, whose shrinking reservoirs find themselves under more pressure as the island tries to transform itself into a digital hub.

Following protests in August and September, authorities told the firms opening data centres in Batam that they must build their own desalination plants instead of relying on reservoirs for freshwater.
But locals say they are increasingly concerned that they must now compete with servers for water.

"Reliable data on data centre water use in Indonesia remains scarce, partly because companies treat it as proprietary information," says Agus Hasan, a professor at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology.

"We should build [data centres] rationally, transparently, and responsibly, and insist on seeing the numbers... [Otherwise] those kept in the dark while their taps run dry will push back, and rightly so," he adds.
A backlash has been building against data centres across the world, from the US to the UK to parts of Asia, as tech companies pour billions into AI infrastructure.

People are worried about how the huge, windowless buildings might change their neighbourhoods, the constant hum of machines, the security lights that could stay on all night, and the pressure this puts on water and energy resources.
While electricity powers the centres, the water keeps the servers from frying - engineers deploy elaborate cooling systems, which consume a lot of water.

Research in the US suggests a typical data centre consumes around 300,000 gallons of water a day, or about as much as 1,000 US households. A larger, 50MW facility could take as much water as 2,200 households per day, and enough electricity to power 22,000 homes, according to Malaysia's central bank.
It's unclear how much water or electricity the data centres in Batam are consuming.
But the island routinely faces water shortages, and the levels are worse this year, possibly because of a historic "super" El Niño.
Devoid of natural freshwater sources, Batam's 1.3 million people rely on rainwater collected in six artificial reservoirs.

Nongsa reservoir, which supplies water to Bakau Serip, where Dewi lives, would dry up over the next month with no rainfall, simulations by local environmental non-profit group Akar Bhumi Indonesia suggest.

"The water shortage is affecting our livelihoods... Money that should be used to buy rice is now spent on water drums," Dewi says. "My husband has to wait up overnight to get water, and then go straight to work the next morning."

Batam's water utility had earlier said that it would consider measures like cloud seeding should the water shortage continue. When asked about the recent protests, they pointed us to earlier statements.

Authorities in Batam have approved 10 data centres, six of which will be located in Nongsa Digital Park. Two are up and running, while a third is under construction. At least six more are currently under review for approval, BP Batam told the BBC.
Official figures put investment in data centres on the island at more than $6.7bn (£5.1bn) as of mid-2026, spurred in part by demand from Singapore, which is just an hour away by ferry.

Singapore paused construction of data centres in 2019, citing land and energy constraints. It lifted the ban in 2022 after introducing new efficiency standards, which prompted investors to look elsewhere.
Singapore has long been promoting the Riau Islands, which includes Batam, and the Malaysian state of Johor as "complementary" regions.

Quick to absorb the spillover, Johor approved data centre projects worth tens of billions. But this soon drew the ire of residents frustrated with noise, dust and water shortages. The state has since tried to regulate how much water and electricity data centres consume.

Across the strait, Batam is just as attractive to investors - from the US, China, Australia, Singapore - because of relatively low operating costs, proximity to Singapore and connections to major subsea cable routes.

Nongsa is home to a 13,000-sq-m data centre by Hong Kong-based private equity firm Gaw Capital and Indonesian developer Sinar Primera. In April, Singapore's DayOne signed a deal with an Indonesian state utility to build one of the country's largest data centres - around 450MW capacity, enough to power 350,000 average households. In June, DayOne, chip maker Nvidia and Australian AI start-up Firmus Technologies announced a 360MW "AI factory".
By 2030, power demand from data centres in Batam is expected to cross 1,100MW, which is enough to power nearly a million homes, according to the official estimates.
The BBC has contacted DayOne, Sinar Primera and Gaw Capital for comment.
Meanwhile, the spate of construction is worrying locals in Batam who urged authorities to prioritise their needs.

"Don't just sit at the top and keep approving these projects. Come down here and see for yourselves what we are wrestling with," says Marlinda, who lives in the district of Sei Beduk, which is also facing water shortages.
"We want the government to pay attention to ordinary people," another resident told the BBC.
"Don't make billion-rupiah investments while ordinary people are made to suffer... We are not asking for anything extravagant. We just want our water supply restored."

articles.title: Canada falls 4-3 to Denmark in women's soccer friendly in Toronto
articles.summary: Olivia Holdt scored twice and had an assist to lead Denmark to a 4-3 victory over Canada in a women's international soccer friendly on Monday at BMO Field in Toronto.

image.caption: Canada goalkeeper Kailen Sheridan, left, and teammate Janine Sonis react after Denmark's Olivia Holdt, not shown, scored her country's third goal during first half of Monday's international friendly at BMO Field in Toronto. (Chris Young/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Soccer·New
Olivia Holdt scored twice and had an assist to lead Denmark to a 4-3 victory over Canada in a women's international soccer friendly on Monday at BMO Field in Toronto.
The teams played to a 1-1 draw on Friday in Montreal
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Oct 12, 2026 6:17 PM EDT | Last Updated: 12 minutes ago
Pernille Harder and Janni Thomsen also tallied for the visitors, who blitzed the hosts with three goals in a nine-minute span in the opening half.
Olivia Smith, Evelyne Viens and Delaney Pridham scored for Canada in front of an announced crowd of 12,112 on a warm, mostly sunny afternoon at the lakefront stadium.
The teams played to a 1-1 draw on Friday in Montreal. Smith scored a late equalizer for the hosts in that game and Canada won the unofficial shootout 4-2.

On Monday, the ninth-ranked Canadians started with a 4-2-3-1 formation while the 12th-ranked Danes went with a 3-4-3. Kailen Sheridan started in net for Canada and Jessie Fleming wore the captain's armband.
Canada comes up just short against Denmark in Toronto FIFA friendly

Pridham opened the scoring in the 10th minute after Kaylee Hunter headed the ball low into a packed penalty area. Pridham swiveled and beat goalkeeper Freja Thisgaard for her first goal with the women's senior team.
Canada kept the pressure on and was nearly rewarded moments later when Smith's shot from outside the area glanced off Thisgaard and hit the post.
Denmark scoring surge
Defensive miscues contributed to the Denmark scoring surge.

Holdt took possession of a loose ball after Canada's Julia Grosso couldn't corral a pass from defender Kadeisha Buchanan at midfield. The Danish forward took a few strides inside the halfway line and launched a shot that sailed over Sheridan's head and bounced into the net in the 24th minute.

An errant pass attempt by Buchanan moments later created another turnover. A strike from Sofie Bredgaard hit the crossbar but Denmark controlled the rebound and Harder beat Sheridan in the 27th minute.
In the 32nd minute, Ashley Lawrence's pass to Jade Rose was turned over down low and the ball found its way to an open Holdt, who earned her first international brace.
The tempo picked up in the second half as Pridham and Buchanan came off for Viens and Shelina Zadorsky.

Canada cut the deficit in the 49th minute after some heady work by Smith, who found Viens at the top of the area. Viens made a sliding shot attempt that deflected high off a defender and bounced off the grass and into the top corner.
Thomsen restored Denmark's two-goal cushion in the 61st minute as she coolly slotted a ball between two defenders and past Sheridan.
Smith scored from outside the box in the 70th minute. Her strike was misplayed by Thisgaard, who got down low to gather the ball but had it roll between her legs and over the line.
Casey Stoney is still seeking her first victory against a top-15 opponent since taking over as Canada's head coach in January 2025.
Upcoming CONCACAF W Championship
The friendlies served as a measuring stick ahead of Canada's opening match against No. 54 Panama at the CONCACAF W Championship on Nov. 28.

The tournament is a qualifier for both the 2027 FIFA Women's World Cup in Brazil and the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. Denmark has already qualified for the World Cup after finishing atop its UEFA qualifying group.
Left back Allysha Chapman came on in the 89th minute for her 100th and final international appearance for Canada. She was feted during a ceremony after the game.

Fleming, Buchanan and Lawrence were honoured before the game for reaching 150 career international appearances. At halftime, Melissa Tancredi was acknowledged for her induction into the Canada Soccer Hall of Fame.
Canada fell to 3-4-1 in eight all-time meetings against Denmark.

articles.title: Emergency medical help for Christa Pike was delayed due to confusion, 911 tapes reveal
articles.summary: Emergency help for Christa Pike was delayed by confusion among first responders and Tennessee prison officials following her failed lethal injection last month, according to 911 dispatch recordings…

image.caption: 911 recordings suggest emergency care was delayed after the failed execution of Christa Pike, seen here in December 2007. (J. Miles Cary/ Knoxville News Sentinel/USA Today Network/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

Emergency help for Christa Pike was delayed by confusion among first responders and Tennessee prison officials following her failed lethal injection last month, according to 911 dispatch recordings reviewed by The Associated Press.
First responders not sure whether request for emergency help in execution chamber was legitimate

The recordings show that precious minutes elapsed as officials and responders tried to figure out whether a request for emergency help in the execution chamber was legitimate. The first call came in at 8:40 p.m. local time on Sept. 30, and it was about half an hour before prison officials affirmed it was legitimate and began letting responders through the prison gates.

"Per supervisors here at the DEC [Department of Emergency Communications], we have been informed it is a false call," one unidentified person says at 9:03 p.m. "There is no medical assistance needed at Riverbend Prison."

items: Tennessee governor orders outside review after death row inmate Christa Pike survives execution attempt
After day of delays, witnesses say Tennessee unable to carry out execution of Christa Pike

blocks.text: Four minutes later, a responder reported: "Somebody is outside the gate at the prison telling us that it's real and demanding us to go in. They say they are some sort of state official. I need somebody to get out to the gate and talk to those people."
It wasn't until 9:11 p.m. that prison officials affirmed the call for help was legitimate, the calls show.
Pike discharged from hospital

Pike, 50, was hospitalized after surviving two doses of pentobarbital as the state attempted to execute her for the 1995 beating and stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer. At one point, Pike was on a ventilator, and her lawyers did not expect her to survive.

However, they said Pike woke up and began talking and walking with assistance, and she has since been discharged and is back at the Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center, the women's prison where she was housed for 30 years.

The Tennessee Department of Correction has not said what went wrong in the attempted execution. Medical and lethal injection experts have focused on whether a problem with the IV line caused the drug to pool in her tissue instead of entering her bloodstream.

articles.title: Cyberattack defrosts French supermarket freezers, spoiling food at 100s of stores
articles.summary: Hackers raised the temperature of refrigerators and freezers at hundreds of French supermarkets to as high as 50 C overnight, causing fires ‌and spoiling food.

image.caption: A woman walks past empty frozen-food refrigerators at an Intermarché supermarket in Névez, France, on Monday, following a cyberattack affecting the French supermarket chains. (Fred Tanneau/AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: World·New
Hackers raised the temperature of refrigerators and freezers at hundreds of French supermarkets to as high as 50 C overnight, causing fires ‌and spoiling food.
Freezer temperatures were remotely raised to as high as 50 C at stores across France
The Paris prosecutor's office said on Monday that a "large-scale" attack was "affecting connected refrigerators in several major food retailers across France," leading to food losses and fires.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has instructed France's National Cybersecurity Agency (ANSSI) to investigate, a person in his office said.

France was co-ordinating with European counterparts because other countries could also be affected, the person said, adding that authorities were assessing whether other French companies were at risk.
Félix Aimé, a senior ​cyber threat intelligence analyst at Sekoia Threat Detection and Research, said Spain, Portugal, Poland, Germany and Belgium ​had also been affected.
Carrefour said 80 of its supermarkets were hit, while Monoprix, which operates about 490 stores in France, said five per cent of its stores were affected.

A frozen food aisle at a supermarket near Nantes, closed after a cyberattack targeted refrigeration systems at French supermarket chains, causing food losses and fires at several stores. (Stephane Mahe/Reuters)
All affected food thrown out

Les Mousquetaires, owner of retailer Intermarché, said fridges at around 150 of its stores were heated up to 50 ​C for six hours overnight. A spokesperson said all affected food had been discarded to eliminate health risks.

Paris resident Geert de Clercq ⁠witnessed staff at an Intermarché in central Paris ⁠throwing cartfuls of defrosted frozen foods into a giant trash container, with molten ice ‌cream sloshing out of broken tubs on the street.
Coopérative U CEO Dominique Schelcher said his supermarket group had also been targeted.
"Targeting equipment essential to the preservation of fresh products and to the food supply of the French people is of extreme gravity and is unprecedented," he wrote on X.
Food retailers E.Leclerc and Auchan did not respond to requests for comment.

There was no immediate estimate of industry-wide losses, but Intermarché CEO Thierry Cotillard told BFM TV ⁠the "unprecedented" attack would represent losses amounting to "tens of millions of euros nationwide in a single day."
Christel Delberghe, director general at European retail association Eurocommerce, said, "This incident underlines the importance of resilience across the entire supply chain."
AI can make cyberattacks faster and smarter
Control panels accessible over internet

Supermarket cold aisles are typically run by control panels that manage an entire store's fridges and freezers and can be accessed over ‌the internet, which lets maintenance companies adjust them from anywhere.
The source close to Lecornu said ANSSI had identified a vulnerability in software supplied by Danish company Danfoss.
Danfoss said it was "aware of incidents in France affecting a limited number of refrigeration management systems."

The affected units "were running outdated firmware," Danfoss said, adding that it had "long advised customers to keep supported systems updated with the latest firmware and to migrate legacy systems to current-generation solutions."
Want to protect yourself from today’s cybersecurity and AI threats? Here are a few tips

On Aug. 9, cybersecurity firm ​Claroty's Team82 published research detailing vulnerabilities in the Danfoss AK-SM 800A controller. According to the report, software updates issued by Danfoss addressed issues that could have allowed attackers to bypass authentication controls and execute code on compromised devices.
The attacks resemble disruptions ⁠reported at about a dozen U.S. military commissaries in late August that led to food losses after fridges were affected.
Dutch security issue

Dutch ​retailer Ahold Delhaize, which operates the Netherlands's largest supermarket chain Albert Heijn and has major operations in the U.S., said it was dealing with a "security issue" on its network and ​had taken several systems offline as a precaution.
A message ⁠on the retailer's smartphone app said it was unable to deliver groceries because of a "cybersecurity incident."
Online orders account for about 10 per cent of Albert Heijn sales. Physical stores remained open, while Dutch news agency ANP reported that rival retailers had seen a surge in delivery orders.
Ahold Delhaize said there was no reason to see a link between the incidents in France and its supermarkets.
Ahold is the fourth-largest grocery retailer in the U.S. Websites for its Stop & Shop, Giant, Hannaford and Food Lion chains displayed notices saying "site temporarily down."
It was unclear whether other operations had been ⁠affected.

articles.title: Breaking Bad actor RJ Mitte dies aged 34
articles.summary: The actor, who played the defiant son of drug kingpin Walter White in the drama series, dies aged 34.

blocks.text: US actor RJ Mitte, best known for his role as the defiant son of drug kingpin Walter White in the drama series Breaking Bad, has died aged 34.
"It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of beloved actor, philanthropist, and passionate disability rights advocate RJ Mitte," his representative told the BBC.
He died in Brownsville, Texas. No immediate cause of death was provided.

Mitte, who lived with cerebral palsy, drew on his own experience for his role as Walter White Jr in the Emmy-winning drama series starring Bryan Cranston and Aaron Paul. He earned a Screen Actors Guild Award in 2014 for his work on the series.
"Mitte brought authenticity to the role and built a platform on disability awareness and inclusion," his representative Sean Reilly said in a statement to the BBC.
Mitte also served as an ambassador for United Cerebral Palsy and Shriners Children's.

He created The Mitte Foundation as well, to support philanthropic efforts and community initiatives, using his platform "to challenge stereotypes and promote greater representation for people with disabilities", Reilly said.
Breaking Bad aired on US cable broadcaster AMC for five seasons from 2008 to 2013.

The anti-hero drama created by Vince Gilligan earned a whopping 58 Primetime Emmy nominations and won 16, including two for Outstanding Drama Series in 2013 and 2014. It is widely credited as being one of the best US TV series of the 21st century.

Cranston plays a high school chemistry teacher in New Mexico who turns to a life of crime to support his family after a cancer diagnosis. As he descends deeper into the underbelly of the meth trade, he drifts further from his son, Walt Jr, who made his displeasure known with levity through much of the series.

articles.title: Bolivia investigates ex-president Evo Morales over alleged ties to 2009 killings
articles.summary:
Leftist former leader accused of involvement in shooting of three Europeans in Santa Cruz and torture of two others

Bolivia’s attorney general has announced an investigation into leftist…

blocks.text: Bolivia’s attorney general has announced an investigation into leftist former president Evo Morales, alleging his involvement in the murder and torture of European citizens in 2009.
Seventeen years ago, police raided a hotel in the city of Santa Cruz, shooting dead Eduardo Rózsa Flores, a Bolivian-Croatian, Michael Dwyer, an Irishman, and Árpád Magyarosi, a Hungarian-Romanian.
Bolivian-Croatian citizen Mario Tadic and Elöd Tóásó from Hungary survived and reported being tortured after their arrest.
The Morales administration in power at the time claimed that Rózsa Flores was leading efforts to promote a separatist movement, with funding from the rightwing economic elite of Santa Cruz.
Acting attorney general José Armando Urioste announced the preliminary investigation into Morales just one week into the job on Monday.

In a letter to the supreme court, Urioste said authorities were gathering evidence against Morales and his former vice-president Álvaro García Linera “for the alleged commission of the crimes of murder, abuse, torture and unlawful detention”.
The investigation comes after a complaint filed by rightwing lawmakers Tomasa Yarhui and Rodrigo Antonio.
When the raid occurred, Morales told the press during an official visit to Venezuela that he had ordered the detention of the foreigners, whom he called “mercenaries”.
Family members and victims brought the case before the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights, which concluded in 2021 that the government had violated human rights.
Neither of the accused has commented on the latest inquiry.

Morales, the first-ever Indigenous person to lead Bolivia, is currently in hiding from two active arrest warrants against him. One relates to his alleged role in massive protests that paralysed the country for 53 days earlier this year. The other accuses him of trafficking a minor with whom he is said to have had a daughter. Morales denies the allegations.

articles.title: RJ Mitte, actor best known for Breaking Bad role, dies aged 34
articles.summary:
Mitte, who played Walter White Jr on acclaimed show, had cerebral palsy and advocated for disability representation

The

blocks.text: The Breaking Bad actor RJ Mitte has died aged 34, his representatives confirmed on Monday.

“It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of beloved actor, philanthropist, and passionate disability rights advocate RJ Mitte,” Mitte’s representatives said in a statement provided to Variety and Deadline.
No cause of death was given.
Mitte, who played Walter White Jr on 56 episodes of the acclaimed AMC show, had cerebral palsy, a condition he shared with his Breaking Bad character.
In 2015, he spoke to the Guardian about being a disabled actor who plays disabled characters.
“You accept the risks and you accept these will be the parts you play. But it’s all about how you play those parts – you have to show the inner strength that people have.”

Mitte was an outspoken advocate for disability representation in entertainment, and served in various philanthropic roles, including as an ambassador for United Cerebral Palsy and as president of the Mitte Foundation.

articles.title: Analysis: Trump's global headaches worsen weeks before crucial elections
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump has had a whirlwind weekend, announcing a diesel deal with Russia and an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine. With the midterms coming up, it looks like Trump is…

blocks.text: With elections that will decide control of Congress just weeks away and American voters already casting ballots in some battlegrounds, President Donald Trump has turned his eyes overseas – and to Russia, in particular - for help tackling one of his most pressing problems.
World affairs seldom provide easy answers, however, and developments elsewhere have threatened to undermine his efforts to bring down fuel prices before they provide any political benefit.

A whirlwind weekend started on Friday afternoon, as Trump announced a new deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin that would provide the US with hundreds of millions of tons of Russian diesel fuel in the coming months.

High energy prices, particularly for midwestern agricultural states that rely on diesel to power farm machinery and carry their goods to market, have been a growing source of frustration for American voters.

Polls suggest they view the Iran War as the leading cause for their woes, and overall support for Trump, and approval of his handling of the war and the US economy in particular, has dropped precipitously.

Trump heralded his Russian deal in a Truth Social post as bringing "lower prices for Americans," while he ordered his Treasury Department to suspend US restrictions that prevented Russian diesel from being sold on global markets.
Two days later, Trump was back on his social media website, touting a new energy ceasefire agreement between Russia and Ukraine.
The truth, however, was more complicated.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he had no advanced notice of the agreement, although he said his nation would abide by it. Russia, for its part, was silent. And on Sunday night, it launched a new wave of attacks on Ukrainian power plants.
"It's clear that Putin does not read Truth Social," Zelensky noted wryly on Monday. He added: "This winter, if Russia does not agree to an energy ceasefire, we will respond."

It now appears Trump's celebration of the "energy truce" may have been a familiar move for this president, touting an agreement before it had been sealed and delivered. In the past, for instance, he has prematurely announced Middle East ceasefires and sweeping peace agreements.

Whether it is impatience on the president's part with the slow pace of diplomacy or a savvy negotiating tactic to push a deal across the finish line, the result has been to set off a scramble as the world decides what it means – and how to react.
Those reactions didn't take long to arrive.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who has become a vocal critic of the president's on the international stage, offered "strong support" for the energy ceasefire, but condemned the diesel deal as undermining peace and stability in Europe and helping Russia to finance its "illegal, unjustifiable war against Ukraine".

In the US, Trump's diesel announcement prompted similar concern, even among members of his own party. Four Republican senators joined with Democrats in a letter calling on the president to "immediately reverse course".

"Congress explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin's brutal war against Ukraine," the senators wrote in a statement released on Sunday. "President Trump's decision to allow Russian diesel imports to the US runs directly counter to that law."

What could be worse for the president than the criticisms is that the announced ceasefire has had little effect on the price of diesel, which continues to sit below its record highs but still well above $6 a gallon.
Meanwhile, as the latest twists in the Russia-Ukraine conflict unfolded, new violence in the Middle East threaten to further strain global energy markets, regardless of what happens with Russian oil.

A wave of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, including strikes on airports and energy infrastructure that killed at least 13 over the weekend, have threatened to escalate a decade-long conflict that had been simmering throughout the US-Iran war.

"This is the Houthis sending a message that it's not just military targets, it's not just energy infrastructure, they're going to strike at civilian airports that could kill a lot of people," Michael Ratney, former US ambassador to Saudi Arabia, told the BBC.

The US-Iran war was a conflict that none of the Arab nations in the region wanted, he said, and the latest Houthi offensive was a foreseeable result. With the US and Iran currently in an extended stand-off, any new hostilities could lead to more regional conflict and send oil prices soaring once more.
"I do think it gets uglier before it really deescalates," he said.

In recent weeks, Trump has pointed to Ukraine, not the Middle East, as the primary source of the world's energy woes. He cites increased oil tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, which had been effectively shut by Iran's military threat.
That may, however, be wishful thinking – an attempt to convince the American public to direct their energy-related anger toward a conflict that began under a different president's watch.
There is only one president at a time, however. And when American voters casts their ballots they tend to hold those who are currently in power responsible.
After a rough weekend that again proved there are no easy fixes to the global energy crisis, that may be the worst news of all for the US president.

articles.title: Qantas flight grounded after bedbug outbreak
articles.summary: The flight from Italy to Australia was cancelled after passengers on the plane's previous journey complained of bug bites.

blocks.text: A Qantas flight from Italy to Australia was cancelled on Saturday, after an outbreak of bedbugs on the plane.
During the previous flight on Friday - a nearly 17-hour journey from Perth to Rome - some passengers had complained that they were being bitten by bugs, according to the Sydney Morning Herald.
They were reportedly given antihistamines to help ease the itch of the bites, but supplies ran out.
The Boeing 787 Dreamliner had to be grounded for "a deep clean", a Qantas spokesperson told the BBC.

"We sincerely apologise to customers for the cancellation of Saturday's Rome to Perth service, which allowed our engineers and maintenance teams to carry out a deep clean of the aircraft after an issue was identified on a small number of economy seats," the spokesperson said.
All affected customers were provided with accommodation and were rebooked on alternative flights within 48 hours of their original departure, the carrier said.

Bedbugs are small, wingless parasites that can live on clothes, furniture and bedding. Their bites can be itchy but they do not usually cause more serious health problems, the NHS website says, external.

But they can be difficult and expensive to get rid of. Treatment includes washing all bedding, clothing, and household materials like curtains on a hot wash and tumble dry, or they can be put in plastic bags in a freezer for three or four days.
Bedbugs causing travel chaos is not unusual - less than two weeks ago, several Southeastern train services in England were cancelled after drivers discovered the creepy-crawlies in their cabs.
In 2017, British Airways apologised to a family travelling from Vancouver to London, after they were left covered in bug bites from an overnight flight.

And Turkish Airlines faced with a PR nightmare last year after the New York Times reported, external of several instances of bedbug infestations on its planes - and allegations at the time that the airline did nothing about it.

articles.title: Prominent U.S. archbishop compares planned livestream of firing squad execution to terrorist practices
articles.summary: Catholics serving in the U.S. army should not participate in the firing squad execution of Fort Hood ‌shooter Nidal Hasan that the Pentagon is planning to livestream in December, a prominent U.S.…

image.caption: U.S. Military Services Archbishop Timothy Broglio, seen here in 2025, has raised a series of objections to the unprecedented plan to ​broadcast the execution of a former U.S. army officer who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009. (Stephanie Scarbrough/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

Catholics serving in the U.S. army should not participate in the firing squad execution of Fort Hood ‌shooter Nidal Hasan that the Pentagon is planning to livestream in December, a prominent U.S. archbishop said on Monday.
Timothy Broglio urged Catholic members assigned to the firing squad to request religious exemption

In an unusually strongly worded statement, Archbishop Timothy Broglio, who oversees the spiritual care of Catholic members of the U.S. armed forces, raised a series of objections to the unprecedented plan to ​broadcast the execution of Hasan, who killed 13 people at Fort ​Hood, Texas, in a 2009 shooting spree.

Broglio said he presided at the funeral of one of Hasan's victims, and lamented the shooting. But the Ohio-born archbishop asked whether the U.S. ​wanted to "imitate the terrorists of this world and make a public spectacle of barbarically ⁠killing our adversaries."
"I oblige any Catholics ⁠assigned to the firing squad to request to be ‌excused from this action contrary to the teaching of the Church," Broglio said.
U.S. army regulations do allow for soldiers to request religious exemptions or accommodations, and the army has yet to say how it intends to select members of the firing squad.
The Pentagon says Nidal Hasan will be executed by firing squad in a livestreamed broadcast in December. (Bell County Sheriff's Office/Handout/Reuters)
Backlash from Republicans, international observers

U.S. War Secretary Pete ⁠Hegseth announced plans to livestream the shooting last week, triggering a backlash among Republicans in Congress, religious leaders and international observers. U.S. President Donald Trump approved Hasan's execution by firing squad but has said he is still deciding whether to allow the ‌livestreaming to proceed.

The event would be extraordinary, even for a country that has long employed capital punishment. A government execution has never been broadcast or livestreamed, according to death penalty experts, and the U.S. military has not executed anyone by firing squad since 1945. Hasan, now 56, requires a wheelchair, having been ​shot by police during his arrest.

items: Vance, Republican lawmakers and religious leaders oppose Pentagon plan to livestream an execution
The U.S. plans to livestream an execution. Here's how that compares to global practice

blocks.text: Hegseth said last week he wants U.S. soldiers to execute Hasan at the time, day of the week and ⁠location of Hasan's shooting spree. Hegseth has argued that making the event public will help serve as a deterrent.

Broglio ⁠questioned whether the effect of a livestreamed execution on young viewers had been considered. He said the U.S. military ⁠had ⁠a good reputation and asked if there ​was "really a value to throwing them in the same boat with terrorists by broadcasting the image of the execution of ​a man in a wheelchair to ⁠the whole world."

Broglio's statement was issued shortly after he met on Monday in Rome with Pope Leo, who has clashed with Trump and his Pentagon over issues including the Iran war. Leo on Saturday condemned the death penalty, without mentioning the Hasan case specifically.
U.S. Vice-President JD Vance, a convert to Catholicism, has said that if it does ultimately get livestreamed, he would ⁠not watch it.

articles.title: Windsor residents react to thank you banner from Detroit on Thanksgiving
articles.summary: A banner was flown above the Detroit River on Monday to thank Canadians during Thanksgiving. The initiative was organized by groups in Detroit, who wanted to commemorate the unique relationship…

blocks.text: Windsor

A banner was flown above the Detroit River on Monday to thank Canadians during Thanksgiving. The initiative was organized by groups in Detroit, who wanted to commemorate the unique relationship between Windsor and the American city.
The initiative was organized by groups from the U.S. side of the Detroit River
Here's why this Thanksgiving banner flew over the Detroit River
Windsor residents are reacting to a thank you banner that was flown over the Detroit River on Monday.
The nine-by-three-metre aerial banner, which reads "Detroit and Canada are bridged in friendship,” was organized by the Downtown Detroit Partnership (DDP) and Metro Detroit.
Eric Larson, CEO of the DDP, said the gesture is about reminding Windsorites of the importance of U.S.-Canada friendship at a time of cross-border friction.

"What better time than on Canada's Thanksgiving to recognize and really send an expression of gratitude," Larson said. "On the U.S. side, we find ourselves saying sorry a lot more than what used to be the custom."
Windsor residents are being impacted by tariffs on Canada's automotive sector, with Stellantis saying they contributed to recent layoffs.

items: Stellantis says tariffs, consumer demand driving weeks-long layoffs at Windsor plant

blocks.text: In July, tensions, tariffs and delays over the opening of the Gordie Howe International Bridge meant that only Canadian officials attended the official ribbon-cutting ceremony.
Larson said that Monday's banner event is a small gesture in recognizing Canada's importance.
"It's just the ability to recognize Canada's continued consistent leadership," he said.
Not crossing the border
The banner was flown along the Detroit River both morning and afternoon, and was visible to residents on both sides of the border.
Windsorites expressed gratitude at the gesture but acknowledged that they are unwilling to cross into the United States as trade tensions continue.

items: Windsor businesses looking for tariff help are still waiting

blocks.text: Windsor resident Jack Paterson said tensions with the Trump administration have meant that he has avoided crossing over into Detroit.
"The Americans are not our problem, it's the president and the Republican Party in power," Paterson said. " They stirred it up, divided everywhere and it's unsettling."
The banner was flown above the Detroit River for Canadian Thanksgiving. (Justin Escoto/CBC)
Despite the tensions, Paterson said he thinks that the banner reinforces the strength of Windsor and Detroit's unique relationship.
"I'm really moved by it just because we're not enemies of any kind with the American people," he said. "We enjoyed for years going over. We have relatives. It's all connected. We're all connected."
Local resident Priscilla Boismier came to the Detroit River to see the banner. (Justin Escoto/CBC)
Similarly, Priscilla Boismier said that while the aerial banner is a positive gesture, she is still hesitant to visit the American side of the river any time soon.
"It's a nice gesture considering what we're going through," Boismier said. "I don't have a passport. I don't intend to get a passport until Donald Trump is out of office."
For another local, Wayne Jahn, the banner is symbolic of Detroit's attachment to its neighbour.
"Michiganers love Canadians and vice versa," Jahn said. "We love them. But the situation dictates our reactions, and it's just too bad it's that way."
Once a regular visitor, Wayne Jahn says he hasn't crossed into the U.S. for two years. (Justin Escoto/CBC)
For Eric Larson, the banner is just a small way in which residents on both sides of the border can be reminded of their interconnectivity.
"We hope and expect this to be a moment in time and we can, you know, return to what has been a very successful, both economically and socially, relationship," he said.
"It's about how North America operates as one ecosystem."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Oliver Thompson is a writer, producer and musician. Originally from the UK, where he worked for the BBC, Oliver moved to Canada in 2018.
With files from Justin Escoto

articles.title: Archbishop of US military condemns Pentagon plans to livestream execution
articles.summary:
Timothy Broglio says Catholics on army firing squad should ask to be excused since it clashes with church teachings

The archbishop who oversees the spiritual care of

blocks.text: The archbishop who oversees the spiritual care of Catholics serving in the US military condemned the Pentagon’s proposed plans to livestream the firing squad execution of Nidal Hasan later this year.

Archbishop Timothy Broglio also stipulated in a Monday statement that any Catholic soldier assigned to the US army firing squad should ask to be excused from that duty, which he described as contrary to the teachings of the church. He joins other Catholic leaders in speaking out against the death penalty and the live stream plans.
Hasan, an army psychiatrist convicted of killing 13 people in 2009 at Fort Hood in Texas, is scheduled to be executed by firing squad on 3 December.
Pete Hegseth, the US defense secretary, announced last week that Hasan’s execution would be public, and the Pentagon later confirmed it would be livestreamed.
Broglio recalled that he presided over the funeral of Michael Grant Cahill, the only civilian killed in that attack.
The crime committed by Hasan “was heinous, but does exposing the public to his execution serve any purpose?” Broglio asked.

“The US military generally enjoys a good reputation in the world,” Broglio added. “Is there really a value to throwing them in the same boat with terrorists by broadcasting the image of the execution of a man in a wheelchair to the whole world?”

blocks.text: Live streamed firing squad execution ‘absolutely disgusting’, says Watt

Labor cabinet minister, Murray Watt says a planned live streamed execution in the US would be extremely distressing for the public, but won’t commit to legislative change to prevent Australians being able to watch it.
The eSafety commissioner, Julie Inman-Grant has said she does not have powers to “proactively prevent” the stream on 3 December.
Watt tells ABC News Breakfast the government is trying to take “as much action as we can” to deal with rapidly evolving technology.

double quotation markI just find the idea of a public streaming of a firing squad execution absolutely disgusting. When I first heard that was being proposed, I couldn’t believe that it was real. I think all Australians would agree that this is a very distressing thing to have publicised … We’ve seen now that the eSafety Commissioner has said they don’t have those powers. I wouldn’t want to commit to any legislative change at this point in time, but what I do think it shows is this rapidly evolving situation that we’ve got with technology, which is why our government is trying to take as much action as we can, as quickly as we can.”

blocks.caption: Ben Doherty

blocks.text: Ben Doherty
Greens say big tech has been ‘laughing all the way to the bank’ and ‘we need proper regulations’

Sarah Hanson-Young is leading the Greens’ negotiations with the government over legislation designed to hold tech companies responsible for preventing harm to Australians, in particular children. The legislation is expected to be tabled in parliament this week.

Hanson-Young, the Greens’ manager of business in the Senate, said the party would wait to see the details of the legislation before deciding whether to support it. But the senator said the Greens supported the imperative, telling the ABC’s 7:30 program that big tech companies had been “running amok for far too long and we want laws that will actually hold them to account”.
Hanson-Young added:

double quotation markPutting in place a duty of care on these big tech platforms is something that’s well and truly overdue. And these big tech companies, social media platforms have been getting away with profiting off content that has been harmful, of technologies that have been designed to be deliberately addictive, even though they know the harm that that can do. And they’ve just been laughing all the way to the bank. We need proper regulations on these tech companies.

Australia sending tanks, weapons, infantry and ammunition to Ukraine has put Greens politicians at odds.

Charities and not-for-profit organisations will receive a $630m funding boost from the federal government after the Fair Work Commission awarded pay rises for health, disability and community services workers.
